ADAPT: On the International Day of Persons with Disabilities, we’re proud to highlight the [Straz Strong Foundation](https://www.strazstrongfoundation.com/), created by Humboldt Broncos crash survivor Ryan Straschnitzki. Straz Strong helps people adapt by supporting access to adaptive sports, technologies, and opportunities that promote independence and inclusion. Their work showcases the strength of communities that come together to break barriers and champion resilience across Canada.
ADOPT: Canada has a program called Adopt-A-Highway, where volunteers and organizations can 'adopt' a section of highway to help keep it clean and litter-free. The Adopt-A-Highway program, which originated in the United States and was later adopted in Canada, encourages civic engagement and community involvement in maintaining the cleanliness of roadways. In Canada, volunteers commit to cleaning up litter along a designated stretch of highway several times a year, helping to beautify the landscape and protect the environment. So, the next time you're driving along a Canadian highway, take a moment to appreciate the efforts of those who have 'adopted' a stretch of road and made a positive difference in their communities.
AGAIN: "On the Road Again" was a beloved Canadian television show that aired from 1987 to 2007 on CBC! Hosted by the iconic Wayne Rostad, the show traveled across Canada, showcasing the unique stories and traditions of everyday Canadians in towns big and small. Each episode celebrated the diverse cultures, landscapes, and people that make Canada so special.
ALARM: Robert Foulis is known as the inventor of the world's first steam-operated fog alarm, which was installed on Partridge Island in the Bay of Fundy in 1859, just off the coast of Saint John, New Brunswick. While Foulis never patented or even profited from his life-saving innovation, his steam foghorn invention assisted fogbound mariners for over a century.
ALERT: Alert, in the Qikiqtaaluk Region of Nunavut, Canada, is the northernmost continuously inhabited place in the world, on Ellesmere Island (Queen Elizabeth Islands) just 817 kilometres from the North Pole. Alert was named after HMS Alert, a British ship that wintered in the area from 1875-76.
ALGAE: Algae thrive in Canada’s waters, from the Atlantic coast to the Great Lakes and all the way to the Pacific. Green Cladophora in the Great Lakes supports fish and helps monitor water quality, while coastal seaweeds like rockweed shelter marine life along British Columbia’s shores. These simple organisms are unsung heroes, keeping Canada’s freshwater and marine ecosystems healthy.
ALIEN: In 1967, a proposal was made to build the world's first UFO Landing Pad as a landmark for the town of St. Paul, Alberta. The Government of Canada responded to this proposition and, during the grand opening on June 3 1967, St. Paul was declared the Centennial Capital of Canada. Aliens have yet to land in St. Paul, but in 1998 the town hosted a UFO conference for believers and the merely curious.
ALLOY: An alloy is a mixture of two or more metals, or a metal and another element, designed to enhance strength, durability, or other properties. In Canada, alloys are essential in industries from aerospace and automotive manufacturing to construction and energy. Alloys of copper, nickel, and steel are also used in everyday items like Canadian coins, highlighting how these metal blends are both practical and integral to Canadian life.
AMBER: Canada is home to rare and fascinating amber deposits, including finds at Cedar Lake in Manitoba, where ancient tree resin has been preserved for millions of years. Amber has also been discovered in other parts of the country, offering a glimpse into prehistoric forests and the insects and plant life they once contained. These golden fossils provide a natural time capsule of Canada’s distant past.
ANGEL: Abigail Becker (1830–1905), known as the Angel of Long Point, was a Canadian woman credited with saving the lives of numerous sailors caught in storms along the shores of Long Point, located on Lake Erie in Ontario. When the storms had passed, she would wade in the water as far as she could to rescue trapped seamen from their doomed ships.
ANIME: Did you know that [Anime North](https://www.animenorth.com/) is Canada's largest fan-run anime convention? Founded in 1997 by Toronto anime enthusiast Donald Simmons, it began as a one-day event with around 600 attendees. Today, it attracts tens of thousands of fans annually to celebrate anime, manga, music, games, and Japanese culture. This year's convention takes place from May 23-25, 2025, at the Toronto Congress Centre.
APRON: Wok with Yan was a Chinese cuisine cooking show starring Stephen Yan that was first produced in Vancouver, British Columbia in the late 1970s. It ran until 1995 with over 500 episodes, and each show featured Yan wearing of an apron with a different pun on the word "wok." The humorous aprons complemented his humour that consisted of spontaneous one-liners and playing with the food & cookware. "Wokkey Night in Canada" is our absolute favourite apron!
ARROW: Canada's response to the threat of Soviet nuclear bombers was the Avro Arrow. A marvel of engineering, it was a twin-engine, all-weather supersonic interceptor. Only five Avro Arrow planes were ever built, yet this innovative jet fighter put Canada on top of the aviation world in the 1950s.
ASPEN: Aspen are a deciduous, hardwood tree of the genus Populus, belonging to the willow family. Trembling aspen and largetooth aspen are native to Canada; the former, found from the treeline to northern Mexico, is the most widely distributed tree in North America. Trembling aspen grows on most soils, doing best on well-drained, moist, sandy or gravelly loams. As a fast-growing pioneer tree species, it is ideal for quickly restoring a wide range of forest functions after disturbances.
ATLAS: The Armstrong Whitworth Atlas was a British single-engine two-seat biplane. It served as an army co-operation aircraft for the Royal Canadian Air Force in the 1920s and 1930s. April 1, 2024 marked 100 years of service for the Royal Canadian Air Force as a distinct military element. The [RCAF Centennial](https://rcaf2024arc.ca/) is an opportunity to showcase Air Force personnel and their accomplishments, demonstrate air and space power, enhance the reputation of the RCAF, and proudly honour its distinguished history and heritage.
ATTIC: Attic Records was a Canadian independent record label, founded in 1974 by Alexander Mair and Tom Williams. The label was known for developing Canadian talent, including Anvil, Lee Aaron, Maestro Fresh Wes, The Nylons, Teenage Head, and Triumph. The company was also active in distributing international acts not affiliated with a major label, most successfully with Jennifer Warnes, "Weird Al" Yankovic, Katrina and the Waves, and Creed.
AUGER: Ice fishing is a popular winter pastime in Canada that is enjoyed on many Canadian lakes! Small holes are drilled through the frozen lake surfaces using ice augers, allowing for the fun activity of fishing during the winter months! Billed as the "Ice Fishing Capital of Canada," more people fish on Lake Simcoe, Ontario in winter than all other seasons combined.
AWARD: The 2023 Juno Awards took place in Edmonton, Alberta last night! The annual awards ceremony celebrates outstanding achievements in Canadian music. The Juno Awards began in 1964 as the RPM Gold Leaf Awards, and in 1971 they were renamed the Juno Awards after the Roman goddess and in tribute to Pierre Juneau, the first chairperson of the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC) who was responsible for introducing the Canadian content quota to Canadian radio that year.
AXIOM: An axiom is a basic rule accepted as true without needing proof, and it’s where all logical thinking begins. World Logic Day on January 14 celebrates these foundational ideas, the same way games like Canuckle and Canoku start with simple rules that guide every word guess and emoji placement. From letters to patterns, great puzzles are built one solid axiom at a time.
BACON: Canadian bacon comes from the loin of the pig instead of the side or belly.
BALSA: Balsa wood is lightweight yet incredibly strong, making it a go-to material for Canadian crafters and hobbyists! Native to South America, balsa is used in model airplanes, ping pong paddles, and even surfboards. Many Canadian builders appreciate its ease of use and buoyancy, making it perfect for crafting floatable objects. So next time you spot a model plane or a small raft in Canada, there's a good chance balsa wood is behind the design!
BANDS: Today is [National Indigenous Veterans Day](https://www.veterans.gc.ca/en/remembrance/people-and-stories/indigenous-veterans), a time to honour the First Nations, Inuit, and Métis peoples who have served in uniform. Thousands of Indigenous veterans from communities and bands across Canada volunteered in both World Wars, Korea, and beyond – often travelling far from home to defend a country that did not yet grant them full rights. Their courage, resilience, and leadership are now formally recognized and remembered each November 8, as Canadians pay tribute to the vital role Indigenous veterans have played in our shared history.
BANKS: Today is National Food Bank Day! Held on the first Friday in September, National Food Bank Day encourages you to commit to contributing to the cause that believes no one should go to bed hungry. Founded in 1989, [Food Banks Canada](https://foodbankscanada.ca/) is a national organization working to reduce food insecurity countrywide. Food Banks Canada's mission is to provide national leadership to relieve hunger today and prevent hunger tomorrow.
BARON: Anyone outside of Western Canada might not know or understand the cult following behind the unassuming [Burger Baron](https://burgerbaronedmonton.com/) restaurant. The popular fast-food chain, with its distinctive sign, popular mushroom burger and 25 locations around Alberta, has been a part of the Prairie dining scene since the 1950s. Founded in 1957 in either Calgary or Lethbridge, Alberta (the location and ownership of the first site is disputed), Burger Baron was one of the first drive-in restaurant chains in Western Canada. Many of the owners are Lebanese Canadians, connected to Rudy Kemaldean of Edmonton. Among other things, Burger Baron is famous for being endorsed by former Edmonton Oilers hockey coach Glen Sather and other former members of the Edmonton Oilers.
BATON: Canada has a strong tradition of excellence in relay races, with its teams achieving notable success on the world stage. The Canadian men's 4x100m relay team famously won gold at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics, a triumph that echoed the country's prowess in track and field. More recently, the men's 4x100m team clinched silver at the 2020 Tokyo Olympics, further solidifying Canada's status as a powerhouse in relay events. These achievements highlight the strength and teamwork that define [Canadian athletics](https://olympic.ca/sports/athletics/).
BEACH: Canada is home to the two longest freshwater beaches in the world: Wasaga Beach (14 km) on the Georgian Bay in Ontario and Sauble Beach (11 km) on the Bruce Peninsula, along the eastern shore of Lake Huron.
BEADS: Beading has a very long artistic and cultural history among the Indigenous people in Canada. At least 8,000 years before Europeans came to Canada, First Nations people were using beads in elaborate designs and for trade. Today, you can find beautiful First Nations beadwork at powwows, First Nations arts stores and museums across Canada. June 21st is National Indigenous Peoples Day. Take the opportunity to learn more about the cultural and linguistic diversity as well as the contributions of First Nations, Inuit and Métis Peoples.
BEECH: The [American Beech tree](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/beech) is a common sight in the forests of eastern Canada and in Ontario and Quebec. Known for its smooth, grey bark and vibrant fall colours, this tree can live for more than 300 years! Beech trees play an important role in Canadian ecosystems, providing food for wildlife such as squirrels, birds, and even black bears, who enjoy feasting on its nuts. Whether you're hiking through a forest or simply admiring their beauty, beech trees are a quiet giant in Canada's natural landscape!
BEETS: Sugar beets have played a key role in Canada's sugar production for over a century! While most of Canada's sugar comes from imported cane, sugar beets are grown domestically - mainly in Alberta. In the town of Taber, home to Canada's last remaining sugar beet processing plant, 200 local farm families supply the refinery with approximately 840,000 tonnes of sugar beets each year. This yields 125,000 tonnes of sugar, making up 8–10% of Canada's total sugar consumption! From root to sweet treat, these beets keep Canada's sugar industry thriving!
BELLS: It's time to ring in the New Year! Churches, cathedrals and towers across Canada will be ringing the bells tonight at midnight to signal the start of 2023. There are 11 carillons in Canada, ranging from the historic Hamilton cathedral to the more modern Exhibition Place carillon in Toronto. The Peace Tower Carillon on Parliament Hill in Ottawa is the most frequently played and the best known carillon. It has 53 bells, and was inaugurated on July 1, 1927 to mark the 60th anniversary of Confederation. The Cathedral of the Transfiguration in Markham, Ontario contains one of the world’s largest sets of bells. They were cast in bronze and weigh in at a whopping 32,000 pounds (over 14,500kg)!
BELTS: Wampum are tubular purple and white beads made from shells. Wampum are used primarily by Indigenous peoples of the Eastern Woodlands for ornamental, ceremonial, diplomatic and commercial purposes. Belts made of wampum were used to mark agreements between peoples. Wampum belts and other wampum bead artifacts continue to hold significance for Indigenous peoples and any treaties or agreements they might represent.
BERET: The beret is a form of headdress with a long history of use in the Canadian Army. Different colours of berets symbolize membership of a particular type of armed force or unit. Distinctive blue berets are worn by [United Nations peacekeepers](https://peacekeeping.un.org/en). One of the first big peacekeeping missions was established in 1956 by the United Nations and Canada played a leading role in this idea. Canada has taken part in dozens of multinational peace support efforts over the years and continues to support various peacekeeping missions today.
BEZEL: A bezel is a frame that holds a gem, watch face, or even a coin – adding both protection and style. In Canada, bezels are a popular way to turn meaningful items into wearable keepsakes, from Indigenous-made jewelry to custom-crafted pendants. The Royal Canadian Mint even offers sterling silver bezel kits, allowing collectors to transform special coins into necklaces, brooches, or keychains, letting Canadian craftsmanship shine one coin at a time. Canada was the first country in the world to introduce coloured coin technology back in 2004, starting with the iconic poppy quarter. From glow-in-the-dark dinosaurs to shimmering maple leaves, Canadian coins are known for pushing boundaries – and bezels help keep that beauty on full display.
BICEP: Canadian arm wrestling legend Devon Larratt is known around the world for his powerful biceps and unmatched technique! Born in Victoria, British Columbia, Larratt served in the Canadian Armed Forces before becoming a dominant force in professional arm wrestling. With multiple world titles and viral matchups under his belt, he's helped put Canada on the map in this intense sport of strength and strategy.
BINGO: The game of Bingo has been a beloved pastime in Canada for decades! In fact, the first official Canadian Bingo hall opened in the 1940s in British Columbia, and the game quickly became a popular way to raise money for charities, schools, and local communities. Whether played at a community centre or as a family game night favourite, Bingo remains a fun way to bring Canadians together! From coast to coast, Canadians have enjoyed shouting "Bingo!" as a way to win big and support their communities at the same time.
BIRCH: The white birch is the most widely distributed of native birch trees, and grows in every region of Canada. The bark has long been used for making canoes and ornaments.
BIRDS: Point Pelee National Park is Canada's smallest National Park by size, but it comes to life in a big way every May for the annual [Festival of Birds](https://www.festivalofbirds.ca/). In spring, birds return from their winter migration to nest and breed, pass through before heading further north, or are permanent year-round residents of this southernmost point of mainland Canada. Over 370 species of birds can be found at Point Pelee National Park. This event is one of the biggest and best attended bird festivals in the country. Celebrate spring migration at the 2024 Festival of Birds from May 1 to May 20.
BISON: Bison are North America's largest land animal, with bulls weighing up to 2000 lbs and cows up to 1000 lbs.
BLAND: Despite the name, Blanding’s turtles aren’t bland at all! This bright-eyed freshwater species, found in southern Ontario, Quebec, and parts of the Maritimes, has a striking yellow throat and domed shell. Sadly, these turtles are endangered, and conservation efforts across Canada are helping protect their wetlands and nesting sites so they can continue to thrive.
BLAST: Every day, the Royal Artillery fires the noon gun at the [Halifax Citadel National Historic Site](https://parks.canada.ca/lhn-nhs/ns/halifax) in Halifax, Nova Scotia. The 19th-century British fort fires one of the oldest continuous noon guns in the world. The cannon’s blast has been part of Halifax’s daily rituals since 1857. The present noon gun is a reproduction 12 pounder, smooth-bore muzzle loading gun used during the reign of King George III (1760-1820).
BLAZE: In Canada's vast wilderness, a blaze isn't just a fiery flash - it's also a mark on a tree used to guide hikers along a trail! Trail blazes, often painted or carved, help outdoor adventurers find their way through forests, mountains, and national parks across the country. The tradition of blazing trails goes back centuries, including by Indigenous Peoples who navigated the land with deep knowledge and skill.
BLESS: Canada is home to a unique maritime tradition known as the 'Blessing of the Fleet'! Each year in Digby, Nova Scotia, locals gather to participate in this special ceremony, which dates back over a century. The blessing of the scallop and deep sea fishing fleet is a time-honored tradition where fishermen and their vessels are blessed by clergy for a safe and bountiful fishing season. This event not only celebrates the rich maritime heritage of Nova Scotia but also serves as a symbol of community unity and support for those who make their living from the sea. It is a cherished tradition that brings together residents and visitors alike to offer prayers and well-wishes for the fishermen and their families.
BLING: Hotline Bling by Canadian artist Drake became one of the defining hits of 2015, reaching No. 2 on the Billboard Hot 100 and dominating charts around the world. Known for its minimalist production and instantly recognizable music video, the track spent weeks in the top tier of the charts and earned multiple Grammy wins, further cementing Drake’s global influence as a Canadian music powerhouse.
BLITZ: Today is the [110th CFL Grey Cup](https://www.greycupfestival.ca/)! When you hear the term blitz you probably think of football, but The Canadian Wildlife Federation and the Nature Conservancy of Canada use [Bioblitzes](https://cwf-fcf.org/en/explore/bioblitz/) to help determine the health of an ecosystem. A Bioblitz is a participatory search for species within a limited area and a limited timeframe that takes a "snapshot" of as many living things as possible. Biodiversity - literally the variety of life - is an indicator that an area is ecologically stable and healthy. Through use of the [iNaturalist Canada app](https://inaturalist.ca/), the species records are compiled into a single data set to help researchers, scientists and policy-makers to help them make informed decisions about wildlife management.
BLOOD: This week is National Blood Donor Week and today is World Blood Donor Day! One in two people in Canada are eligible to donate blood, but only one in 81 actually do. [Canadian Blood Services](https://www.blood.ca/) is responsible for the safety of the national blood supply system (along with [Héma-Québec](https://www.hema-quebec.qc.ca/) in Québec) and Canada has one of the safest blood systems in the world! If you'd like to be a blood donor, visit [blood.ca](https://www.blood.ca/) or [hema-quebec.qc.ca](https://www.hema-quebec.qc.ca/) to join Canada’s Lifeline and book an appointment today. #ItsInYouToGive
BLOOM: Today marks the start of the [Canadian Tulip Festival](https://tulipfestival.ca/) in Ottawa, with over 100 tulip varieties and more than one million blooms over 14,000 m². The Festival preserves the memorable role of the Canadian troops in the liberation of the Netherlands and Europe, as well as commemorates the birth of Dutch Princess Margriet in Ottawa during World War II - the only royal personage ever born in Canada. Each year, the Netherlands continue to give 20,000 bulbs to Canada as a gesture of gratitude. In 2001, the tulip became Ottawa’s official flower.
BLUES: The [Maple Blues Awards](https://www.mapleblues.ca/) is Canada’s national blues awards program. Its goal is to promote blues music across Canada and to recognize outstanding achievement in the field. The Maple Blues Awards have been presented by the Toronto Blues Society since their inception in 1997.
BOILS: Lobster boils are a beloved culinary tradition on Canada's East Coast! Lobster boils are a festive occasion where friends and family gather to enjoy fresh lobster, along with an array of other seafood and seasonal delights. Typically, lobsters are cooked in large pots of boiling water seasoned with spices, herbs, and sometimes beer, infusing them with irresistible flavor. As the lobsters cook to perfection, the aroma fills the air, creating an atmosphere of anticipation and excitement. Once ready, the succulent lobster meat is served alongside melted butter, corn on the cob, potatoes, and other accompaniments, creating a feast fit for any maritime celebration.
BOOKS: Happy National Read a Book Day! Reading is one of the most popular pastimes in Canada, with over 80% of adults admitting to reading for pleasure. There are so many incredible books written by famous Canadian authors, and today is a great day to pick up your favourite Canadian book! Check out [CBC Books](https://www.cbc.ca/books) to learn more about books in Canada!
BORER: In Canada, the emerald ash borer and bronze birch borer are two well-known tree borers found in our forests. The emerald ash borer is an invasive species that affects ash trees, while the bronze birch borer is native to North America and targets birch trees. Both insects live beneath the bark, where they tunnel through wood and disrupt the flow of water and nutrients, making them important considerations in Canadian forest health and tree management.
BORES: Canada is home to some of the world’s most dramatic tidal bores, including roaring waves that surge up rivers in the Bay of Fundy. These phenomena occur when the incoming tide pushes against a river’s current, creating a wall of water that can travel for kilometres. Adventurous kayakers and rafters can ride these powerful bores, experiencing firsthand one of the most spectacular natural events in Canada.
BRAND: Canada is home to many iconic brands and locally owned companies that reflect the country’s creativity, innovation, and regional pride. From everyday essentials to globally recognized names like Tim Hortons, Lululemon, Canada Goose, Aritzia, and Roots, Canadian brands span food, fashion, retail, and outdoor gear. Together, they are a strong part of the national identity, showcasing homegrown quality and entrepreneurial spirit and connecting communities in every part of the country.
BRAVE: On November 11th, we remember and honour all the individuals who have and continue to serve in Canada's military services. Attending Remembrance Day ceremonies on November 11th is a well known way to honour the brave men and women who served Canada in times of war, military conflict and peace. For more than 100 years, millions of Canadians have proudly served our country in uniform. On this Remembrance Day, we honour those brave soldiers who fought for our country and made the ultimate sacrifice. Lest we forget.
BRAVO: In the Canadian military, "Bravo" is more than just an exclamation of praise; it's the code word for the letter "B" in the NATO phonetic alphabet, which ensures clear communication across the Canadian Armed Forces and beyond. The phonetic alphabet - from "Alpha" to "Zulu" - is used worldwide, helping Canadian military personnel coordinate and reduce misunderstandings during missions. Bravo is also commonly used to name companies within various units like the Bravo Company, 1st Battalion, The Royal Canadian Regiment (1 RCR) Battle Group. Additionally, the term Bravo Zulu (BZ) is also a naval signal meaning "well done", and is commonly used across all branches to commend service members for a job well executed.
BRINE: Brine isn’t just salty water – it’s the starting point for one of Canada’s biggest salt success stories. At its Goderich operation on Lake Huron, [Sifto Canada](https://siftocanada.com/) operates the world’s largest rock salt mine, producing millions of tonnes of bulk salt each year. A separate nearby facility pumps up underground brine, then evaporates and refines it into around 95,000 tonnes high-purity, food-grade salt each year. From seasoning kitchens to preserving food across the country, Canadian brine plays a quietly essential role at the table.
BROOK: Canada is home to countless brooks that meander through lush forests and rugged landscapes. These babbling waterways provide essential habitats for fish like brook trout, a prized catch for anglers in Canadian waters. Whether you're hiking in Algonquin Park or fishing in Newfoundland's rivers, encountering a brook is a tranquil reminder of Canada's pristine natural beauty. So, next time you wander through Canada's wilderness, listen closely - the whispers of a brook might just lead you to an unforgettable adventure!
BRUSH: Today is [Curling Day in Canada](https://www.curlingdayincanada.ca/)! On this day celebrating all things curling, we celebrate one of the sport's most essential tools: the brush! In curling, the brush (or broom) is used to sweep the ice in the path of a moving stone. Sweeping warms the ice and helps control the stone’s speed and direction - making it a critical part of the game. Canadians can cheer on teams at the [Scotties Tournament of Hearts](https://www.curling.ca/2025scotties/) in Thunder Bay, or try their hand at sweeping on the ice themselves!
BUDDY: On the east coast predominantly (but also heard nationwide), buddy is a way to talk about a person in Canada without using a name. When you call someone "bud" or "buddy" in Canada, that person could literally be your best friend or a total stranger. It is a friendly colloquialism used as a term of endearment or camaraderie. Peace By Chocolate even has a special edition [Hey Buddy chocolate bar](https://peacebychocolate.ca/products/92g-hey-buddy-canada-bar)!
BUTTE: Situated in the Big Muddy Badlands in Saskatchewan, Castle Butte is a grand, reddish free-standing structure with a circumference of 0.5 km and an elevation of 60 metres. A relic from the Ice Age, it is a striking formation that served as a landmark for Indigenous people, the North West Mounted Police (NWMP) and early prairie settlers. Other notable Canadian buttes include Pilot Butte (Saskatchewan), Lone Butte (British Columbia), Nebogwawin Butte (Manitoba), Nahanni Butte (Northwest Territories), and Mud Buttes (Alberta). It goes without saying that these buttes are some of our country's finest assets! Read more about [Canada's Nicest Buttes](https://www.familyfuncanada.com/canadas-nicest-buttes/).
BYLAW: From coast to coast, Canada is home to some wonderfully strange and amusing bylaws that reflect the quirks and character of its communities. In Dawson City, Yukon, it's illegal to disturb a moose, including honking at one! In Calgary, Alberta, you're not allowed to put your feet on benches, planters, or sculptures in public spaces. And In Souris, Prince Edward Island, you can't build a snowman taller than 30 inches on a corner lot – safety first, even for frosty friends! These odd rules show how unique (and Canadian!) our local bylaws can be.
CABIN: Cabin is another name for a cottage, and Canada has no shortage of weekend getaway spots!
CACHE: Geocaching is the real-world treasure hunt where participants use GPS satellites and coordinates to hide and retrieve containers or caches hidden in outdoor locations. There are millions of caches all around Canada! In Ontario, deep in the Haliburton Highlands in the Municipality of Highlands East and at the South Gate of Algonquin Park a string of seven hamlets make up the [Geocaching Capital of Canada](https://www.geocachingcapitalofcanada.com/): Irondale, Gooderham, Tory Hill, Wilberforce, Harcourt, Highland Grove and Cardiff. Get out there and explore!
CADET: In the Canadian Armed Forces, the appointment of officer cadet is held by beginning officers, as well as students attending the Royal Military College of Canada in Kingston, Ontario and the Collège militaire royal de Saint-Jean in Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu, Québec. Officer cadets and naval cadets complete the Regular Officer Training Plan to become commissioned officers in the Canadian Armed Forces.
CAKES: Edmonton's most iconic cakes aren't sweet - they're crispy, savoury, and packed with green onions! [Green onion cakes](https://www.greenonioncakeman.com/) became a local favourite after Siu To introduced them at his Edmonton restaurant in 1978. Originally from Northern China, To brought this delicious pan-fried treat to the city, where it quickly took off. Today, green onion cakes are a beloved Edmonton specialty, served at restaurants, festivals, and even hockey games!
CAMPS: Over 5.7 million Canadian adults camp each year and the camping industry contributes a total of $4.7 billion annually to Canada's economy.
CANADA: The name Canada comes from the St. Lawrence Iroquoian word kanata, meaning "village" or "settlement." When French explorer Jacques Cartier heard the word in 1535, he used it to refer to the land, and over time, it became the name of the entire country! On July 1, 1867, Canada officially became a nation, uniting its first provinces in Confederation. As we celebrate Canada Day, let's reflect on the rich history, diverse cultures, and incredible landscapes that make Canada so special!
CANES: While candy canes bring sweetness and festive charm to the holiday season, Canada is also home to a revolutionary cane designed for accessibility. At just 14 years old, Canadian student Riya Karumanchi invented the SmartCane, an innovative device to aid visually impaired individuals. Her design incorporates advanced features like ultrasonic sensors, GPS integration, and haptic feedback to detect obstacles and enhance navigation. Her invention has since received widespread recognition, securing funding from major tech companies like Microsoft and Google, and establishing Riya as a young leader in accessibility innovation. Much like the joy candy canes bring, the SmartCane embodies Canadian ingenuity, spreading hope and empowerment globally.
CANOE: In Canada, the canoe has long been associated with the fur trade and the romantic figure of the voyageur.
CANOLA: Developed in Canada in the 1970s, canola is a heart-healthy oilseed crop prized around the world. From cooking oil to margarine, Canadian farmers produce millions of tonnes each year, making it one of the country’s top agricultural exports. Canola is a portmanteau of CANada and OLA (meaning low acid oil).
CANUCK: The word Canuck is a proud and playful nickname for Canadians! While its origins are debated, it has been used since at least the 19th century to describe people from Canada. From Johnny Canuck, a folk hero who stood up to tyranny, to the Vancouver Canucks hockey team, the word has become a symbol of Canadian identity. It even inspired the name of our game - Canuckle - a fun and truly Canadian word game!
CAPER: The "Canadian Caper" was the joint covert rescue by the Canadian government and the CIA of six American diplomats who had evaded capture during the seizure of the United States embassy in Tehran, Iran, on November 4, 1979. An article written about these events was published in Wired in 2007. The article was used loosely as the basis of the 2012 film Argo.
CAPES: Canada is home to some stunning coastal landscapes adorned with picturesque capes! Along its vast coastline, Canada boasts numerous capes that offer breathtaking views of the surrounding seas and landscapes. One iconic example is Cape Breton Island's Cabot Trail in Nova Scotia, where rugged cliffs meet the Atlantic Ocean, creating a dramatic and awe-inspiring vista. Cape Scott Provincial Park on Vancouver Island is renowned for its remote wilderness and rugged coastline, while Cape Columbia located on Ellesmere Island in the Qikiqtaaluk Region of Nunavut is the northernmost point of land of Canada and offers incredible views of the Canadian Arctic. Cape Spear in Newfoundland and Labrador holds the distinction of being the easternmost point in North America. Canada's capes provide endless opportunities for adventure and discovery!
CARAT: Happy Mother's Day from Canuckle! Canadian mines produced 18.6 million carats of rough diamonds valued at $2.25 billion in 2019, making Canada the world's third largest producer of rough diamonds by value.
CARDS: [Kelvington, Saskatchewan](https://www.townofkelvington.com/) is known as "Canada's Hockey Factory"! A giant hockey cards monument was built to celebrate Kelvington's famous hockey players, including Lloyd Gronsdahl, Barry Melrose, Joe Kocur, Wendel Clark, Kerry Clark, and Kory Kocur.
CAROL: For the past several weeks, the most popular songs around have been Christmas carols. Many of our favourites have European roots, but one that is still sung can claim to be the first Canadian Christmas carol. The "Huron Carol" (or "Twas in the Moon of Wintertime") was written by Jean de Brébeuf, a Jesuit missionary at Sainte-Marie among the Hurons in Canada. Brebeuf's hymn, written in both Huron and French, is now over 380 years old. The song remains a common Christmas hymn in Canadian churches, and it has become a cherished part of Canadian Christmas.
CARTS: Carts were essential for travel and trade in early Canada, and the [Red River Cart](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/red-river-cart) is one of the most famous. Developed by the Métis during the settlement of the Prairies in the mid- to late-1800s, these two-wheeled wooden carts could carry up to 450 kg of goods across long distances, pulled by oxen or horses. The cart takes its name from the Red River, along which the Red River Colony was settled, and the Métis had their own Michif words for it, including aen wagon and aen charet. These carts became a lasting symbol of Métis ingenuity and resilience on the frontier.
CARVE: With its many carved pumpkins, sculptures and special effects, [Pumpkins After Dark](https://pumpkinsafterdark.com/) brings magic across Canada. Pumpkins After Dark is Canada’s award-winning outdoor Halloween event, with locations in Burnaby, Calgary, Edmonton, Milton and Ottawa. Featuring over 10,000+ hand-carved pumpkins, this one-of-a-kind walk-through experience is the must-see event of the spooky season.
CAVES: Canada is home to some spectacular natural caves waiting to be explored! While Canada may be known for its vast wilderness and towering mountains, it also boasts a hidden underground world filled with breathtaking caverns and geological wonders. Some notable examples include the Bonnechere Caves and Bruce Peninsula Caves in Ontario, the Canmore Caverns in Alberta, the Horne Lake Caves on Vancouver Island, and the Castleguard Cave in Banff National Park, the longest cave in Canada. Whether you're spelunking through narrow passageways or admiring dazzling rock formations, exploring caves in Canada is an unforgettable adventure that reveals the hidden beauty beneath the surface of the Great White North.
CELLO: The cello’s rich, singing tone has been brought to life by many notable Canadian musicians, including virtuoso [Ofra Harnoy](https://ofraharnoy.ca/), a multiple JUNO Award winner; Montreal-born [Stéphane Tétreault](https://stephanetetreault.com/), who has performed internationally on a famed Stradivarius; and Rachel Mercer, Principal Cellist of the [National Arts Centre Orchestra](https://nac-cna.ca/en/orchestra) in Ottawa. From solo recitals to chamber music and symphony halls, these cellists help bring the deep voice of the cello to life across Canada and around the world.
CELLS: Stem cells were first discovered by Canadians Dr. James Till and Dr. Ernest McCulloch who were both pioneers in biomedical research. Stem cells can self-renew and can be artificially grown, leading to all kinds of possibilities for the cure of disease and the rebuilding of tissue. Till and McCulloch were jointly nominated and inducted into the Canadian Medical Hall of Fame.
CENTS: Street Cents is a newsmagazine TV series directed at teenagers that originally aired on CBC Television between 1989 and 2006. Street Cents focused on consumer and media awareness for young people. The show has won several Gemini Awards and even an International Emmy for Best Youth Programming or Series, and was lauded by critics for its efforts to be inclusive and representative of Canada's youth. Jonathan Torrens was one of the original hosts of the show. Street Cents returned in a new format in 2022, led by a group of dynamic content creators. Targeted to teens, the new version of the beloved youth brand has [launched on TikTok](https://www.tiktok.com/@streetcents) with a focus on making financial literacy useful, relatable and entertaining through daily short form video content.
CHAIN: Did you know that a group of lynx is called a "chain"? The Canada lynx, a native species to Canada, is known for its distinctive tufted ears and large, padded paws that act like snowshoes in the winter. These elusive cats are most commonly found in the boreal forests of Canada, where they primarily hunt snowshoe hares. While lynx are typically solitary animals, the term "chain" is used to describe a group of them when they do come together. Seeing a chain of lynx in the wild is a rare and remarkable sight, reflecting the rich biodiversity of Canada's wilderness.
CHANT: Today is [National Indigenous Peoples Day](https://www.rcaanc-cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1100100013718/1708446948967)! On June 21, we recognize and celebrate the history, heritage, resilience and diversity of First Nations, Inuit and Métis across Canada. Chants play a vital role in Indigenous culture in Canada, used in ceremonies, healing, and storytelling for generations. These rhythmic vocalizations help preserve history, connect communities, and honour ancestors. Chants, alongside traditional songs, are a way for Indigenous peoples to maintain their cultural identity and pass knowledge from one generation to the next. They are a powerful form of expression and resilience within Canada’s rich cultural mosaic.
CHASM: [Chasm Provincial Park](https://bcparks.ca/chasm-park/) is a provincial park in British Columbia, Canada, located near the town of Clinton. The park was originally created in 1940 to preserve and promote a feature known as the Painted Chasm, or simply The Chasm, a gorge created from melting glacial waters eroding a lava plateau over a 10 million year span called the Chilcotin Group. The Chasm is approximately 600 metres wide and 8 kilometres long, and lies adjacent to the route of the Cariboo Road.
CHEEK: In Newfoundland and Labrador, cod cheek is a local delicacy! This tender, flavourful piece of meat comes from just below the cod’s eye and is prized for its melt-in-your-mouth texture. Pan-fried or battered, cod cheeks are a true taste of Atlantic Canada - proof that every part of the fish can be something to savour!
CHIEF: In many Indigenous cultures in Canada, chiefs are the leaders of bands, clans and/or First Nations. Chiefs act as cultural and spiritual leaders and also serve as links between their people and the municipal, provincial and federal governments. RoseAnne Archibald is the current National Chief of the Assembly of First Nations (AFN) in Canada.
CHILD: Canada declared November 20th as [National Child Day](https://nationalchildday.org/) to celebrate the rights of children. It was chosen in recognition of Canada's commitment to upholding the rights of children, and to commemorate the day the United Nations adopted the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC) on November 20, 1989.
CHILL: In 2001, Canada took the lead to promote an international standard for wind chill. A team of scientists and medical experts from Canada and the US worked together to develop the current wind chill index. This index represents the degree of "chill" that your skin senses, and is based on the loss of heat from the face. Wind chills below -70 have been recorded in northern communities in Canada. On January 13, 1975 at Kugaaruk, Nunavut, the air temperature was -51C and the winds were 56km/h, producing a bone-chilling wind chill of -78!
CHIME: The Peace Tower’s 53 bells chime high above Parliament Hill, ringing out everything from O Canada to classic folk tunes. Played like a giant piano, this grand carillon is one of the largest in the world! Since 2008, Canada’s official Dominion Carillonneur, Dr. Andrea McCrady, has performed thousands of live recitals from the tower, keeping this uniquely Canadian tradition ringing loud and proud in the heart of Ottawa with every chime.
CHOIR: Canada's world-renowned and oldest-surviving mixed-voice amateur choir, the [Toronto Mendelssohn Choir](https://www.tmchoir.org/), was founded in 1894 by Augustus Stephen Vogt. It is one of Canada's oldest, largest, and most recognized choral ensembles, renowned for over 125 years for delivering the highest standard of musical performance.
CIVIC: Canadian citizens have the civic duty to serve on a jury if called to do so and the civic responsibility to vote in Canadian elections. Federal election voter turnout in Canada rose sharply in the 2015 federal election to 68.3% of eligible voters, the highest turnout since 1993. Voter turnout decreased to 67% in 2019 and to 62.2% in 2021.
CIVIL: [Canada History Week 2023](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/history-week.html) takes place from November 20 to 26. This year’s theme is the History of Black Achievement in Canada. The week encourages Canadians to reflect upon and engage with Canada’s past. Viola Desmond was a Canadian civil and women's rights activist and businesswoman of Black Nova Scotian descent. In 1946, she challenged racial segregation at a cinema in New Glasgow, Nova Scotia, by refusing to leave a whites-only area of the Roseland Theatre. Viola was forcibly removed and jailed, sparking the civil rights movement in Canada. #HistoryWeek2023
CLEAR: With its crystal-clear waters, sandy beaches, and beautiful surrounding forests, [Clear Lake](https://discoverclearlake.com/) is one of the best-known destinations in Riding Mountain National Park. Located near the resort town of Wasagaming, the lake attracts visitors year-round for hiking, boating, wildlife viewing, skiing, and ice fishing. From spotting moose and bison in the summer to skating and snowy adventures in winter, Clear Lake showcases Manitoba’s natural beauty in every season.
CLERK: The [Clerk of the Privy Council](https://www.canada.ca/en/privy-council/corporate/clerk.html) is the professional head of the Public Service of Canada. As the deputy minister for the Privy Council Office (the Prime Minister's department), the clerk is the senior civil servant in the Government of Canada and serves as the secretary to the Cabinet.
CLIFF: Baffin Island, Canada is home to Mount Thor, the world's tallest vertical cliff. In fact, it's steeper than vertical, with a 105-degree overhang. Check out this [article by Jeopardy champ Ken Jennings](https://www.cntraveler.com/stories/2013-06-10/mount-thor-canada-maphead-ken-jennings) all about Mount Thor!
CLIMB: Did you know that sport climbing is making its second appearance in the 2024 Paris Olympics? This dynamic and challenging sport has gained popularity worldwide, including in Canada. [Canadian sport climbers](https://olympic.ca/sports/sport-climbing/) have been making their mark on the international stage, with athletes like [Sean McColl](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/sean-mccoll/) and Alannah Yip leading the way. Both climbers have represented Canada in various international competitions, showcasing their skills and determination.
CLOTH: The J-Cloth, a staple in kitchens and cleaning routines around the world, was invented in Canada! In 1963, the J-Cloth was created by the Johnson & Johnson company in Montreal. This versatile, durable, and highly absorbent cloth revolutionized household cleaning with its unique design and efficiency. The J-Cloth has become a beloved cleaning tool in homes, restaurants, and industries across the globe.
CLOUD: Cloudberries are a member of the Rosaceae family and are a relative of the raspberry. These amber berries are a rare find as they are native to cool temperate regions, alpine and Arctic tundra and boreal forest. Cloudberries are also known as bakeapples or bake-apple berries in Atlantic Canada. This herbaceous perennial produces amber-colored edible fruit similar to the blackberry.
COAST: Canada has the longest coastline in the world, measuring 243,042 km!
COBRA: There are plenty of animals that are considered to be icons in Canada including beavers, moose and polar bears. However, anyone who lives in the Great White North knows that Canada geese are the country's true mascots, despite their notoriously bad attitude. They hiss, they honk, and worst of all, they chase you down if you get too close. Cobra Chickens is a slang term for Canada Geese that gained popularity in 2018 after a post on Twitter went viral from a farm worker. Consider yourself lucky if you've never been chased by a cobra chicken!
COCOA: During the holiday season, Canadians love nothing more than a cozy cup of hot cocoa to warm up on chilly winter days. Canada is one of the world's top consumers of chocolate, and the holidays bring out the best cocoa traditions – whether it's sipping a rich hot chocolate by the fire or indulging in chocolatey desserts after a holiday feast. The [Vancouver Hot Chocolate Festival](https://hotchocolatefest.com/) celebrates this sweet tradition each winter, with local chocolatiers creating unique and festive flavours just for the occasion. From peppermint cocoa to gingerbread chocolate, Canadians know how to make their cocoa merry and bright!
COINS: Canada has some iconic coins, including the $1 loonie and the $2 toonie. DYK: In 2017, the Canadian Mint ran a contest and Canadians chose "Churchill" as the toonie polar bear's official name, a reference both to Winston Churchill and to the common polar bear sightings in Churchill, Manitoba. Canada has even commemorated the coins with monuments: the "Big Loonie" in Echo Bay, Ontario and the "Giant Toonie" in Campbellford, Ontario.
COLTS: The [Barrie Colts](https://chl.ca/ohl-colts/) are a junior ice hockey team in Ontario Hockey League (OHL), based in Barrie, Ontario. The Colts joined the OHL in 1995, and won the J. Ross Robertson Cup during the 1999–2000 OHL season. The team has produced several NHL stars, including Mark Scheifele, Aaron Ekblad, and Alex Pietrangelo, all of whom have represented Team Canada on the international stage. The 2025 OHL Playoffs are officially underway and the Colts are the second seed in the Eastern Conference.
COMET: The de Havilland Comet is the world's first commercial jet airliner. On May 29th 1953, the first of two 40 passenger de Havilland Comets arrived in Ottawa. With the arrival of this aircraft, the Royal Canadian Air Force became the first air force in the world to operate jet transports and the first operator to make scheduled trans-Atlantic crossings.
COMIC: Today is International Read Comics in Public Day! Did you know that comic book characters Wolverine and Deadpool are both from Canada? Many other Canadian superheroes have appeared on comic book stands over the years, including Johnny Canuck, Nelvana of the Northern Lights, Captain Canuck, Northguard & Fleur de Lys, and Northstar and Weapon Alpha (aka Guardian), members of Alpha Flight, a team of Canadian superheroes. Although not Canadian himself, Superman was co-created by a Canadian: Toronto-born artist Joe Shuster created the superhero with American writer Jerry Siegel.
CONCH: [Caraquet, New Brunswick](https://caraquet.ca/), is home to the world's largest conch! This massive seashell sculpture was built to celebrate the region's coastal heritage and attract visitors to this charming seaside community. Caraquet, known as the "Acadian Capital," is rich in maritime culture and traditions, making this larger-than-life conch a fitting landmark. Whether you're a fan of the ocean, Acadian history, or just love quirky roadside attractions, this giant shell is a must-see on your next trip to the East Coast!
CONGA: The conga drum is a key part of Afro-Cuban music, and Canada has many talented conga players! Juno-winning artist Alex Cuba blends smooth melodies with vibrant conga rhythms, creating a unique sound loved across the country. Congas bring rich beats to jazz, Latin, and world music scenes - especially in Toronto's vibrant Latin community. Festivals like the [Canadian Latin Fest](https://www.canadianlatinfest.org/) happening in Nathan Phillips Square this weekend celebrate this lively culture, making congas a vital part of Canada's diverse musical heritage.
COVER: The [Hartland Covered Bridge](https://www.pc.gc.ca/apps/dfhd/page_nhs_eng.aspx?id=181) in Hartland, New Brunswick, is the world's longest covered bridge, at 391 metres (1,282 feet) long. It crosses the Saint John River from Hartland to Somerville, New Brunswick. The bridge was designated a National Historic Site in 1980, and the Winter Olympic Torch was carried through the bridge in 1988. Canada Post released a postage stamp honouring the bridge in 1995.
CRABS: Canada is the largest producer of snow crab in the world, accounting for about two-thirds of the global supply! The provinces of Newfoundland and Quebec provide Canada and the world with hundreds of tonnes of snow crab each year. Snow crabs have white flesh with a tinge of pink and a slightly salty flavour offering the perfect balance of sweet and briny.
CRAFT: In the past decade, Canada has seen a rapidly growing number of craft breweries popping up. Craft breweries have become so popular in Canada that a new association, Canadian Craft Brewers Association, was formed in May 2019. Sales of craft beer increased tenfold from 2008 to 2018, and it now accounts for 6% of the Canadian market. December 10th is National Lager Day! Lagers are some of the most popular beer styles in the world and Canada is no exception. Celebrate with a craft lager from your favourite Canadian brewery!
CRASH: [Crash Adams](https://www.crashadamsmusic.com/), the Toronto-based pop duo, performed their original song “Optimist” on America’s Got Talent in 2025, earning four “yes” votes from the judges. They were previously nominated for Breakthrough Group of the Year at the 2024 Juno Awards, highlighting their rise in the Canadian music scene. Their energetic blend of pop, rock, and electronic music has won them a devoted fanbase.
CRAVE: [Crave](https://www.crave.ca/) is a popular Canadian streaming service offering a wide range of content and programming. Launched by Bell Media in 2014, Crave provides Canadians with access to a rich library of movies, TV shows, and original content. It has become a go-to platform for Canadian viewers craving top-quality entertainment, including hit series like "Game of Thrones," "The Handmaid's Tale," and Canadian originals like "Letterkenny." With its extensive selection and exclusive offerings, Crave has cemented itself as a key player in the Canadian streaming landscape.
CREAM: The iconic Twinkie – a golden sponge cake with a creamy centre – was invented in 1930 by Canadian-born baker James Dewar. Working at the Continental Baking Company in Illinois, Dewar came up with the idea as a way to use shortcake pans year-round. Early versions were filled with lemon or banana cream, but during WWII, a banana shortage led to the switch to vanilla cream. That classic creamy filling has been a sweet part of snack history ever since – with a surprising Canadian connection!
CREEK: Having premiered on CBC in 2015, Schitt's Creek was Canada's best-kept sitcom secret. In its sixth and final season, the quirky and hilarious Canadian comedy Schitt's Creek pulled off a sweep, taking home seven primetime awards and nine Emmys in all.
CREWS: Paris 2024 will see Canada's first breaking Olympian, as the sport makes its Olympic debut. In [breaking](https://olympic.ca/sports/breaking/), crews are a collective of B-Boys and B-Girls who come together as a team, under one crew name. Being in a crew is an official, important commitment as a crew is a family who train together, battle together, support each other and share the same mindset towards breaking as a dance and culture. [Philip Kim](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/philip-kim/), aka B-Boy Phil Wizard, is one of the most creative and original breakers on the hip-hop dance scene and he is representing Canada in Paris 2024!
CRIED: [The Girl Who Cried Pearls](https://www.nfb.ca/film/the-girl-who-cried-pearls/) made history in 2026 by winning the Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film. Produced by the National Film Board of Canada, the stop-motion film was created by Montréal-based directors Chris Lavis and Maciek Szczerbowski, and is set in early 20th-century Montréal. Featuring Canadian voice actor Colm Feore, it’s a powerful example of homegrown storytelling earning global recognition.
CRIER: Before newspapers or social media, Canadian towns relied on the town crier to spread the news. Ringing a bell and shouting “Hear Ye! Hear Ye!”, they announced royal proclamations, local events, and important updates. Today, town criers are a cherished part of Canada’s history, keeping this lively tradition alive at festivals and ceremonies!
CROPS: Canada is the world’s largest grower and exporter of flax seed, canola, oats, mustard seeds, pulses (peas, beans, and lentils) and durum wheat.
CROSS: The Victoria Cross was created in 1993 and is the highest award within the Canadian honours system, taking precedence over all other orders, decorations, and medals. The Victoria Cross is awarded for "the most conspicuous bravery, a daring or pre-eminent act of valour or self-sacrifice or extreme devotion to duty, in the presence of the enemy". To date, no Canadian Victoria Cross has been conferred.
CRUDE: Canada has the 3rd largest oil reserves in the world and is the 4th largest oil producer and exporter.
CRUMB: [Nanaimo Bars](https://www.nanaimo.ca/about-nanaimo/nanaimo-bars) are a Canadian dessert classic from Nanaimo, British Columbia. This no-bake treat has a crumb-based bottom layer made from crushed graham crackers, cocoa, and coconut, topped with a creamy custard icing and finished with a smooth chocolate layer. A perfect blend of textures and flavours, Nanaimo Bars are a sweet Canadian favourite enjoyed across the country!
CUBIC: Canada is one of the world's top producers of diamonds, with mines in the Northwest Territories, Ontario, and Quebec. Diamonds, which are also the birthstone for April, form deep underground in a cubic crystal structure, giving them their signature sparkle! The first Canadian diamond mine, Ekati, opened in the Northwest Territories in 1998, and today, Canada is known for its high-quality, ethically sourced gems.
CURLS: Canada is a country that curls! According to [Curling Canada](https://www.curling.ca/), there are 1,000 curling rinks across the country. Canada has won 12 medals since curling became an Olympic sport in 1998, the most most any country has won in curling at the Olympic Winter Games! Canada has also won a record 59 golds at the World Curling Championships across the men's, women's, mixed and wheelchair events. Hurry hard!
CYBER: Did you know that Canada is a global leader in cybersecurity research and innovation? With the increasing reliance on digital technologies and the internet, cybersecurity has become a critical aspect of protecting individuals, businesses, and governments from cyber threats. In Canada, organizations such as the [Canadian Cyber Threat Exchange](https://cctx.ca/) (CCTX) and the [Canadian Centre for Cyber Security](https://www.cyber.gc.ca/) (CCCS) work tirelessly to enhance the nation's cybersecurity posture and collaborate with international partners to address cyber threats.
CYCLE: Today is World Bicycle Day! It's a global celebration supported by the United Nations held each year on June 3rd and aims to promote physical activity and the use of bicycles for transportation. Canada boasts an extensive network of cycling infrastructure, ranging from urban bike lanes to scenic rural trails. By participating in World Bicycle Day, Canadians can raise awareness about the benefits of cycling, encourage their fellow citizens to take up this healthy and eco-friendly habit, and advocate for continued improvements to cycling infrastructure in their communities.
DAILY: Daily Planet was a Canadian television program featuring daily news, discussion and commentary on the scientific aspects of current events and discoveries. The show first aired on January 1, 1995, the same day as the premiere of Discovery Channel Canada, under the name @discovery.ca with Jay Ingram as the host. Ingram previously hosted the science program Quirks and Quarks on CBC Radio One from 1979 (when he took over the show from David Suzuki) to 1992.
DAIRY: The Dairy Farmers of Canada logo guarantees a product is made with 100% Canadian milk and milk ingredients, and is free of antibiotics.
DEALS: Deals are the highlight of Boxing Day, when Canadians flock to stores and online shops to snag post-holiday bargains. It’s one of the biggest shopping days of the year in Canada, with nearly six in ten Canadians planning to shop in some way. From electronics to winter gear, retailers across the country offer deep discounts, making it a favourite day for shoppers hunting for a steal and extending the holiday cheer a little further.
DECOY: Hunters in Canada have been using decoys for generations to attract waterfowl like ducks and geese during hunting season. Decoy carving is even considered an art form, particularly in communities along the East Coast, where handmade decoys were once essential for a successful hunt. Decoys play a symbolic role in connecting Canadians with their heritage and the outdoors, a reflection of the country's strong ties to nature and conservation.
DEEDS: November 13th is [World Kindness Day](https://www.randomactsofkindness.org/world-kindness-day)! The purpose of World Kindness Day is to highlight and encourage good deeds in your community. In Canada, the Chevrolet Good Deeds Cup seeks to inspire young Canadians to do good by transforming the positive values learned through hockey into Good Deeds within their communities. The program has made an incredible impact in communities coast to coast to coast amounting more than 1,000 Good Deeds and over $600,000 to charities.
DELTA: Happy World Rivers Day! Deltas are wetlands that form as rivers empty their water and sediment into another body of water, such as an ocean, lake, or another river. Among the largest deltas in Canada are those of the Mackenzie and Saskatchewan rivers, as well as the Peace-Athabasca Delta. The Mackenzie Delta in Northwest Territories is one of the world's largest river deltas.
DEMON: In 2025, Netflix’s KPop Demon Hunters thrilled audiences with a fictional K-Pop girl group battling demons through music. Co-directed by Maggie Kang – born in Seoul, raised in Toronto, and a Sheridan College animation grad – the film blends Korean mythology with Canadian creativity. Its hit song Golden made Billboard history, topping both the Hot 100 and Global 200 charts.
DEPOT: In early Canadian history, a depot was more than just a storage spot – it was a lifeline. Trading depots were key hubs during the fur trade era, where Indigenous peoples, voyageurs, and European traders exchanged goods like furs, tools, and textiles. Major depots, such as those run by the Hudson’s Bay Company and North West Company, helped shape trade routes and settlements across Canada. These depots laid the groundwork for many towns and cities we know today!
DERBY: It's the final weekend of the 2023 [Calgary Stampede](https://www.calgarystampede.com/) - the world's largest outdoor rodeo! This year, the Stampede is celebrating 100 years of chuckwagon racing at the Cowboys Rangeland Derby! The world’s first Chuckwagon Race was staged at the Calgary Stampede in 1923. A true throwback to the wild west, the event was inspired by the tradition of cowboys breaking camp and racing home. And while some of the rules have since changed, the rush has never left. YAHOO!
DEUCE: In curling, a deuce is when a team scores two points in a single end, giving them a strong advantage on the scoreboard. The new [Rock League](https://www.rockleague.com/) kicks off in Toronto from April 6-12, featuring an exciting new format and players from across Canada and around the world. With the slogan “Curling Unleashed,” competitors will be sliding, sweeping, and chasing deuces in a week of fast-paced, international curling action.
DEVIL: The Devil’s Brigade was an elite Canadian-American commando unit during the Second World War. They were renowned for their daring missions, night raids and unconventional fighting tactics. A legacy that paved the way for modern Canadian Forces special operations units. They were also referred to as "The Black Devils" because the brigade's members smeared their faces with black boot polish for their covert operations in the dark of the night.
DISCO: Disco fever hit Canada in the 1970s, lighting up dance floors across the country. Montreal became one of North America’s disco capitals with iconic clubs like the Lime Light, where dancers grooved under glittering lights and DJs shaped the scene. Today, disco still thrives with clubs and parties, while Canadian acts like the band Lime and ongoing celebrations keep the rhythm alive coast to coast.
DOCKS: Across Canada, [Victoria Day](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/services/important-commemorative-days/victoria-day.html) weekend is widely seen as the unofficial start of summer, and docks across lakes and cottages are finally coming back to life. Millions of Canadians head to cottages or lake regions each year for the May long weekend, making it one of the busiest travel periods of the spring season. Boats return to the water, families gather along shorelines, and communities across the country kick off the season with sunshine, fresh air, and time by the lake.
DOMES: Canada is home to some famous domes, including Calgary's unmistakeable Saddledome, the SkyDome in Toronto, the Montreal Biodome, and BC's Snow Dome peak which is a "[hydrological apex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_divide)" (a single point where three different watersheds meet).
DOORS: Held in many cities across Canada, Doors Open is an event that invites people to learn more about their local heritage. Doors Open Canada is a national program by Heritage Canada/[National Trust for Canada](https://nationaltrustcanada.ca/) that aims to expose architecture and heritage through the exploration of hidden historical, architectural and cultural gems. Buildings that are normally closed to the public, or which charge an entrance fee, welcome visitors to look around for free.
DOUGH: Today is National Waffle Day! Touton is a traditional dish from Newfoundland produced by frying bread dough on a pan in butter or pork fat. Toutons are often made from leftover bread dough, or dough that was left to rise overnight. This pancake-like dish has emerged as a symbol of Newfoundland identity.
DOZEN: Did you know egg cartons were invented by a Canadian? Egg cartons were invented in 1911 in British Columbia by Joseph Coyle after overhearing a dispute over broken eggs between a local farmer and hotel owner. Coyle was a newspaper man and part-time inventor. He designed the very first egg carton from newspaper, with cushioned slots for each egg. The next time your dozen eggs get home safely, make sure to thank Joseph Coyle!
DRAKE: The Village of Andrew, Alberta is home to the [world's largest mallard duck](https://www.travelalberta.com/listings/worlds-largest-mallard-duck-andrew-5641)! The statue honours the area's wetlands and mallard nesting grounds. It features a male mallard duck (also known as a drake) with a wingspan of 23 feet, weighing 1 tonne and standing seven metres tall. This drake is not quite as famous as Canadian rapper and singer, Drake, who also starred as Jimmy Brooks in the teen drama series Degrassi: The Next Generation.
DRAWN: In Canada, traditional horse-drawn carioles were a common winter sight in the 19th and early 20th centuries. These elegant, narrow sleds, pulled by a single horse, carried families and goods across snowy landscapes, especially in Quebec and Ontario. Today, carioles are celebrated as a charming symbol of Canadian winter heritage and horse-drawn history.
DRESS: Red Dress Day, also known as the National Day of Awareness for Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls and Two-Spirit People, is observed annually on May 5th. The day honours and brings awareness to the thousands of Indigenous women, girls and two-spirit people who have been subject to disproportionate violence in Canada. Red Dress Day was inspired by Métis artist Jaime Black’s REDress Project installation, in which she hung empty, red dresses to represent the missing and murdered women. Red dresses have become symbolic of the crisis as a result of her installation.
DRILL: The [Royal Military College of Canada](https://www.rmc-cmr.ca/) is well known for the quality and diversity of its ceremonial drill. Reaching this high standard can only be gained through the hard work and dedication of each cadet. Cadets are expected to reach and maintain a high standard of personal drill with the service rifle, colours, and the sword.
DRIVE: In Canada’s history, the cattle drive was an essential part of the ranching culture, especially in the western provinces. In the late 1800s, cowboys would drive herds of cattle across vast distances to railheads, where the animals were shipped to markets. These cattle drives, especially in areas like Alberta and Saskatchewan, were grueling yet vital to the growth of Canada’s beef industry. The tradition of cattle driving is still celebrated today in rodeos and ranching festivals, reminding Canadians of the tough, adventurous spirit that shaped the nation’s prairies.
DRUID: Modern druidry has taken root in Canada, where groups gather to celebrate the changing seasons, honour nature, and explore Celtic-inspired spiritual traditions. From coastal ceremonies in Atlantic Canada to forest gatherings in British Columbia, Canadian druids blend ancient symbolism with local landscapes, reminding us how deeply connected many Canadians feel to the land around them.
DUCKS: With roughly 22 different species of duck found in Canada, the most common is the Mallard. Saskatchewan is renowned for having some of the most abundant and productive waterfowl habitat in North America. Check out [Ducks Unlimited Canada](https://www.ducks.ca/) and how they are working to conserve, restore and manage Canadian wetlands.
DUMMY: Canada has a rich tradition of ventriloquism, with incredible performers like Mark Crocker, known for his lovable dummy Elmer, and Cy Leonard, the first ventriloquist to appear on Canadian television. Don Bryan has been recognized as one of the world's top ventriloquists, and he is also a leading expert in the art of creating and carving ventriloquist dummies. These talented artists proved that even a "dummy" can be the star of the show!
DUNES: The world's smallest desert can be found in the Yukon! In truth, the moniker is used in good fun as the Carcross Desert isn't a desert at all. The beautiful 2.5 square kilometre patch of land is a series of sand dunes left over from a glacial lake thousands of years ago. The tiny area is kept dry year-round thanks to the surrounding mountains. In contrast, the Athabasca Sand Dunes in Saskatchewan is the largest active sand surface in Canada at 1925 km² and one of the world's most northerly major sand dunes.
EARTH: Happy Earth Day! 🌎 Every year on April 22, [Earth Day](https://earthday.ca/) marks the anniversary of the birth of the modern environmental movement in 1970. In 1990, the creation of the organization in France and in Canada goes hand in hand with the internationalization of the Earth Day movement. Earth Day in 1990 became a global celebration, with participation by an estimated 200 million people in at least 136 countries. Over the years, Earth Day has become the largest participatory environmental movement on the planet.
EASEL: Altona, Manitoba is home to the [world's largest painting on an easel](https://altona.ca/p/big-easel)! Artist and art educator, Cameron Cross, developed the vision of a giant steel easel displaying the likeness of Vincent Van Gogh's 'Sunflowers' painting. This landmark stands 76'6" high and is on a 3-legged steel easel. It is a symbol of international fine art and celebrates Altona’s reputation as the Sunflower Capital of Canada.
EATER: The Smoke Eaters (aka Smokies) have existed as both junior and senior hockey teams in Canada since the 1920s. The senior Smoke Eaters won two Allan Cup championships, 1938 and 1962, and two Ice Hockey World Championships playing for Canada in 1939 and 1961. The senior Smokies were the last independent ice hockey club to represent Canada in international competition before the Canada men's national ice hockey team was established in 1963. The current Trail Smoke Eaters are a junior A ice hockey team from Trail, British Columbia, that are part of the British Columbia Hockey League. Learn more about the Smoke Eaters in [Craig Baird's Canadian History Ehx podcast episode](https://canadaehx.com/2022/01/11/the-trail-smoke-eaters-2/)!
EAVES: In Canada, the term "eavestroughs" is commonly used to refer to the rain gutters attached to the eaves of a roof! While "gutters" is the more common term elsewhere, Canadians prefer "eavestroughs" to describe these important drainage systems that help manage rainfall and protect buildings from water damage. This uniquely Canadian term reflects the country's distinctive linguistic features and regional vocabulary!
EDICT: An edict is a formal announcement or decree that establishes a law or order. Often associated with monarchies, edicts have been used throughout history to communicate official orders, mandates, and laws. In Canada, royal edicts played a key role in shaping governance and establishing provinces under the Crown. The Quebec Act of 1774, an edict from King George III, protected French civil law and religious rights, helping to preserve Quebec's distinct identity. Even today, Canada remains a constitutional monarchy, with royal proclamations continuing to mark significant national events.
ELBOW: "Elbows Up" is a phrase that means to protect yourself or fight back, and it recently gained attention as Canada flexed its muscle in the ongoing trade dispute with the United States. Just like in hockey, where players use their elbows to shield themselves or push back against opponents, Canada has been using its economic power and strategic policies to stand firm and defend its interests. Whether it's in the rink or the world of international trade, "elbows up" is all about resilience and standing your ground!
ELDER: Elders are respected individuals who play key roles in Indigenous communities. They are important knowledge keepers, and they also help to ensure cultural continuity.
ELVES: [Santa's Village](https://www.santasvillage.ca/) in Bracebridge, Ontario, isn't just a magical summer home for Santa - it's also home to his hardworking 'elves'! Nestled at the 45th parallel, halfway between the North Pole and the equator, it's the perfect spot for Santa’s summer retreat. Since opening in 1955, this charming theme park has welcomed families from near and far, offering a whimsical experience full of holiday cheer during its seasonal operation. The employees - playfully known as elves - help create a world of enchantment, making Santa's Village one of Ontario's most beloved family destinations.
ENTRY: Entry Island is a small, treeless island off the east coast of Quebec with beautiful rolling green hills, a 1969 lighthouse & a seasonal history museum. It is the only inhabited island of the Magdalen Islands not linked to the archipelago. No matter where you decide to go on this 7.2 km² island, you will be charmed by the beauty of its landscape and its animals living in the wild.
EQUAL: In 1927, five women who have since become known as the Famous Five launched a legal challenge that would mark a turning point for equality rights in Canada. Emily Murphy, Nellie McClung, Louise McKinney, Irene Parlby and Henrietta Muir Edwards were journalists, politicians, reformers and activists from Alberta who advocated for equal rights for women in Canada. There are [statues of the Famous Five](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/services/art-monuments/monuments/women-are-persons.html) in both Ottawa and Calgary celebrating the decision of the Privy Council that women are persons and could be elected to the Senate.
EVENT: The Big Event was a professional wrestling spectacle held at Toronto’s Exhibition Stadium on August 28, 1986. Produced by the World Wrestling Federation (WWF), it drew a massive crowd of over 70,000 fans, making it one of the largest wrestling events in Canadian history. This closed-circuit broadcast helped cement Toronto as a major stop on the wrestling map and showcased how Canadians have long embraced live sporting and entertainment events on a grand scale.
EXPAT: Canada is home to a vibrant expat community, with people from around the world making it their home temporarily for work, study, or lifestyle. At the same time, there are over 3 million Canadians living abroad, with popular destinations like the United States, the UK, and Australia. Whether in Canada or overseas, expats play an important role in connecting cultures and expanding global networks.
EXPOS: The Montreal Expos, named after the Expo 67 World's Fair, were the first Major League Baseball franchise located outside the USA, competing from 1969 until 2004. The last World's Fair held in Canada was Expo 86 in Vancouver.
FABLE: Fables of the Green Forest introduced Canadian kids in the 1980s and 1990s to woodland adventures on [TVOntario](https://www.tvo.org/) (TVO). Each episode unfolded like a classic fable, with animal characters learning simple lessons about friendship, courage, and life in the forest. It remains a nostalgic example of how storytelling on TVO helped shape early childhood viewing in Canada.
FACES: [Faces Magazine](https://facesmag.ca/) is Ottawa’s premier lifestyle publication, showcasing the faces behind the city's businesses, sports, and entertainment scene. Faces highlights the best of Ottawa with a uniquely Canadian flair. From restaurants to community leaders, it’s all about connecting people and celebrating what makes the capital great!
FACTS: Did you know that the beloved game Trivial Pursuit was invented by Canadians? Scott Abbott, a sports editor, and Chris Haney, a photo editor, came up with the idea in 1979 while playing Scrabble. The game, which challenges players on their knowledge of a wide range of trivia facts, has since become a global sensation and an iconic part of Canadian pop culture.
FAIRS: With the arrival of the autumn season, Canadians have been attending fairs that celebrate the agricultural heritage and community spirit across the country. These fairs showcase everything from livestock competitions and crafts to local produce, giving visitors a chance to experience the rich bounty of the harvest season. Many fairs feature rides, games and entertainment, along with traditional activities such as pie-eating contests, barn dances, and exhibitions that highlight the skills of local artisans and farmers. These cherished events not only connect communities but also remind us of the importance of agriculture in Canada’s history and culture.
FAITH: Religion in Canada encompasses a wide range of beliefs and customs. The constitution of Canada refers to God and the monarch carries the title of Defender of the Faith, however Canada has no official church and the government is officially committed to religious pluralism. Freedom of religion in Canada is a constitutionally protected right, allowing individuals to assemble and worship without limitation or interference.
FALLS: About 28 million litres of water travel down Niagara Falls every second.
FALSE: Pacific Central Station is a railway station in Vancouver, British Columbia, which acts as the western terminus of Via Rail's cross-country service. The station is located in the False Creek area of Vancouver and is a handsome illustration of Beaux-Arts architectural principles, retaining both the exterior features and interior detailing typical of the style. Designed by the Canadian Northern Railway to serve as the western terminus of its transcontinental route, it was originally named False Creek Station and was designated a heritage railway station in 1991.
FARCE: The Royal Canadian Air Farce was a comedy troupe that was active from 1973 to 2019. It is best known for their various Canadian Broadcasting Corporation series, first on CBC Radio and later on CBC Television. Although their weekly radio series ended in 1997 and their television series ended in 2008, the troupe produced annual New Year's Eve specials on CBC Television until 2019.
FAUNA: Canada's fauna is as diverse as its landscapes, from majestic moose roaming the forests and playful otters frolicking in rivers, to bison grazing the plains and beavers diligently building their dams. With over 200 species of mammals, 400 species of birds, and countless other creatures, Canada is a wildlife lover's dream. Whether you're spotting a moose on a forest trail or hearing the call of a loon across a lake, Canada's fauna never fails to leave you in awe.
FEAST: Réveillon is a traditional all-night feast that starts after church service on Christmas Eve and lasts until the wee hours of Christmas morning.
