First celebrated in 19th-century France, the Canadian menu includes tourtière (a meat pie made with pork and beef or veal), ragoût de pattes de cochon (pigs' feet stew) and bûche de Nöel (a Yule log dessert). This celebration and the traditions and foods associated with it speak to the history of francophones across Canada.
FERNS: Found throughout Canada, fiddlehead ferns are the tightly coiled tips of early spring ferns with a tender texture and mildly nutty flavour. They are only available for a short window of time during the spring and are considered a seasonal delicacy in many parts of Canada.
FETAL: Montreal born Leon Katz was a pioneering biomedical engineer whose work significantly improved patient care and safety throughout Canada. Katz invented, innovated and hand-crafted a wide range of medical devices: Canada's first fetal heart monitor, a scanner-printer to detect radioactive iodine uptake in the thyroid gland, infant incubators, and a high-speed contrast injector for angiography. Notably, using his own original heart-lung bypass machine, he was the perfusionist for Canada’s first successful open heart surgery, and for thousands of subsequent operations.
FIBRE: Fibre optic internet technology has revolutionized connectivity, and here in Canada, it's also helping bridge the digital divide! In Ottawa, the [National Capital FreeNet](https://www.ncf.ca/en/) (NCF) is making waves with its [Community WiFi project](https://www.ncf.ca/en/high-speed-internet/community-wifi/), in partnership with our friends at CIRA. By leveraging fibre connections from [Hiboo Networks](https://www.hiboonetworks.com/), Ottawa-Gatineau's first municipally owned fibre optic-based telecom provider, this pilot project provides free internet access to underserved communities, supporting thousands of individuals living in Ottawa Community Housing. This initiative complements CIRA's annual [Net Good Grants program](https://www.cira.ca/en/grants/?utm_source=canuckle&utm_medium=game&utm_campaign=cira) which provides millions of dollars in funding to community-led projects that address digital challenges in rural, remote, and Indigenous communities across Canada.
FIELD: There are so many different types of fields in Canada: sports fields, wheat fields, oil fields, and ice fields to name a few. The Canadian Prairies are known for their open skies and vast fields of grain, but Canada is also home to the world's largest non-polar ice field in the St. Elias Mountains located in Kluane National Park and Reserve, Yukon Territory.
FIFTY: On June 16, 2025, Canadian ultramarathoner and mental health advocate Sachin "Sach" Latti began running 50 km a day for 75 days across Canada, from Victoria, B.C. to St. John’s, Newfoundland. Known as Canada’s Longest Run for Mental Health, his mission aims to raise $1 million for mental health initiatives. Along the way, Sach is connecting with Canadians from all walks of life, sparking open conversations about mental health and inspiring others to take action. You can follow Sach's journey at [sachinmotion.ca](https://sachinmotion.ca/) and support his cross-Canada run with a donation to the [Sach In Motion Fund](https://form.123formbuilder.com/6647897/sach-in-motion-donation-form). Every step matters. Every donation helps.
FILMS: The film industry in Canada has grown so much over the years that it has been referred to as Hollywood North. Toronto is the home to the [Toronto International Film Festival](https://tiff.net/), which is considered by many in the film industry to be second only to Cannes in terms of influence. James Cameron, born in Kapuskasing, Ontario, is the writer and director of the two highest-grossing movies of all time, Avatar (2009) and Titanic (1997). The two films have combined to gross nearly $500 million dollars. Save the date: April 19, 2023 is [National Canadian Film Day](https://canfilmday.ca/)!
FIRES: Fires have been a natural part of Canada’s landscapes for thousands of years, shaping forests, grasslands, and wildlife habitats. Indigenous peoples have long used controlled burns to renew the land and support healthy ecosystems. Today, wildfire season, which peaks from spring through late summer, remains an important part of life in Canada. Modern wildfire management combines skilled crews, advanced technology, and careful planning to protect communities and the environment while respecting fire’s natural role in the ecosystem.
FIRST: The Canadian Constitution recognizes 3 groups of Indigenous peoples: First Nations, Inuit and Métis. These are 3 distinct peoples with unique histories, languages, cultural practices and spiritual beliefs. More than 1.67 million people in Canada identify themselves as an Aboriginal person, according to the 2016 Census. RoseAnne Archibald is a Canadian First Nations advocate and politician who is the current National Chief of the Assembly of First Nations since July 8, 2021. She is the first female National Chief of the Assembly of First Nations.
FIXER: Property Brothers is a Canadian reality television series that features twin brothers Drew Scott and Jonathan Scott. The Property Brothers help families find, buy, and transform fixer-uppers into dream homes on a strict timeline and budget. The show has aired in over 150 countries around the world!
FLAKE: Edward Anton Maria Asselbergs (1927–1996) was a Dutch-Canadian food chemist famous for inventing the modern process of producing instant mashed potato flakes. He developed the process in 1960 while working for the Canadian Department of Agriculture in Ottawa. The product reached the market in 1962 and it was an instant success!
FLASH: Today is National Lighthouse Day! Canada is home to more than 750 lighthouses, and every lighthouse emits a distinctive series of flashes known as its "characteristic." These flash sequences allow ship captains to time intervals between flashes so that they can identify lighthouses, using a publication called the List of Lights.
FLEET: The [Royal Canadian Navy](https://www.canada.ca/en/navy.html)'s (RCN) fleet is made up of numerous classes of ships, submarines and other support vessels, as well as specialized units that allow Canada to maintain one of the most active blue-water navies in the world. The Royal Canadian Air Force (RCAF) aircraft fleet ranges from huge transport aircraft to helicopters to fighters to patrol aircraft and more. They are used to carry out a multitude of roles at home and abroad, in peace and in conflict, all in support of the RCAF's mission of providing relevant, responsive and effective air power to meet the defence challenges of today and into the future. November 5 to 11 is [Veterans' Week](https://www.veterans.gc.ca/eng/remembrance/commemorative-events/veterans-week), an opportunity for Canadians to honour the extraordinary efforts and sacrifices of our veterans. Thank you for your service!
FLEUR: Today is Saint-Jean-Baptiste Day! A national holiday in the Canadian province of Quebec and celebrated by French Canadians across the country and around the world! The fleur-de-lis (also spelled fleur-de-lys) is featured on the flag of Quebec, known as the "Fleurdelisé". The white cross on a blue field recalls an ancient French military banner, and the four fleurs-de-lis are symbolic of France. In Canada, over 10 million people speak French!
FLOOR: Samuel Perry Jacks, more commonly known as "Sam Jacks", was a Canadian soldier in World War II, inventor, military and civic recreation director, sports coach, and creator of the Canadian sport of ringette. In 1936, Jacks created the game of floor hockey, and developed the first set of rules, and was recognized by the Youth Branch of the United Nations for the creation of the game.
FLUKE: In the world of whale watching, a fluke refers to the tail of a whale, an awe-inspiring sight often visible as the whale dives beneath the surface. Canada is home to some of the best locations for spotting these spectacular flukes, especially in the Bay of Fundy, where humpback and minke whales are frequently seen. A whale's fluke, with its unique patterns and markings, is like a fingerprint, allowing researchers to identify individual whales. With over 12,000 whale sightings annually in the Bay of Fundy, catching a glimpse of a whale's fluke is not just a highlight - it's a quintessential Canadian coastal experience!
FLUSH: Dundurn Castle in Hamilton, Ontario was once home to Sir Allan Napier MacNab, railway magnate, lawyer and Premier of the United Canadas (1854-1856) and his family. The 40-room villa was built in the 1830s and featured the latest conveniences of gas lighting and running water. Sir Allan’s washroom even featured an indoor flushing toilet with running water, which was one of the first in Upper Canada.
FOODS: [McCain Foods](https://www.mccain.com/) is one of Canada’s biggest food success stories, founded in New Brunswick in 1957 and still family-owned today. Best known for its frozen potato products, the company grows and processes potatoes from Canadian farms, helping make fries, hash browns, and many more frozen potato products a staple in freezers across the country. From small-town roots to kitchens around the world, McCain remains proudly Canadian at heart.
FORGE: [Hamilton Forge FC](https://forgefc.canpl.ca/) is a Canadian professional soccer club based in Hamilton, Ontario, that competes in the [Canadian Premier League](https://canpl.ca/), the top tier of Canadian soccer. Forge FC joined the CPL in 2019 as one of the league's seven inaugural teams. The team name represents Hamilton's industrious roots and aligns with its nickname "Steeltown."
FORTS: Parks Canada administers a range of historic forts and fortified places across the country. Forts were the focal points of many important developments in Canada's history. As bases for defence, crossroads of trade, and centres of growing communities, they have been gathering places for generations. The [Fortress of Louisbourg National Historic Site](https://parks.canada.ca/lhn-nhs/ns/louisbourg) is the largest reconstructed 18th-century French fortified town in North America.
FOXES: Four species of foxes live in Canada: arctic, swift, grey, and red being the most common. The grey fox is one of only 2 members of the dog family that can climb trees.
FRAME: A single game of snooker is called a frame. There was a time in the 1980s when Canadians were at the top of the snooker world, with three giants of the sport ranked in the top five spots: Kirk Stevens, "Big" Bill Webeniuk and Cliff Thorburn. In 1980, Thorburn defeated Alex Higgins 18 frames to 16 to win the prestigious World Snooker Championship, becoming the first non-British World Champion. [Cliff Thorburn](https://cliffthorburn.ca/) aka "The Grinder" was inducted into the Canada's Sports Hall of Fame in 2001.
FRIES: Canadians consumed over 240,000 metric tonnes of frozen fries in 2019.
FROST: Canadian winters can be freezing cold. Uncovered skin in freezing temperatures can get frostbite. But that doesn't stop Canadians from having outdoor winter festivals! [Frost Regina](https://frostregina.com/) was just held in Regina, Saskatchewan from Feb 3-12, 2023. This unique city-wide event celebrates the cold winter climate through stunning light installations, local music, captivating art, and rich culture. Frost Regina is where winter comes to life!
FRUIT: Despite a relatively short growing season, Canadian farmers produce a wide range of fruits, including apples, tender fruits (peaches, nectarines, pears, plums, prunes and cherries), grapes, blueberries, cranberries, strawberries and raspberries. Southern Ontario and southern British Columbia (including the Okanagan Valley), which each enjoy about 180 frost-free days every year, produce much of the fruit grown in the country, while Quebec and the Maritimes also have significant fruit production, despite having only about 120 frost-free days per year. Fruits accounted for 18.3% of total farm cash receipts for edible horticulture in Canada in 2021.
FUDGE: Sucre à la crème (sugar with cream) is a classic Canadian fudge from the province of Quebec. A timeless tradition in Québec, sucre à la crème is a smooth, creamy and decadent treat made very simply with, as its name suggests, sugar and cream. This delicacy is traditionally served in the form of small cubes, and is an essential sweet treat for the holiday season!
FUNNY: Canada has given the world laughter in spades! From the slapstick genius of John Candy and Jim Carrey, to the sharp wit of Catherine O’Hara, Martin Short, Eugene Levy, and Andrea Martin, Canadians have been making audiences giggle for decades. Mike Myers, Howie Mandel, Ryan Reynolds, Gerry Dee, Seth Rogen, Dan Aykroyd, Norm Macdonald and Russell Peters have all added their own flavour of humour, proving that whether it’s on screen, stage, improv, or in stand-up, Canada knows how to keep things funny!
FUZZY: Canadian children’s television has given us plenty of unforgettable characters, including Fuzzy and Wuzzy, the lovable dust bunny duo from The Big Comfy Couch! Often popping up from beneath the couch, they shared many playful moments with Loonette the clown and her doll Molly, and were known for finding lost items, playing games, and singing songs.
GAMMA: Today is [Brain Cancer Awareness Day](https://www.braintumour.ca/get-involved/raising-awareness/brain-cancer-awareness-day/)! In Canada, gamma radiation plays a vital role in various scientific and medical fields. The country has been at the forefront of medical advancements using gamma rays, particularly in cancer treatment. The Gamma Knife, a specialized form of radiation therapy, is used to treat brain tumours and other abnormalities with high precision while minimizing damage to surrounding healthy tissue. The technology has become a key tool in Canadian hospitals, enhancing the effectiveness of cancer treatment. You can support the Brain Tumour Foundation of Canada by buying a hat or hoodie at [hatsforhopecanada.ca](https://hatsforhopecanada.ca/).
GENRE: The [Juno Awards](https://junoawards.ca/) celebrate the diversity of Canadian music across multiple genres, from pop and rock to country, hip-hop, jazz, and beyond! Since their inception in 1970, the Junos have evolved to reflect Canada's rich musical landscape, adding new genre categories over the years to spotlight emerging talent. Whether it's indie, electronic, or traditional Indigenous music, the Junos showcase the best of Canada's sound! Tonight, the Junos return to Vancouver, British Columbia, marking the city's fifth time hosting Canada's biggest night in music!
GHOUL: In Canada, Halloween is a time when tales of ghouls and ghosts come alive! Many regions have their own spooky legends, with ghouls often depicted as eerie creatures lurking in graveyards or abandoned places. For example, the historic city of Montreal is famous for its haunted sites, including the Old Port, where locals share stories of ghoulish apparitions. Whether it's the restless spirits of pioneers or mythical creatures from Indigenous folklore, Canada's rich tapestry of ghost stories adds a uniquely chilling flavour to Halloween celebrations. So this October, embrace the spooky season and keep an eye out for ghouls as you wander through haunted sites!
GIANT: The Sibley Peninsula just outside of Thunder Bay, Ontario is home to The Sleeping Giant, a series of cliffs which resemble a giant lying on its back. The formation is part of Sleeping Giant Provincial Park and it was voted number one on a list of The Seven Wonders of Canada, and 2007 competition sponsored by CBC. Another famous Canadian giant was "The Friendly Giant", a children's television program that aired on CBC from 1958-1985 with over 3,000 episodes!
GIVER: The slang word give'r is used in Canada to mean to give it all you've got or to try as hard as possible at something. Also, today is the International Day of Charity! The day was chosen to commemorate the anniversary of the passing away of Mother Teresa of Calcutta, who received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979 for her humanitarian work. Canadians are known to be a very generous bunch of givers. In 2021, Canadians gave over $11.8 billion to charitable organizations. Consider donating to your favourite charity today, and just give'r!
GIZMO: Canada has a proud history of tech innovation, with groundbreaking gizmos like the Canadarm, the BlackBerry smartphone, and the IMAX theatre system. Inventions like these have shaped industries around the world showing that Canadian tech has made a global impact. The Canadarm helped astronauts build the International Space Station, BlackBerry revolutionized mobile communication, and IMAX brought breathtaking visuals to theatres globally. Canada's knack for creating world-changing gizmos shows that tech innovation is truly in our DNA!
GLORY: Glory is what Canadians chase every four years at the Winter Olympics, where unforgettable moments unite the country in celebration. At Vancouver 2010, Canada won 14 gold medals, setting the record for the most golds ever by a host nation. [Team Canada](https://olympic.ca/games/milano-cortina-2026/) continues to shine, chasing sporting glory on the world stage at the 2026 Milano Cortina Games!
GOOFY: In snowboarding, riding goofy means leading with your right foot – the opposite of the more common “regular” stance. Canadian snowboarder [Max Parrot](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/max-parrot/), who rides goofy, captured gold in men’s slopestyle at the 2022 Winter Olympics, showing off his technical tricks, style, and fearless flair on the slopes.
GOOSE: A subspecies known as “giant” Canada geese are the largest geese in the world.
GORGE: Canada is home to some incredible gorges & canyons. One of the best-known canyons in Ontario is the Niagara Gorge, which starts at the base of Niagara Falls, and it ends 11 km downriver, near the town of Queenston, where the famous falls originated some 14,000 years ago. Other notable gorges/canyons in Canada include: Elora Gorge (Ontario's Grand Canyon!), Eau Claire Gorge (Ontario), Grand Falls Gorge (New Brunswick), Coaticook Gorge (Quebec), Ouimet Canyon (Thunder Bay, Ontario), Maligne Canyon (Alberta), Nahanni Canyons (Northwest Territories), Canyon Sainte-Anne (Quebec City, Quebec), and Horseshoe Canyon (Alberta).
GRADE: September in Canada means back to school! Students head into a new grade, ready for fresh notebooks, sharpened pencils, and new adventures in learning. Grades mark more than just progress – they’re milestones filled with growth, challenges, and proud moments. In Quebec, high school finishes at Grade 11, after which students move on to CEGEP to continue their studies. No matter where they are in the country, every grade is a step forward in the journey of learning.
GRAFT: In the Okanagan Valley, renowned for its orchards and vineyards, grafting is a vital horticultural technique. Scion grafting involves joining a young shoot (the scion) from a prized fruit tree onto the rootstock of another, combining strengths to grow healthier, more productive plants. This method helps Okanagan growers cultivate delicious apples, cherries, and grapes suited to the region’s unique climate, supporting one of Canada’s most important fruit-growing areas.
GRAMS: When Canada switched to the metric system in the 1970s, grams replaced ounces as the standard way to measure small weights. Today, you’ll spot grams on everything from nutrition labels to coffee bags – a daily reminder of Canada’s move toward metric and its blend of precision and practicality!
GRANT: The Government of Canada offers funding through grants and contribution (Gs&Cs) programs that help support a variety of jobs, research, training and financial assistance across the country. A grant can provide funding to individuals, nonprofits, community organizations and small businesses to support upcoming projects, programs and initiatives. For many Canadians, the ability to access, stay safe and succeed on the internet is still out of reach. To help close this gap, CIRA is launching its 2024 grants program to support not-for-profits, Indigenous communities, researchers and registered charities across the country that are working to bridge that digital divide. [Learn more about CIRA's Net Good Grants program](https://www.cira.ca/en/grants?utm_source=canuckle)!
GRAPE: In Canada, the two main commercial grape-growing areas are southern Ontario's Niagara Peninsula and the Okanagan and neighbouring Similkameen Valleys in south-central British Columbia. In 2022, approximately 33,000 acres were used for the cultivation of grapes in Canada. The main grape vine varieties grown in Canada are Chardonnay, Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Riesling. Wineries take about 80% of the annual grape production in Canada.
GRASS: In Indigenous culture, braided sweet grass is believed to attract good spirits, energies, and influences. Sweet grass, with its sweet aroma reminding people of the love, kindness, and gentleness provided by Mother Earth, is known to have a calming effect and is often used during talking circles and healings. Sweet grass is often used during smudging to call in the good Spirit.
GREAT: Although it is unknown who coined the term “Great White North” in reference to Canada, the nickname has been in use for many decades. “Great” because it’s the second largest country in the world. “White” because of the amount of Arctic frozen tundra and snow within the country. Finally, “North” because not only does Canada take up most of the northern half of North America, it also stretches nearly to the North Pole! Canada is also home to the Great Lakes, the largest group of freshwater lakes on Earth, as well as Great Bear Lake and Great Slave Lake in the Northwest Territories.
GREEN: With an abundance of trees, parks and green spaces across the country, Canada is very green! Canadian cities consistently rank among the most livable in the world. In 2022, 72% of the land area of 1,016 cities and towns across Canada was classed as green. A few other notable green things in Canada: Anne of Green Gables, The Green Party, the green roofs of the Parliament Buildings, & Mike Weir's Masters green jacket! April 7th was Green Shirt Day in Canada - a day to celebrate the gift of life & the impact of organ donors. Learn more about the Logan Boulet Effect at [greenshirtday.ca](https://greenshirtday.ca).
GRIST: In the 18th and 19th centuries, grist mills were the lifeblood of Canadian rural communities. Powered by water or wind, these mills ground grain into flour, providing the essential ingredient for bread, a staple of everyday life. But they were more than just places of work – they were economic hubs that helped shape Canada's growth. Many still stand today as heritage sites, offering a glimpse into the ingenuity that helped early settlers (and their sourdough starters) thrive.
GROVE: Wander through Vancouver Island's [Cathedral Grove in MacMillan Provincial Park](https://bcparks.ca/macmillan-park/) and you'll experience the unforgettable sight of some the oldest and tallest trees in Canada. The park's name will make perfect sense when you see sunlight filtering through the soaring 80-metre-high canopy. Plan to spend a few hours wandering Cathedral Grove's trail system and gazing up at 800-year-old giant Douglas Fir, Grand Firs, Western Hemlocks, and Western Red Cedar trees.
GROWN: From PEI potatoes to Alberta beef, and Saskatchewan wheat to Québec maple syrup, so many delicious things are proudly grown right here in Canada! Our vast and diverse landscape supports everything from fresh berries to sweet corn, producing some of the finest ingredients and products the world has to offer.
GUESS: Happy American Thanksgiving! [The Guess Who](https://www.theguesswho.com/) was the most successful Canadian rock group of the late 1960s and early 1970s, and Canada’s first rock superstars. Their impressive catalogue of songs includes "These Eyes," "No Time," and "American Woman" (the first song by a Canadian band to hit No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart). The Guess Who won two Juno Awards and a Governor General's Performing Arts Award, and was inducted into the Canadian Music Hall of Fame, Canada's Walk of Fame, the Canadian Songwriters Hall of Fame and the Canadian Music Industry Hall of Fame.
GUIDE: Girl Guides of Canada started on September 7, 1910, and Canada was among the founding members of the World Association of Girl Guides and Girl Scouts (WAGGGS) in 1928. Some well-known former Girl Guides include: Queen Elizabeth II, Margaret Atwood, Celine Dion, Sarah McLachlan, and Dr. Roberta Bondar, who juggled Girl Guide cookies in space!
GUSTO: [Gusto TV](https://gustotv.com/) is a Canadian food and lifestyle channel that serves up delicious programming with a dash of flair! From sizzling cooking competitions to heartwarming travel-meets-food adventures, Gusto is all about flavour, culture, and creativity. Whether you're watching chefs whip up gourmet dishes or exploring global cuisines from a Canadian lens, every show is packed with - you guessed it - gusto!
HEADS: The heads side of a Canadian coin features a portrait of the reigning monarch. For over 70 years, it was Queen Elizabeth II - making hers the longest reign ever depicted on Canadian currency. In 2023, Canada introduced new coins with King Charles III on the heads side, facing left, continuing the royal tradition of alternating profile directions with each new monarch!
HEART: Happy Valentines Day from Canuckle! ❤️ Revered in Canada as the father of biomedical engineering, John Hopps made many contributions to the field of medicine, but he is best known for the invention that keeps hundreds of thousands of hearts beating around the world: the cardiac pacemaker. In 1984, the device that Hopps invented was used to prolong his own life.
HEIST: Over the course of several months in 2011 and 2012, a team of thieves stole approximately 2,700 tonnes of maple syrup from a strategic maple syrup reserve maintained in Quebec. The theft has been popularly dubbed as the [Great Canadian Maple Syrup Heist](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/great-canadian-maple-syrup-heist). At the time of the heist, the stolen maple syrup was valued at nearly $18 million. The heist may be one of the largest thefts in Canadian history.
HERON: Great blue herons are Canada's most widespread heron and are found from the Maritimes to British Columbia. As the largest heron in North America, the great blue heron stands about one metre tall.
HERTZ: Measured in hertz, radio waves power the sounds and signals that surround us – and Canadian inventor Reginald Fessenden helped make it all possible. Born in Quebec, Fessenden was a true pioneer of wireless communication. In 1906, he made history by broadcasting the first voice and music over radio waves, sending “O Holy Night” across the air. His groundbreaking work paved the way for radio, television, and the technology that connects us today. He also laid the groundwork for AM radio, sonar, and even early radar – innovations that still echo through modern communication.
HIDES: On May 15, we mark [Moose Hide Campaign Day](https://moosehidecampaign.ca/), a national day of action for the Indigenous-led grassroots movement to engage men and boys in ending violence towards women and children. The Moose Hide Campaign began with a small patch of moose hide, worn as a symbol of commitment to safety and healing. Today, millions across Canada wear these hides to stand up against gender-based violence. To support them in igniting powerful change, please consider [donating to the Moose Hide Campaign](https://moosehidecampaign.ca/donate/) today.
HIPPO: The [house hippo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TijcoS8qHIE) is the subject of a Canadian television public service announcement (PSA) produced by Concerned Children's Advertisers in 1999. The fake infomercial about the fictional critters was created in order to raise awareness about the importance of media literacy. It was produced in the style of [Hinterland Who's Who](https://www.hww.ca/), the Canadian educational series that ran in the 1960s and 1970s. Two decades later, Ottawa-based not-for-profit [MediaSmarts](https://mediasmarts.ca/) brought back the house hippo in a [new commerical](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5R_tOSRynZU) as part of a media literacy campaign called [Break the Fake](https://mediasmarts.ca/break-fake). Real or not, the house hippo will always be a nostalgic piece of Canadiana.
HIVES: Beekeeping is buzzing across Canada, with more than 800,000 honeybee hives managed nationwide. These hives not only produce millions of kilograms of honey each year, but also play a vital role in pollinating crops from blueberries in Nova Scotia to canola in the Prairies. In Ottawa, [Gees Bees Honey Company](https://www.geesbees.ca/) has created a buzz by bringing beekeeping into the city, setting up hives in urban spaces and teaching people about the importance of pollinators. Whether in city backyards or rural farms, Canada’s hives help keep our food system sweet and thriving.
HOARY: It's Groundhog Day! Each year on February 2, Canadians watch eagerly as the groundhog emerges to predict whether winter will linger or spring will arrive early. Famous prognosticators like Wiarton Willie in Ontario and Fred la marmotte in Val‑d’Espoir, Quebec, help mark the occasion, while Canada is also home to the hoary marmot, a frosty, winter-loving relative. Like groundhogs, hoary marmots spend much of winter asleep, only to waken and enjoy the first hints of spring. From playful festivals to ancient folklore, Groundhog Day reminds us that even small creatures can give big signs about the seasons!
HOBBY: Hobby farms have become increasingly popular in Canada, especially among those looking to escape the hustle and bustle of city life. A hobby farm in Canada typically consists of a small acreage of land, usually between 5-10 acres, and is used to grow crops, raise animals, and/or provide a rural lifestyle. Other common activities on a hobby farm in Canada include beekeeping, keeping horses, and maintaining an orchard.
HOIST: Today is [National Flag Day](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/national-flag-canada-day.html)! When it comes to flags, the hoist is the part of the flag closest to the flagpole. On February 15, 1965, the new National Flag of Canada was officially hoisted for the first time on Parliament Hill. As the flag was raised, it symbolized a new chapter in Canada's history. With its bold red and white maple leaf design, the flag quickly became a unifying symbol of national pride. As we celebrate 60 years of this iconic emblem, Canadians continue to hoist their flag high with pride from coast to coast to coast.
HOMER: Today marks the start of the Major League Baseball Postseason! [Sam Bat](https://canada.sambat.com/), officially The Original Maple Bat Corporation, is a Canadian company based in the town of Carleton Place, Ontario that manufactures baseball bats. It was the first company to supply baseball bats manufactured from maple wood to professional baseball players. Loved by baseball players at all levels worldwide, the legendary Sam Bat was used by Barry Bonds to to break the world record for both most homers in a season and a career. The records continued with Miguel Cabrera using a Sam Bat to win the Triple Crown in 2012, and Giancarlo Stanton using a Sam Bat to win the 2016 Home Run Derby.
HONEY: Canadian honey is recognized around the world for its high quality. Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta produce 80% of Canada's honey crop. Canada is the world's sixth largest producer of honey. The average honey yield per hive in Canada is twice the world's average due to our long and warm summer days and a vast supply of nectar producing crops!
HOOPS: Invented by Canadian James Naismith in 1891 while he was teaching at the YMCA in Springfield, Massachusetts, basketball is now one of the most popular sports in the world. The first game used a soccer ball and peach baskets as hoops, which gave the sport its name. Basketball was born!
HORNS: The [Great Horned Owl](https://www.hww.ca/en/wildlife/birds/great-horned-owl.html) is one of Canada’s commonest large birds of prey. This nocturnal predator ranges through all urban and rural wooded areas of Canada. The majestic owl is named after its iconic “horns” that are actually bunches of feathers and is the provincial bird of Alberta. Voted upon in 1977 by children in the province, the Great Horned Owl represents Alberta’s impressive biodiversity!
HOTEL: There are many iconic hotels in Canada known for their history, their cultural significance, and their incredible architecture, including the Banff Springs Hotel, Château Frontenac, Château Laurier, Château Lake Louise, and the Empress Hotel, but there is only one hotel in Canada that is made entirely of snow and ice. The "[Hôtel de Glace](https://www.valcartier.com/en/lodging/hotel-de-glace-ice-hotel/)" (Ice Hotel) in Saint-Gabriel-de-Valcartier, Quebec is the oldest ice hotel in North America. Located just a short drive from Quebec City, this architectural marvel is a wonder to behold. Guests can explore the grand hall, an ice slide, a chapel, and a bar, where all furniture is made of ice and drinks are served in ice glasses.
HOUND: In Sault Ste. Marie, the [Soo Greyhounds](https://chl.ca/ohl-greyhounds/) are a junior hockey powerhouse with deep roots and loyal fans. They’ve won three OHL championships and the 1993 Memorial Cup, and even helped launch Wayne Gretzky’s career – he played his first season of major junior hockey there at just 16. The Greyhounds continue to be a symbol of hockey passion in northern Ontario.
HOUSE: The House of Commons of Canada is a democratically elected body whose members are known as members of Parliament (MPs). It is the lower house of the Parliament of Canada (the Senate is the upper house) and provides a link between Canadians and their Parliament. Many laws in Canada first begin as bills in the House of Commons.
HOWDY: At the 1988 Calgary Winter Olympics, friendly polar bear twins Hidy and Howdy welcomed fans with big smiles and western greetings, and they’re still fondly remembered in Canada today. Nearly 40 years later, as the [2026 Winter Olympics](https://www.olympics.com/en/milano-cortina-2026) kick off in Milano Cortina on February 6, those cheerful mascots remind us how fun and festive the Olympic spirit can be – and that every Games starts with a warm “hello,” no matter the country.
HUMAN: The [Canadian Museum for Human Rights](https://humanrights.ca/) in the city of Winnipeg, Manitoba is first museum in the world dedicated exclusively to human rights. The museum is adjacent to The Forks and is located on Indigenous ancestral lands on Treaty One Territory. The purpose of the museum is to "explore the subject of human rights with a special but not exclusive reference to Canada, to enhance the public's understanding of human rights, to promote respect for others and to encourage reflection and dialogue."
HUNTS: [National Hunting, Trapping, and Fishing Heritage Day](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/annualstatutes/2014_26/FullText.html) is celebrated on September 21, 2024, across Canada! This special day recognizes the long-standing traditions of hunting, trapping, and fishing, which have been integral to Canada’s cultural and economic history, especially for Indigenous communities and early settlers. Whether hunting for sport or sustenance, these activities remain a significant part of life in many parts of the country.
HYDRA: Hydra was a crucial and secure radio communications link in Canada during the Second World War. Part of [Camp X](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/camp-x) (a training school for covert agents and a radio communications centre that operated on the shores of Lake Ontario between Whitby and Oshawa), Hydra sent and received Allied radio (including telegraph) signals from around the world. Hydra was the most sophisticated telecommunications centre of its time and was instrumental in coding/decoding information vital to the allied war effort.
ICING: Happy National Donut Day! Canada is so sweet, it has two National Donut Days each year: the summer edition in June and another sweet treat on November 5th. Donuts, often topped with delicious layers of icing, are a beloved snack enjoyed coast to coast. Whether at a local bakery or shared with family and friends, these sugary delights help mark the day. So, on this second National Donut Day, don't forget to indulge in your favourite iced donut. Cheers to celebrating Canada's donut love, twice a year!
IDIOM: An idiom is a phrase whose meaning isn’t obvious from the words themselves. Canada has plenty of its own: you might hear someone say “Give’r” to mean “go for it,” “double-double” for a coffee with two creams and two sugars, “snowbirds” for Canadians who head south in the winter, or the classic “Eh?” at the end of a sentence to check for agreement. These colourful expressions show how Canadians have turned everyday language into something uniquely their own, full of humour, culture, and local flavour.
IGLOO: Igloo comes from the Inkuktitut word “iglu” meaning house.
INLET: The west coast of Canada is one of the major fjord coastlines of the world, hosting about 150 inlets. The remote and rugged coastline of British Columbia is indented with stunning inlets that cut deep into the Coast Mountains of the BC mainland north of Vancouver. Inlets can be found across the country from coast to coast to coast!
ISLES: Happy St. Patrick's Day from O'Canuckle! Canada is home to many isles with strong Irish heritage! Newfoundland is often called "the most Irish place outside of Ireland," with its distinct dialect, music, and place names reflecting its strong ties to the Emerald Isle. Prince Edward Island and Cape Breton Island also saw Irish settlers shape their communities, contributing to lively traditions of storytelling, music, and St. Patrick's Day celebrations. From coast to coast, Canadians proudly honour their Irish heritage - Sláinte!
IVORY: International Inuit Day on November 7 celebrates the rich cultural heritage of Inuit communities across Canada's Arctic, including their incredible craftsmanship. Among their many innovations, Inuit carvers have long used natural materials like ivory to craft intricate art pieces and practical tools. Traditional Inuit snow goggles (Inuktitut: ilgaak or iggaak), often made from ivory or bone, were designed with narrow slits to protect against the bright Arctic sun reflecting off the snow - an innovative design to prevent snow blindness.
JAZZY: Canada is home to numerous jazz festivals each year, including the [Festival International de Jazz de Montréal](https://www.montrealjazzfest.com/) (FIJM) which attracts over 2 million visitors annually and is recognized by Guinness World Records as the largest jazz festival on the planet. A number of Canadian jazz artists have achieved international prominence, including Oscar Peterson, Maynard Ferguson, Gil Evans, and Diana Krall.
JEANS: The all-denim look, affectionately known as the Canadian tuxedo, has become a classic style statement! It all started in 1951 when American singer Bing Crosby was denied entry to a Vancouver hotel for wearing head-to-toe denim. Levi's heard about it and made him a custom denim tuxedo jacket to go with his denim jeans - and the rest is fashion history! Whether you wear your jeans dressed up or dressed down, they'll always have a place in Canadian style lore.
JETTY: In Canada, jetties are a common sight along the coastlines, providing protection for harbours and enhancing the beauty of waterfront areas. One notable example is the [Chambly Jetty](https://parks.canada.ca/lhn-nhs/qc/chambly/culture/architecture/jetee-federal-wharf) in Quebec, which stretches into the Richelieu River. This historic jetty was originally built to help guide boats and protect the harbour from strong currents. Today, it's a popular spot for locals and visitors alike, offering scenic views and a glimpse into Canada's maritime heritage.
JEWEL: Looking for the biggest jewel in Canada? The town of Black Diamond, Alberta, is home to the world's largest black diamond! This striking monument was unveiled during the town's centennial Jubilee in 2007, paying homage to its namesake and rich coal mining history. Standing 1.22 metres wide and crafted from painted aluminum, the diamond is more than just a dazzling sight - it symbolizes the resilience and ingenuity of the community that once thrived on coal mining. On January 1, 2023, Black Diamond took on a new chapter in its history by amalgamating with its neighbour, Turner Valley, to form the town of Diamond Valley. Today, Diamond Valley is celebrated not only for its jewel, but also for its vibrant arts scene and stunning foothills views, making it a true gem of Alberta!
JOLLY: Toronto mother Susan Olivia Poole was an Indigenous Canadian inventor who invented the Jolly Jumper after her first child was born in 1910. In 1948 they were produced for the retail market, and by 1957, the Jolly Jumper was patented.
JUICE: Canada is a nation that loves its juice – from classic apple and orange varieties to tart cranberry and sweet grape juice. Canadian farmers produce millions of litres of fruit juice each year, and juice has long been a staple at breakfasts, school lunches, and summer picnics across the country. Whether freshly pressed or store-bought, it’s a tasty reminder of Canada’s rich fruit-growing regions.
KARMA: Karma is the idea that what you put into the world comes back to you – a philosophy that inspired [Farming Karma](https://www.farmingkarma.ca/), a family-run Canadian beverage company based in Kelowna, British Columbia. Founded by Karma and Kuku Gill, longtime Okanagan orchardists, the brand grew out of decades of BC fruit farming and a desire to turn homegrown apples and cherries into better-for-you sodas. Today, Farming Karma products are made with real fruit from the family’s orchards and enjoyed across Canada, carrying a simple message at its core: good fruit, good people, and good karma.
KITTY: During the Klondike Gold Rush, Kathleen "Klondike Kate" Rockwell, affectionately known as "Kitty," became one of the Yukon's most celebrated entertainers. Drawn by tales of fortune, Kitty arrived in Dawson City in 1900 and quickly found fame as a dancer. She dazzled packed saloons with her vaudeville routines, including her signature "Flame Dance," which transformed her red sequined dress and flowing chiffon into a fiery spectacle. A symbol of resilience and charm, Kitty brought joy and excitement to the often grueling lives of miners who had flocked to the north in search of gold. Kitty's name remains synonymous with the Klondike spirit, capturing the allure and larger-than-life characters that defined one of Canada's most legendary eras.
KNOLL: Knolls are found throughout Canada, and the term generally refers to small, rounded hills or mounds that often create scenic viewpoints or unique natural features in the landscape. Knolls are a common geographical feature, especially in hilly or mountainous regions, and are present in various places across the country. High Knoll in Minnekhada Regional Park near Coquitlam, British Columbia, is a popular hiking destination with impressive views. Additionally, knoll-like formations appear in areas across Alberta and Ontario, adding character to the natural landscape and offering vantage points in parks and along hiking trails. Knolls can also be found in more northern areas of Canada where glacial activity historically shaped the terrain, leaving behind knolls, drumlins, and other geological features.
LABEL: More than ever, Canadians are looking to the label to guide their choices. Amid rising trade tensions and growing national pride, more shoppers are seeking out goods labelled “Made in Canada” and “Product of Canada.” A recent survey found that 84% of Canadians check labels to see where items are made, and 77% say they’ll choose Canadian – even if it costs more. That little label is a symbol of pride, connecting Canadians to the people and places behind every product.
LABOUR: In Canada, Labour Day is celebrated on the first Monday of September to honour the contributions of workers and the labour movement. The holiday dates back to 1894, when Canada became one of the first countries to make Labour Day a national holiday after workers rallied for shorter workdays and safer conditions. And yes, we always spell it with an “OU”—because it wouldn’t be truly Canadian labour without it, eh?
LAKES: Canada has more lakes than the rest of the world combined! Almost 9% of Canada's total surface area is covered by freshwater.
LANCE: One of the most prominent symbols of Canada is the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) "Mountie," wearing their red serge uniform and brown Stetson. Put many of these Mounties on black horses, have them perform intricate formations in front of a crowd, and you have another of Canada's most recognizable icons: the [RCMP Musical Ride](https://rcmp.ca/en/corporate-information/musical-ride). The riders carry lances, while the Officer in Charge carries a sword. "The Charge" is one of the final and the most powerful manoeuvres performed by the RCMP Musical Ride. The finely trained horses are lined up and held in position by their riders until the rider lowers the lance and bellows "Charge!" and the horses and riders thunder forward in battle cry of times past.
LANES: Did you know that 5-pin bowling was invented in 1909 by Canadian Thomas F. Ryan in Toronto? Bowling alleys have a rich history in Canada. Hamilton's [Skyway Bowl](https://www.skywaybowl.com/) is home to City 10-pin - the oldest bowling league on the planet that has been rolling for over 120 years! Since opening in 1930, [Commodore Lanes & Billiards](https://www.commodorelanes.ca/) in Vancouver is one of Canada's oldest surviving recreation centres. [Steelheads and Strikes](https://www.steelheadsandstrikes.com/) in Arnprior is the oldest, continually operating bowling alley in the country, with the original lanes dating back to the 1930 as well. If you can spare some time to play, go hit the lanes and give bowling a try...it may be right up your alley!
LAPEL: On November 11, Canadians commemorate Remembrance Day by wearing a red poppy on their lapels to honour military personnel who served and sacrificed in conflicts. The poppy is worn on the left side, close to the heart, symbolizing respect and remembrance. Inspired by the iconic World War I poem "In Flanders Fields" by Lieutenant Colonel John McCrae, this tradition of wearing poppies began in 1921, and the phrase "lest we forget" serves as a powerful reminder of the importance of remembering those who served Canada. This simple yet significant act of wearing a poppy reminds us all of the courage and sacrifice of past generations and honours their memory with deep reverence.
LARGE: With a landmass of almost 10 million square kilometres, Canada is the second-largest country in the world.
LAYER: Nanaimo Bars are a Canadian dessert staple originating in Nanaimo, a city on Vancouver Island in British Columbia. It consists of three layers: a graham wafer crumb and shredded coconut base, a custard-flavoured butter icing filling, and a chocolate ganache topping. The Nanaimo bar was popularized nationwide after being highlighted as a classic Canadian dessert at Expo 86. In 2006, the Nanaimo bar was declared Canada’s favourite confection by a reader’s poll in the National Post.
LEAFS: One of the NHL's founding teams, the Toronto Maple Leafs have won 13 Stanley Cups, the most recent being in 1967.
LEMON: One of the greatest mysteries of the Canadian Rockies is the legend of the so-called “Lost Lemon Mine.” The Lost Lemon Mine is a legendary gold deposit reputedly somewhere between the Crowsnest Pass and the Highwood River in southwestern Alberta, discovered about 1870 by prospectors Frank Lemon and "Blackjack." Thousands have since searched for the fabulous lode; many have died mysteriously. Check out Craig Baird's [Canadian History Ehx podcast](https://canadaehx.com/2023/06/02/the-lost-lemon-mine/) to learn more!
LEVEE: Happy New Year from Canuckle! In Canada, the word "levee" has a unique historical and cultural significance! Originating from the French word "lever," meaning "to rise," a levee is a New Year's Day reception traditionally hosted by the Governor General, Lieutenant Governors, military establishments, and municipalities. This custom dates back to the 17th century, introduced by French colonial governors. Today, it is a cherished Canadian tradition where citizens gather to exchange New Year's greetings, enjoy refreshments, and celebrate community spirit.
LIGHT: With the world's longest coastline and more than half the earth's area covered in lakes, Canada is home to more than 750 lighthouses. Lighthouses across Canada have long symbolized strength, safety and safe harbour. The first lighthouse in Canada was built in Louisbourg on Cape Breton Island, Nova Scotia, in 1734. Did you know that every lighthouse has a distinctive flash pattern?
LIMIT: Did you know that in Canada, even your change has a limit? Under the [Currency Act](https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/c-52/page-1.html), there are caps on how much you can use in coins for one purchase: up to $25 in loonies, $40 in toonies, $10 in dimes, $10 in quarters, and just $5 in nickels. These limits exist to stop “coin overload” at the counter – so while a store can accept more, they don’t have to once those limits are reached. So next time, leave the big bag of loonies and toonies at home!
LINES: Canadian engineer John D. Millar devised what now seems a straightforward manner of helping drivers to share the road - painting lines to divide lanes and to separate traffic moving in opposite directions. Millar was working for the Ontario Department of Transport when he came up with the idea in 1930. A stretch of highway between Quebec and Ontario was the first to receive the treatment. Millar’s idea soon received wide acceptance - within a few years, white painted lines were standard not only on highways in Ontario but all across North America, and accident rates dropped significantly. Yellow, dashed, and double lines followed as ways of providing additional information to drivers.
LINGO: Before Canuckle brought daily word fun to Canadians, there was Lingo – the classic word game show that combined luck, logic, and quick thinking! Produced in Vancouver and originally airing in the late 1980s, Lingo featured contestants guessing five-letter words to fill a bingo-style grid, with each correct guess bringing them closer to a winning line. A Canadian version later aired in the late 1990s, hosted by Paul Houde, introducing a new generation to the fun of wordplay. Decades later, Canadians are still hooked on guessing words – proving that a love for lingo never goes out of style!
LIONS: The [Canadian Football League](https://www.cfl.ca/) season is underway! The [BC Lions](https://www.bclions.com/) are a professional Canadian football team based in Vancouver, British Columbia. The Lions played their first season in 1954, and have played every season since, making them the oldest professional sports franchise in British Columbia. They have appeared in the league's Grey Cup championship game 10 times, winning six, with their most recent championship occurring in 2011. The team is named for the Lions, a pair of mountain peaks overlooking the team's home city of Vancouver.
LLAMA: Did you know that llamas are not only found in South America but also have a growing presence in Canada? Llamas have been introduced to Canadian farms and are primarily used for their wool, as pack animals, and in eco-friendly agricultural practices. These gentle and intelligent creatures are well-suited to the Canadian climate and can be found on farms across the country, particularly in British Columbia and Ontario. Additionally, llamas have become popular attractions at petting zoos and educational farms, where visitors can learn about their unique characteristics and benefits.
LOBBY: In Canada, the art of lobbying has a long history – dating back to the days when political leaders would meet with key figures in government corridors to sway decisions. Today, lobbying is a crucial part of Canadian politics, with professional lobbyists working to represent everything from environmental causes to business interests. The Centre Block of Parliament Hill, with its grand lobbies, is where many of these important discussions still take place, shaping laws and policies that impact the nation.
LOCAL: According to a new report by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, over nine in ten Canadians (92%) said they love having small businesses in their community, but only 13% do most of their shopping locally. Small businesses are the cornerstones of our communities and foster a strong sense of community. We encourage Canadians to prioritize shopping local not just during the holiday season, but all year long! #ShopLocal
LOCKS: With so many canals and waterways across the country, Canada is home to numerous locks to help watercraft navigate all the different levels of water. The Rideau Canal Locks in Ottawa are the oldest continuously operating canal system in North America. In use since 1832, these locks are still operated by hand today.
LODGE: A beaver home is called a lodge. Beavers live in wetland habitats along lakes and rivers and are some of the best architects in the wild. Some even call them the original Canadian lumberjacks!
LOONIE: The loonie, Canada’s one-dollar coin, made its debut in 1987. Featuring the iconic common loon, it quickly picked up its feathery nickname and became a symbol of Canadian currency. Introduced to replace the paper dollar bill, it saved the government millions in printing costs and even inspired a giant roadside attraction—the “Big Loonie” monument in Echo Bay, Ontario. Today, the loonie is more than just spare change—it’s a true piece of Canadian identity.
LOONS: Loons have beautiful, crimson red eyes, but this is only during mating season.
LOVER: Lover's Arch is located at Hopewell Rocks Provincial Park on the coast of the Bay of Fundy in New Brunswick, and it is said that the two opposing rocks that make up the formation resemble two people kissing. The arch has a span of 30 feet and a height of about 18 feet. Access by foot is only possible two hours either side of low tide, but you can paddle through it during high tide!
LOWER: The Province of Lower Canada was a British colony on the lower Saint Lawrence River and the shores of the Gulf of Saint Lawrence (1791-1841). It covered the southern portion of the current Province of Quebec and the Labrador region of the current Province of Newfoundland and Labrador.
LUMEN: [Winterlude](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/winterlude.html) is underway in Ottawa and Gatineau, and this year's festivities feature [Lumen Eira](https://limbicmedia.ca/projects/lumen-eira-night-walk/) - a mesmorizing illumination experience animating Confederation Park. This dazzling display blends light and sound, transforming the park into a winter wonderland after dark. Trees glow and pulse with colours synchronized to custom soundscapes, inspired by nature and imagination. Let the interplay of light, sound, and winter's magic draw you into a world where reality is suspended, and imagination takes centre stage!
LUNAR: Happy Lunar New Year! The Lunar New Year is an event celebrated by millions of people across the world on the first new moon of their calendar. It marks the beginning of the new year based on the lunar calendar or lunisolar calendar. It is one of the largest celebrations for Canada's Chinese population, and it is also celebrated by Canadians from Vietnam, Korea and Southeast Asia, among others.
LUNCH: The [Cuban Lunch](https://cubanlunch.ca/) bar was a chocolate bar originally produced in Winnipeg by the Paulin Chambers Company factory for over 100 years. In 1991, the factory closed and production of the iconic Canadian treat ceased. A couple from Camrose, Alberta revived the popular peanut-and-chocolate candy in 2018. Crystal Regehr Westergard, along with her husband Bert, started the comeback venture as a way to cheer up her 85-year-old mother by bringing her favourite candy to her nursing home. The term "Cuban lunch" came into use before WWI, during the Spanish-American War. A Cuban Lunch was a soldier's rectangular chocolate ration, and the slang term held on in common use.
LUNGS: Canada's boreal forest is referred to as the 'lungs of the Earth' as it is among the world's biggest producers of oxygen. The boreal forest stretches across the country, playing a crucial role in regulating the Earth's climate. Just like our lungs provide oxygen to our bodies, the boreal forest acts as a vital carbon sink, absorbing and storing large amounts of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. With its pristine lakes, dense forests, and wide-open spaces, the boreal forest is not only a treasure trove of biodiversity but also a symbol of Canada's natural beauty and environmental stewardship.
LYRIC: The [Lyric Theatre](https://lyrictheatre.ca/) is a performing arts theatre located in Swift Current, Saskatchewan. The building was declared a municipal heritage property in 2007. The theatre was originally built as a Vaudeville and silent film theatre with 400 seats. From 1918 to 1981, the theatre was operated as a movie theatre, but throughout its history has hosted a variety of events including orchestras, lectures, balls, church services, pet and poultry shows and dance classes, as well as serving as makeshift isolation quarters during the Spanish Flu epidemic of 1918.
MACRO: In economics, macro means looking at the big picture – growth, innovation, and how whole economies thrive. Canadian economist Peter Howitt shared the [2025 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/economic-sciences/2025/howitt/facts/) for groundbreaking research showing how new ideas drive long-term growth. His work in macroeconomics helped the world understand how innovation fuels prosperity – a truly big-picture contribution from a brilliant Canadian mind!
MAGIC: The [International Brotherhood of Magicians](https://www.magician.org/) (I.B.M.) is an organization for both professional and amateur close-up and stage magicians, with approximately 15,000 members worldwide. It was founded in Winnipeg, Manitoba in 1922, and is now the largest organization of magicians in the world. Winnipeg was also home to one of Canada's most famous magicians, Doug Henning, who had a storied career around the world. He retired in the mid-1980s, selling some of his most famous illusions to another famous magician, David Copperfield.
MAGMA: Did you know that Canada is home to several active and dormant volcanoes, where magma from deep within the Earth's crust occasionally makes its presence known? While Canada is not typically associated with volcanic activity, the country does have a number of volcanic regions, particularly in British Columbia and Yukon. Even though you may not see flowing lava or erupting volcanoes in Canada, the presence of magma beneath the surface is a fascinating reminder of the Earth's ever-changing landscape.
MAJOR: In the Canadian military, the role of Pipe Major holds significant importance. A Pipe Major is responsible for leading and coordinating the regimental bagpipe band, which plays a crucial role in ceremonial events and military parades. The Pipe Major is a respected and revered figure in the Canadian military, embodying the spirit and heritage of the regiment through the stirring melodies of the bagpipes.
MANGA: Manga, the Japanese style of comics and graphic novels, has a growing fanbase across Canada. Readers enjoy a wide range of genres, from action-packed adventures to heartwarming slice-of-life stories. Canadian artists are creating their own manga-inspired works, and conventions like Anime North and Ottawa Comiccon celebrate this art form, showing how Canada embraces global storytelling and visual creativity. Michael Nicoll Yahgulanaas, a Haida artist, has blended Indigenous storytelling with manga aesthetics, creating works like Red: A Haida Manga.
MANIA: Canada experienced "Trudeaumania" in the late 1960s and early 1970s, a wave of excitement sparked by Pierre Trudeau, the charismatic leader of the Liberal Party. With his progressive policies, youthful energy, and charm, Trudeau became a symbol of change and modernity during a transformative period in Canadian history. His rise to power as Prime Minister in 1968 captivated Canadians from coast to coast. "Trudeaumania" saw fans attending packed rallies, sporting Trudeau-inspired fashion, and collecting buttons and memorabilia. This phenomenon left a lasting impact on Canadian politics and culture, marking a unique and spirited chapter in the nation's political history.
MANIC: Quebec is home to [Manic‑5](https://www.hydroquebec.com/facility-tours/tours-general-public/daniel-johnson-manic-5-cote-nord.html), the world’s largest multiple‑arch‑and‑buttress dam, spanning the Manicouagan River. Since its completion in 1970, it has generated hydroelectric power for Quebec and beyond, making it a cornerstone of the province’s clean energy system. Now known as the Daniel‑Johnson Dam, the steady hum of this engineering marvel is a reminder of the massive, reliable infrastructure that keeps Canada running.
MAPLE: The maple leaf is one of the most recognizable symbols of Canada and is featured on the national flag.
MASKS: Today marks the start of the 2023-24 National Hockey League Season! The goaltender mask is now a mandatory piece of equipment, but that wasn't always the case. The first goaltender to wear a mask in any level of organized ice hockey was Elizabeth Graham of Queen’s University in 1927 who wore a fencing mask. The first NHL goalie to wear a mask full-time was Jacques Plante of the Montreal Canadiens. During the 1959 season, Plante wore a face-hugging fibreglass mask created by Bill Burchmore, a children’s hockey coach and Canadiens fan who worked at Fiberglas Canada in Montreal. Goalie masks have certainly come a long way since then!
MASON: June 26th was coined National Canoe Day by [The Canadian Canoe Museum](https://canoemuseum.ca/) following a CBC campaign that, in 2007, declared the canoe one of the Seven Wonders of Canada. The canoe has long been an important symbol of Canada’s Indigenous peoples and their cultures. Used as the principal means of water transportation, Indigenous peoples have been making dugout and birchbark canoes for centuries. Bill Mason was a Canadian naturalist, author, artist, filmmaker, and conservationist, noted primarily for his popular canoeing books, films, and art as well as his documentaries on wolves. Mason once said: "I have always believed that the Canadian wooden canoe is one of the greatest achievements of mankind. There is nothing that is so aesthetically pleasing and yet so functional and versatile as the canoe. It is as much a part of our land as the rocks and trees and lakes and rivers." Bill Mason’s 16 foot red Prospector canoe is on display at The Canadian Canoe Museum in Peterborough, Ontario.
MEDAL: Feb 18 marks the start of the [2023 Canada Winter Games](https://www.canadagames.ca/previous-games/pei-2023) in Prince Edward Island! Over 2,500 young athletes will be competing for hard-earned medals. Canadian athletes have won numerous medals on the world stage, and Canada has won at least one medal at every Olympics in which it has competed. Canada has won 551 Olympic medals in total (326 Summer, 225 Winter). Go Canada Go!
MEDIA: Today is Bell Let's Talk Day - a campaign started by Bell Canada/Bell Media in an effort to raise awareness and combat stigma surrounding mental illness in Canada. Bell Let's Talk has a vision of a Canada where everyone can get the mental health support they need. On January 25 and every day throughout the year, we can all take meaningful action to create positive change.
MELEE: In hockey, a melee breaks out when tempers flare and players pile into a full-on scrum! Canadian fans know the thrill of a bench-clearing brawl, where sticks fly and penalty boxes fill. One of the wildest moments came in 2004, when the Ottawa Senators and Philadelphia Flyers combined for an NHL-record 419 penalty minutes after multiple fights erupted late in the game. Whether it’s a heated rivalry or playoff tension, few things capture the chaos and passion of the game like a classic Canadian hockey melee!
MELON: The Montreal melon, also known as the Montreal market muskmelon or the Montreal nutmeg melon, is a variety of melon recently rediscovered and cultivated in Montreal, Quebec. It was originally widely grown between the St. Lawrence River and Mount Royal, on the Montreal Plain. In its prime from the late 19th century until World War II, it was one of the most popular varieties of melon on the east coast of North America.
METRE: Canada officially uses the metric system of measurement, and metre is the standard spelling of the metric unit for length.
METRO: Metro systems help move millions of Canadians every day, with rapid transit networks operating in cities like Toronto, Montréal, Vancouver, and Edmonton. [Canada’s first true metro](https://www.stm.info/en/info/networks/metro) opened in Montréal in 1966, designed with rubber-tired trains to allow for quieter rides and steeper grades. Even during heavy snowfall, these systems are built to keep commuters moving and cities connected year-round.
MEZZO: In celebration of World Opera Day on October 25th, let's shine a spotlight on some of Canada's incredible mezzo-soprano talents! Mezzo-sopranos sing in the vocal range between soprano and contralto, often playing some of the most dynamic characters in opera. Wallis Giunta, an award-winning Canadian mezzo-soprano, has wowed audiences internationally with her performances. Another iconic Canadian mezzo is Catherine Robbin, whose illustrious career has been celebrated around the world. Canada's opera scene continues to thrive, with these talented voices leading the way on the global stage. Learn more about the Canadian Opera Company at [coc.ca](https://www.coc.ca/).
MISTY: Niagara Falls is a misty wonder on both sides of the border! While the Maid of the Mist is a historic boat tour in the United States, Canada’s [Niagara City Cruises](https://www.cityexperiences.com/niagara-ca/city-cruises/niagara/) lets visitors experience the spray up close and feel the power of this natural marvel. This iconic ride has thrilled generations, offering an unforgettable view of one of Canada’s most famous landmarks. It’s a truly misty adventure you won’t forget!
MOCHA: Happy National Coffee Day! A caffè mocha is a chocolatey twist on a latte – made with espresso, steamed milk, and chocolate. It’s also known as a Mocaccino or Mochaccino, and Canadian coffee shops like Second Cup Café serve their own take on this sweet favourite. Canadians are passionate about their coffee, with 71% drinking it regularly – more than tap water! Whether you enjoy it hot or iced, a mocha is a perfect way to celebrate the day with a cozy Canadian cup.
MODAL: Modal is a soft, breathable fabric made from beech-tree pulp, prized for its comfort, flexibility, and durability. In Canada, Montreal-based company [Manmade](https://manmadebrand.com/) uses modal to make everyday essentials like boxer briefs and t-shirts, combining comfort with thoughtful design. Their innovative approach even earned them a deal on Dragon’s Den, helping the company grow into a true Canadian success story and proving that smart ideas and quality materials can take Canadian brands to the next level.
MODEL: [Little Canada](https://little-canada.ca/) is an incredible attraction in Toronto that features highly detailed 1:87 scale models of Canadian cities and landmarks! The brainchild of Dutch-Canadian Jean-Louis Brenninkmeijer, this miniature wonderland inspired by his love of model trains showcases the beauty and diversity of Canada in a unique and captivating way. The skilled model makers at Little Canada have meticulously recreated iconic Canadian sites such as Niagara Falls, the Parliament Buildings in Ottawa, and the Toronto skyline, down to the smallest detail. Visitors can marvel at the intricate craftsmanship and feel a sense of national pride as they explore these miniaturized versions of beloved Canadian locations. Little Canada offers a magical journey through the country, celebrating its rich heritage and stunning landscapes in a truly extraordinary way.
MOIST: [Moist](https://moistonline.com/) is a Canadian rock band that formed in 1992. They released three studio albums in the 1990s, becoming a staple of Canadian rock music. The band, led by frontman David Usher, became a staple of the Canadian alternative rock scene in the 1990s. Moist has been nominated for ten Juno Awards, winning two, including Best New Group at the 1995 Juno Awards.
MONEY: People from around the world refer to Canadian Money as "rainbow money" or "Monopoly money" thanks to its bright colours and unique artwork.
MOTOR: Happy Father's Day from Canuckle! The 2023 Formula 1 Canadian Grand Prix is on today in Montréal! The F1 Canadian Grand Prix (F1 Grand Prix du Canada) is an annual motor racing event that has been held in Montréal since 1978. Circuit Gilles-Villeneuve, the track on which the motor race is run, is located on Île Notre-Dame at Parc Jean-Drapeau, right in the heart of the majestic Saint Lawrence River. The event is synonymous with festivities and the start of Montréal's summer season. Start your engines!
MOUND: The Kay-Nah-Chi-Wah-Nung Historical Centre, or Manitou Mounds, is Canada's premier concentration of ancient burial mounds. Manitou Mounds National Historic Site, as it was once called, is a vast network of 30 village sites and 15 ancient burial mounds constructed from approximately 5000 BP during the Archaic Period, to 360 BP. It is one of the "most significant centres of early habitation and ceremonial burial in Canada."
MOUSE: Toopy and Binoo is an animated series based on the popular French Canadian book series created by Dominique Jolin that features Toopy the mouse and his best friend Binoo the cat. A total of 175 episodes were produced overall. The show has been broadcast in over 179 countries and dubbed into 30 languages, and a film adaptation was released on August 11, 2023 in theatres across Canada.
MUNCH: One of Canada's most nostalgic snack brands has made a triumphant return, 20 years after disappearing from shelves. Munchies, the Hostess chips beloved by those who grew up in the '80s and '90s, are back, along with their iconic characters - Red, Yellow, and Orange. Canadians are sure to be munching on these tasty treats once again, savouring the familiar crunch and a taste of the past!
NAKED: Did you know Canada is home to some famous nude beaches, like Vancouver's [Wreck Beach](https://visit.ubc.ca/see-and-do/gardens-and-nature/wreck-beach/), one of the largest in North America? Not only do Canadians have a reputation for embracing natural beauty, but we’ve also got "naked" talent in our music scene! From the bold and fearless rocker [Bif Naked](https://herroyalmajestys.com/bif-naked/), to the fun and quirky [Barenaked Ladies](https://www.barenakedladies.com/), Canadian culture has a knack for celebrating individuality. So whether you're enjoying nature or jamming out, there's always a place for "naked" fun in Canada!
NATAL: In Nova Scotia, Natal Day is celebrated on the first Monday in August and marks the "birth" of the Halifax–Dartmouth area. The name comes from the Latin natalis, meaning birth – fitting for a holiday that honours the founding of Halifax in 1749 and the growth of neighbouring communities. First celebrated in 1895, Natal Day has grown into a beloved long weekend tradition filled with parades, fireworks, concerts, and one of Canada’s oldest road races. It’s a joyful celebration of Nova Scotia’s history and coastal spirit!
NICKEL: Canada has a long history with nickel, so much so that our five-cent coin earned its name from the metal! The town of Sudbury, Ontario became one of the world’s leading sources of nickel after a massive deposit was discovered in the late 1800s—thanks to a meteor strike over 1.8 billion years ago! To celebrate this mining heritage, Sudbury is home to the [Big Nickel](https://www.sciencenorth.ca/dynamic-earth), a 9-metre-tall replica of a 1951 Canadian nickel. It’s one of Canada’s most iconic roadside attractions!
NIGHT: Hockey Night in Canada (HNIC) is a weekly Saturday night broadcast of NHL games. It has been a staple in Canadian homes since the first radio broadcast in 1931. HNIC began airing on Saturday nights on CBC Television in 1952. It is Canada’s longest-running television program and the Guinness World Record holder as the longest-running TV sports program. Instant replay even made its world debut on a 1955 Hockey Night in Canada broadcast.
NINJA: The [Canadian Ninja League](https://www.canadianninjaleague.org/) is a competition that features obstacle courses inspired by the popular television show American Ninja Warrior(™). Across Canada, Ninja gyms host regional competitions through-out the year where participants compete in various stages of challenging obstacles to demonstrate their speed, strength, and agility. The [Canadian Ninja League National Finals](https://www.canadianninjaleague.org/2023-national-finals) are in Edmonton Nov 24-26, 2023!
NITRO: In the iconic [Heritage Minute about the Canadian Pacific Railway](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EE3ISzalVuo), titled 'Nitro,' a young Chinese railway worker bravely risks his life to set a dangerous nitroglycerine charge, helping carve a path through the rugged Canadian Rockies in the 1880s. His actions are a powerful symbol of the perilous work undertaken by thousands of Chinese labourers who played a vital role in building Canada's first transcontinental railway. Between 1880 and 1885, over 15,000 Chinese workers toiled under hazardous conditions, constructing some of the most challenging sections of the railway in British Columbia.
NOISE: Happy National Acadian Day! Tintamarre is an Acadian tradition of marching through one's community making noise with improvised instruments and other noisemakers. The term originates from the Acadian French word meaning "clangour" or "din" meaning noise. The practice is intended to demonstrate the vitality and solidarity of Acadian society, and to express their pride in their Acadian heritage.
NOSED: The Eastern hog-nosed snake is a fascinating creature that gets its name from the distinct upturned scale on the tip of its snout. While Canada doesn't have cobras, this unique snake can mimic one by flattening its head into a dramatic, cobra-like hood to ward off threats. Found in Southern Ontario, south of the Canadian Shield, the Eastern hog-nosed snake is a master of disguise and one of Canada's most intriguing reptiles.
NOVEL: Canadian authors have given the world some outstanding must read novels, including "The Handmaid's Tale" by Margaret Atwood, "The Book of Negroes" by Lawrence Hill, "Indian Horse" by Richard Wagamese, "Anne of Green Gables" by Lucy Maud Montgomery, "Life of Pi" by Yann Martel, and "Five Little Indians" by Michelle Good, just to name a few. Canadian literature has certainly made its mark!
NURSE: Happy [National Nursing Week](https://www.cna-aiic.ca/en/news-events/national-nursing-week)! Annual celebrations take place in Canada from the Monday to the Sunday of the same week as Florence Nightingale’s birthday on May 12. The week draws attention to nurses, increasing the awareness of the many contributions of nursing to the well-being of Canadians. The first integrated nursing degree program in Canada was started at the University of Toronto in 1942. Today, Canada is one of the few countries in the world requiring a bachelor’s degree for entry to practice as a registered nurse (RN). In 2021, there were 312,382 RNs licensed to practise in Canada. Thank you to all the nurses for everything you do!
NYMPH: In Canada’s cold freshwater ecosystems, including trout streams in the Rockies, many insects such as mayflies and dragonflies spend the early part of their lives as aquatic nymphs. These underwater stages can last from months to years as they develop in rivers and lakes. Mayfly nymphs are especially important in the food chain, serving as a key food source for native trout and other freshwater fish across Canada.
OCEAN: With marine waters spanning its west, north, and east coasts, Canada is an ocean nation. Canadians are influenced in many ways by the Pacific, Arctic, and Atlantic Oceans. Celebrate World Oceans Day on June 8th!
ODEON: [Cineplex Odeon](https://www.cineplex.com/) is one of Canada’s most iconic movie theatre chains, known for bringing the big-screen experience to audiences from coast to coast. Cineplex began in 1979 at Toronto’s Eaton Centre, while Odeon Theatres had been operating in Canada since the 1940s. The two merged in 1984 to form Cineplex Odeon, where Canadians have enjoyed everything from Hollywood hits to homegrown productions ever since.
ONION: The onion is Canada's most important condiment crop. It is a biennial, herbaceous plant of the Amaryllidaceae family. In 2022, the annual Canadian production of dry onions was over 287,000 metric tons, worth approximately $157.2 million. Dry onions are mainly produced in Quebec (46%), Ontario (37%) and Alberta (10%). There is even a species of onion called the Canada onion (Allium canadense) that is native to eastern North America.
OPERA: World Opera Day is celebrated each year October 25th. It raises awareness for the positive impact and value of opera for society. Throughout the 20th century, great operatic singers have populated Canada’s cultural landscape - from Raoul Jobin, Portia White, Maureen Forrester and Jon Vickers to Gerald Finley, Rihab Chaieb, Rebecca Cuddy and Measha Brueggergosman. Over the years, opera singers from Canada have made Canadians proud on stages around the world! Learn more about the Canadian Opera Company at [coc.ca](https://www.coc.ca/).
OPTIC: Fibre-optic cables carry data as pulses of light, letting information travel vast distances at incredible speeds. In Canada, optic-based networks expand internet access to rural, remote, and northern communities, connecting them to essential services. As more fibre reaches farther corners of the country, optical technology continues to play a quiet but powerful role in helping Canadians stay connected, no matter where they live.
ORBIT: The Manitoba government launched the Orbit program in 1965, which saw unique fibreglass sphere trashcans placed along the province's highways in an effort to reduce the amount of litter. The program lasted roughly till the 1990s across Manitoba highways.
ORDER: The Order of Canada is how our country honours people who make extraordinary contributions to the nation.
OVENS: [Ovens Natural Park](https://www.ovenspark.com/) is a privately owned 180-acre pristine reserve of coastal forest, located on the Atlantic coast of Nova Scotia, along the scenic Lighthouse Route near Lunenburg. For hundreds of years, people have been drawn to the incredible beauty, diverse geography, fascinating history, and spiritual solace that make The Ovens Natural Park so unique. Every year, thousands of park visitors hike the spectacular trails along the cliffs to view the famous sea caves, or "Ovens" for which the park was named.
