OZONE: September 16 is [World Ozone Day](https://www.un.org/en/observances/ozone-day)! Canada is known for its commitment to environmental conservation, including efforts to protect the ozone layer through initiatives such as the [Montreal Protocol](https://www.canada.ca/en/environment-climate-change/corporate/international-affairs/partnerships-organizations/ozone-layer-depletion-montreal-convention.html). The Montreal Protocol has succeeded in halting the damage to the ozone layer and is helping the world in the battle against climate change. In Canada and around the world, the Montreal Protocol regulates the production and consumption of numerous substances that deplete the ozone layer, the Earth’s atmospheric shield that prevents UV radiation from harming humans and other forms of life. It is considered one of the most successful, global environmental agreements of all time.
PAGES: In Canada’s House of Commons, pages are post-secondary students selected from across the country through the [Page Program](https://www.ourcommons.ca/about/pageprogram/index-e.html) to support the daily work of Parliament. Dressed in traditional uniforms, they assist Members of Parliament by delivering documents, carrying messages, and helping proceedings run smoothly during debates and Question Period. The role is highly competitive and offers a unique behind-the-scenes look at Canada’s democratic process.
PAINT: Norman Breakey from Toronto created the first paint roller in 1939. Unfortunately, he didn't patent the innovation and knock-offs quickly emerged. He may not get the credit he deserves, but Norman's invention has aided generations of painters. Next time you are painting a wall or ceiling, take a moment to remember Canadian Norman Breakey!
PAIRS: Canadian pair skaters Deanna Stellato-Dudek and Maxime Deschamps made history at the 2024 World Figure Skating Championships in Montreal by clinching the gold medal in the pairs event. Their exceptional performance captivated audiences and judges alike, earning them top marks and solidifying their status as world champions. Notably, Stellato-Dudek, at 40, became the oldest woman to win a figure skating world title in any discipline, breaking a record set over a century ago. Their victory marked the first world title for a Canadian pair since 2016, highlighting their remarkable skill, grace, and athleticism on the ice.
PAPAL: The word papal refers to the pope, the leader of the Catholic Church. Following the recent passing of Pope Francis, many Canadians are reflecting on his 2022 papal visit to Canada – a "pilgrimage of penance" during which he delivered a historic apology for the Catholic Church's role in residential schools. His words at Maskwacîs, Alberta marked a significant moment in the ongoing journey of truth and reconciliation with Indigenous Peoples.
PAPER: Charles Fenerty was a Canadian inventor who invented the wood pulp process for papermaking, which was first adapted into the production of newsprint and later the modern paper we use today. Fenerty was born in Sackville, Nova Scotia and was also a well-known poet of his time, publishing more than 35 (known) poems.
PARKA: Originally created by the Inuit to keep warm in the Canadian Arctic, the first parkas were made from whale, seal or caribou skin and often coated with fish oil for waterproofing.
PARRY: In fencing, a parry is a defensive move used to block an opponent’s attack – an essential skill in a sport where speed and precision are everything. In Canada, fencing has been gaining momentum on the world stage, highlighted by [Eleanor Harvey](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/eleanor-harvey/)'s historic bronze medal in women’s foil at the Paris 2024 Olympics, marking the country’s first-ever Olympic podium in the sport.
PASTA: Kraft Dinner Macaroni & Cheese pasta, aka "KD", is the classic Canadian comfort food. Canada buys over 1.7 million boxes of KD each week, which is approximately 24% of what the company produces globally. On average, every Canadian eats more than three boxes of KD per year! KD is the most popular grocery item in Canada, and some consider it to be Canada’s true national dish.
PASTE: In 1884, Canadian chemist and pharmacist Marcellus Gilmore Edson received a patent for the manufacture of a peanut paste, which he named “peanut-candy.” Edson's patent for peanut-candy has been recognized as a forerunner to the commercially available peanut butter or spread.
PEACH: Ontario produces 82% of Canada’s peaches and nectarines. Three of the biggest peach festivals in Canada all get underway in August: Ontario's Winona Peach Festival & [Niagara-on-the-Lake Peach Festival](https://www.niagaraonthelake.com/peachfestival2024) and British Columbia's [Penticton Peach Festival](https://peachfest.com/). Happy peach season!
PEAKS: Canada’s Yukon Territory is home to 8 of Canada’s tallest mountains, with Mount Logan topping them all at 5956m high. BC’s Snow Dome peak is a unique “three-ocean peak”, where if you poured a cup of water at the summit, the water could flow into the Pacific Ocean to the west, the Arctic Ocean to the north, or the Atlantic Ocean to the east.
PECAN: Pecans bring a rich, nutty flavour to Canadian holiday baking, starring in festive favourites like pecan pies, spiced cookies, and butter tarts. A staple on Christmas tables, these versatile nuts add warmth, crunch, and a touch of sweet tradition to seasonal celebrations across the country.
PEELS: Today is Curling Day in Canada! From coast to coast to coast, Canadians celebrate the strategy, skill, and teamwork that make curling so special. One of the game’s most thrilling shots is the peel – a high-speed takeout designed to remove an opponent’s guard or stone, while sending the delivered stone out of play. Often used to clear the front of the house, the peel is essential for reducing your opponent’s scoring opportunities and shows off skill, timing, and strategy on the ice. Catch exciting shots and perfect peels at the 2026 Scotties in Mississauga, Ontario, as the best teams in Canada compete for the national women’s curling championship!
PEGGY: [Peggy’s Cove](https://novascotia.com/listing/peggys-cove-lighthouse-and-village/), a tiny fishing village in Nova Scotia, is home to one of the most photographed lighthouses in the world! Perched on wave-worn granite rocks, Peggy’s Point Lighthouse has been guiding sailors since 1915. While legends differ on who Peggy was – some say a shipwreck survivor, others a fisherman's wife – the name has become iconic in Canadian coastal lore.
PEONY: Peonies are a beloved flower in Canadian gardens, known for their vibrant blooms and resilience to our northern climate. The [Canadian Peony Society](https://peony.ca/), established in 1998, is dedicated to the cultivation and appreciation of these beautiful flowers. Peonies are often seen as a symbol of prosperity and good fortune in many cultures, and their lush blossoms make them a popular choice for Canadian gardens. With over 30 species of peonies found worldwide, they thrive in Canada's diverse climates from coast to coast!
PETAL: It's tulip time in Ottawa! Every May, over a million tulip petals pop open across the capital for the [Canadian Tulip Festival](https://tulipfestival.ca/) - a blooming beautiful tradition that started with a royal thank-you. Back in 1945, the Dutch royal family sent 100,000 tulip bulbs to Canada to show their gratitude for sheltering Princess Juliana and her daughters during World War II. To ensure Princess Margriet was born a Dutch citizen, the maternity ward at the Ottawa Civic Hospital was temporarily declared international territory. That act of kindness planted the seeds of a friendship that still blossoms today - one tulip petal at a time!
PETTY: Petty Harbour-Maddox Cove is a picturesque fishing village located on the eastern shore of Newfoundland and Labrador, just south of St. John's. This charming community is known for its colourful row houses, stunning coastal views, and rich maritime history. Petty Harbour is not only a haven for fishermen but also a popular spot for tourists seeking to experience Newfoundland's natural beauty and vibrant culture. The village has been featured in various films and television shows, showcasing its stunning landscapes and traditional fishing practices.
PHONE: In 1876, Scottish-born inventor Alexander Graham Bell patented the first practical telephone, a concept that he conceived in Brantford, Ontario.
PIECE: Towering over the Guinness-certified World’s Largest Chess Set in Medicine Hat, Alberta between the library and the Court of King’s Bench is what could be the [World’s Largest Chess Piece](https://chatnewstoday.ca/2021/11/10/checkmate-royal-addition-to-downtown-medicine-hat-could-be-a-record-setter/). Installed in 2021, the king piece stands 20 feet, 11 inches (6.37m) tall and is 9 feet, 3 inches (2.81m) at the base. The current record-holding piece is in St. Louis, standing 20 feet (6.09m) tall and 9 feet, 2 inches (2.79m) at the base. The Medicine Hat Chess Club will be in contact with Guinness World Records to see if there’s a new king in town.
PIERS: Canada’s coastlines are dotted with iconic piers that connect communities to the water. In British Columbia, White Rock is home to [Canada’s longest pier](https://www.whiterockcity.ca/401/Pier-Promenade), stretching an impressive 470 metres into Semiahmoo Bay and offering stunning ocean views year-round. On the opposite coast, Halifax’s [Pier 21](https://pier21.ca/) stands as a National Historic Site and once welcomed nearly one million immigrants to Canada between 1928 and 1971. Together, these piers reflect the country’s deep maritime heritage from sea to sea.
PIGGY: Did you know that before being surpassed in 2015, Canada was home to the biggest piggy bank in the world? This unique attraction in Coleman, Alberta is located in Flumerfelt Park and was created to celebrate thrift and community pride. Nicknamed "Ten Ton Toots," the piggy bank is actually a repurposed locomotive, now featuring a coin slot where visitors can deposit their change. Though not a traditional pig shape, its size and uniqueness make it a memorable Canadian roadside attraction​. Next time you're in the Crowsnest Pass, stop by and "bank" a memory with this Canadian icon!
PIKES: The Glacier Pikes are twin-peaked lava domes rising to about 2,145 metres in Garibaldi Provincial Park, British Columbia. Perched at the southern end of the Sentinel Glacier Neve, they offer stunning views and rugged scrambling for adventurers. First summited in 1911 by members of the British Columbia Mountaineering Club, the Pikes stand as a dramatic landmark in the Coast Mountains.
PILOT: One of Canada's most famous pilots, Billy Bishop was a Canadian flying ace of the First World War. He was officially credited with 72 victories, making him the top Canadian and British Empire ace of the war. The Billy Bishop Toronto City Airport was named in his honour. Today would have been Billy Bishop's 129th birthday!
PINES: Merry Christmas from Canuckle! The Scotch pine reigns as the top Christmas tree in Canada. Scotch pines hardly shed any of their long needles, and their strong, curved branches also hold ornaments well. Canada exported over 2.4 million fresh Christmas trees to countries all over the world in 2021! Pines are the also the arboreal emblem of the provinces of Alberta (Lodgepole pine) and Ontario (Eastern white pine).
PINTO: The Town of Bow Island, Alberta is well known for the dry edible bean industry. An 18 foot high statue of the mascot, "[Pinto MacBean](https://www.bowisland.com/pinto-macbean)" is located adjacent to Highway No. 3 and greets everyone coming into town. Designed by Jane Osborne and unveiled to the public in 1992, Pinto MacBean was created to promote tourism and signifies the importance of the dry edible bean industry to the area.
PINTS: On October 9th, Canadians across the country raise their glasses to celebrate [Canadian Beer Day](https://canadianbeerday.ca/), a day dedicated to the craft, culture, and community that beer fosters from coast to coast. With over 85% of the beer consumed in Canada brewed locally, our pints tell a story of connection, pride, and homegrown flavour. Whether you're enjoying a cold one at a local brewery or sharing a laugh over a pint with friends, Canadian beer brings us together. Cheers to community and great Canadian beer!
PIPER: Rowdy Roddy Piper was one of Canada’s most iconic professional wrestlers. Born in Saskatchewan, he became a global superstar known for his sharp wit, fearless persona, and unforgettable catchphrases. Piper famously entered the ring wearing his signature kilt, accompanied by bagpipe music, a nod to his Scottish heritage. He was inducted into the WWE Hall of Fame in 2005 and remains a legend of sports entertainment.
PIPES: Canada has a long tradition of bagpipe music, especially in communities with strong Scottish roots. Pipe bands are a familiar sight at parades, ceremonies, and Highland games across the country. The [Glengarry Highland Games](https://www.glengarryhighlandgames.com/) in Maxville, Ontario, are one of the largest gatherings of their kind in North America, hosting competitions in piping, drumming, Highland dancing, and heavy athletics. From coast to coast, Canadian pipers help keep this centuries-old musical tradition alive and thriving.
PISTE: In modern [fencing](https://www.fencing.ca), the "piste" is the narrow strip on which fencers duel, and Canadian athletes have shown remarkable prowess on it! At the 2024 Paris Olympics, [Eleanor Harvey](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/eleanor-harvey/) made history by winning a bronze medal in women’s individual foil, marking the first fencing medal ever for Canada in this elegant sport!
PITCH: As the 2022 FIFA Men's World Cup wraps up in Qatar, we are reflecting on the time that the Canada Men's National Soccer team spent on the pitch proudly representing our country. After Canada's 36-year-long wait to return to the men's FIFA World Cup, they inspired fans from coast to coast to coast with their performance. The Canada Women's National Soccer team's success on the pitch includes 3 straight Olympic medals, including gold in 2020! They'll be competing in the [2023 FIFA Women's World Cup](https://www.fifa.com/fifaplus/en/tournaments/womens/womensworldcup/australia-new-zealand2023) in Australia and New Zealand so get ready to cheer them on! #WeCAN
PIVOT: Burdett, Alberta is home to the first pivot irrigation system in Canada. The first water drive pivot irrigation system was introduced to Canada by Donald and Wyman Campbell, who moved to the area from Nebraska during 1962. The system was in operation by May 1962 and was used continuously for 25 years.
PLACE: Located in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada Place is Canada's busiest harbour. Canada Place is the main cruise ship terminal for the region. To mark Expo 86, Canada Place was officially opened as the Canada Pavilion by HRH Prince Charles, Diana, Princess of Wales and former Prime Minister Brian Mulroney. The land that Canada Place is built upon was known as Pier B-C and served as the western terminus for Canadian Pacific Railway's transcontinental railroad.
PLANE: Aviation is an integral part of the Canadian economy. In 2018, the air transport industry, including airlines, and its supply chain, supported over $50 billion of GDP in Canada.
PLANT: The [Bruce Nuclear Generating Station](https://www.brucepower.com/) is a nuclear power plant located on the eastern shore of Lake Huron in Ontario. With eight CANDU pressurized heavy-water reactors, it is the largest operating nuclear power plant in the world! The plant is the largest employer in Bruce County, with over 4000 workers.
PLAYS: Today marks the start of the Stratford Festival's 2024 season! The [Stratford Festival](https://www.stratfordfestival.ca/), located in Stratford, Ontario, is North America's largest classical repertory theatre company. Each season, numerous productions take to the stage, with special emphasis on the plays of Shakespeare. The 2024 Stratford Festival lineup includes 12 plays and runs from April to October.
PLUNGE: Canadians are famous for plunging into the New Year with polar plunges held in icy waters across the country. From lakes to oceans, these frosty traditions combine community spirit, charitable causes, and a fearless embrace of winter – a very Canadian way to kick off January.
POINT: Point Pelee is the southernmost point of mainland Canada, and is an important rest stop for migrating birds. [Point Pelee National Park](https://parks.canada.ca/pn-np/on/pelee) is Canada's second smallest but most ecologically diverse national park, and is home to more than 390 bird species and 70 species of trees, some of which are species at risk.
POLAR: Canada is home to about 16,000 polar bears, which is approximately two-thirds of the world's total estimated population.
POPPY: From the last Friday in October to Remembrance Day, millions of Canadians wear a poppy as a visual pledge to never forget those who sacrificed for our freedom.
POSSE: The Las Vegas Posse were a [Canadian Football League](https://www.cfl.ca/) (CFL) team, that played at the Sam Boyd Silver Bowl in Las Vegas, Nevada, United States, in the league's 1994 season as part of the CFL's American expansion. The team folded after only one season, proving that whatever happens in Vegas doesn't always stay in Vegas.
POUND: Lobster season has officially started in Canada in Quebec and the Atlantic provinces. Canada currently supplies more than half of the world’s supply of “hard-shelled” Atlantic Lobster, considered one of the world’s premier seafood. A lobster pound is where live lobsters are held until they are harvested and sold, like at [Halls Harbour Lobster Pound](https://hallsharbourlobster.com/) in Nova Scotia and [Lobster on the Wharf](https://www.lobsteronthewharf.com/) in PEI, known as MacKinnon's Lobster Pound to locals.
PRANK: April Fools' Day wouldn't be the same without a classic prank, and one of the most iconic prank devices, the whoopee cushion, was invented in Toronto in the 1930s! Created by the JEM Rubber Company, this cheeky contraption has been a prankster's favourite for nearly 100 years, delivering laughs and a few embarrassed giggles along the way. A simple but brilliant invention, the whoopee cushion proves that a well-placed prank never goes out of style!
PRINT: Happy Labour Day! Labour Day has been marked as a statutory public holiday in Canada on the first Monday in September since 1894. However, the origins of Labour Day in Canada can be traced back to numerous local demonstrations and celebrations in earlier decades. Such events assumed political significance in 1872, when an April labour demonstration in Toronto, in support of the printers of the Toronto Typographical Union on strike for a nine-hour day, led directly to the enactment of the Trade Unions Act, a law that confirmed the legality of unions. The Printers' Strike of 1872, part of the Nine Hour Movement, was a key moment in Canadian labour history and marked the start of a shorter workday.
PRISM: [Prism](https://prism.ca/) (styled as PRiSM) is a Canadian rock band formed in Vancouver in 1977. Their classic line-up consisted of lead singer Ron Tabak, guitarist Lindsay Mitchell, keyboardist John Hall, bassist Allen Harlow and drummer Rocket Norton. They have released a total of eight studio albums, three compilation albums and one live album and they won the Canadian music industry Juno Award for 'Group of the Year' in 1981. A pre-fame Bryan Adams contributed as a songwriter to several early Prism releases.
PROOF: Dr. Henri J. Breault, a career paediatrician from Windsor, Ontario, Canada famously invented the childproof safety cap. Breault is known for spearheading a national campaign to prevent accidental childhood poisonings. He advocated for the development of childproof containers with the Palm-N-Turn, a safety cap that drastically reduced child deaths due to poisoning in Canada and around the world.
PUCKS: According to legend, the first hockey pucks used in early outdoor hockey games were pieces of frozen cow dung. Other early versions were made out of wood cut from the branches of trees. Sometimes even stones would suffice. Around 1875, rubber lacrosse balls were sliced in thirds and only the middle section was kept. Eventually, vulcanized rubber became the standard material used for hockey pucks.
PULSE: Pulses are nitrogen-fixing crops that improve the environmental sustainability of cropping systems. Canada is one of the largest pulse producers in the world and the largest exporter, with over 80% of pulses grown being shipped around the world. The four main types of pulses grown in Canada are dry peas, lentils, chickpeas and beans. Learn more at [pulsecanada.com](https://pulsecanada.com/)!
PUNCH: On 1 January 1849, engraver and cartoonist John H. Walker (1831–99) published Punch in Canada, named after the humour magazine in England begun in 1841. It was the first publication in Canada to regularly feature cartoons. Walker drew a full page cartoon for each biweekly issue. Punch in Canada folded after Walker moved it to Toronto in 1850 and tried to publish weekly.
PUPIL: The ophthalmoscope, a small hand-held telescope for looking through the pupil of the eye, allows doctors to see inside the eye and to examine the retina and optic nerve, which are extensions of the brain. In 1864, Toronto doctors pioneered retinal photography by connecting an ophthalmoscope to a camera to photograph the retina of a cat, a first step in photographing the inside of the living human eye and a technique that today is essential all over the world in evaluating and treating patients with eye diseases.
PURSE: Long before modern handbags, Indigenous artisans across Canada crafted beautiful and functional purses using materials from the land. Caribou hide was carefully prepared for durability and softness, then adorned with intricate glass beadwork introduced through early trade. These handmade purses were not only practical – they often carried deep cultural meaning, with patterns and colours reflecting identity, community, and tradition.
QUACK: Canada is a haven for duck lovers! Our country hosts over 11 duck species, and our vast network of wetlands, lakes, and marshes make it a prime stopover in the Mississippi and Atlantic Flyways, two major North American migration routes. Every spring and fall, you can witness flocks of mallards, wood ducks, and teal filling the skies and making quite the racket with their quacks.
QUAIL: Did you know that Canada is home to three fascinating types of quail: the California Quail, the Mountain Quail, and the Northern Bobwhite! These tiny birds bring big personality, whether it’s the California Quail’s fancy feather plume, the Mountain Quail’s love for sneaky hideouts, or the Northern Bobwhite’s cheerful “bob-WHITE!” call. From British Columbia’s grassy hills to Ontario’s fields, these quail are proof that even small birds can make a big impression. These small but mighty birds are a rare treat to see in the Canadian wild, so keep your binoculars handy next time you're exploring their habitats!
QUEEN: Queen Elizabeth II has been Canada's monarch for over 70 years.
QUERY: Before Google, Bing, or Yahoo, there was the Archie Query which launched in 1990 as the world's first internet search engine. Archie, referred to as the "electronic index to the Internet," was developed by Alan Emtage, a postgraduate student and systems administrator at McGill University's School of Computer Science in Montreal, Quebec. The name Archie came from archive, without the "v".
QUEST: At the top of the world in the Yukon and Alaska wilderness of northwestern North America, the [Yukon Quest](https://www.yukonquest.com/) 1,000 Mile International Sled Dog Race, an epic winter sports event takes place every year on the first Saturday of February. Covering 1,000 miles (1,600 km) between Whitehorse, Yukon and Fairbanks, Alaska during the depths of winter, the Yukon Quest is known for excellence in canine care and fostering the traditions of northern travel by dog sled. It has been run every year since 1984 over rough, sometimes hazardous terrain. The Yukon Quest Trail follows historical Gold Rush and mail delivery dog sled routes from the turn of the 20th Century.
QUIET: The Quiet Revolution ("Révolution tranquille" in French) refers to a significant period of socio-political and socio-cultural transformation in French Canada, particularly in Quebec, following the election of 1960. This vivid yet paradoxical description of the period was first used by an anonymous writer in The Globe and Mail. The Quiet Revolution is a major reference point used by successive Québec governments in power since the Liberal defeat in 1966.
QUILT: Quilts were extremely important to the early settlers of Canada, since they had no good way of heating or insulating their homes, especially at night. The first quilts arrived in Canada with immigrants to "New France" in the early 1600s. Today, the [Canadian Quilters' Association](https://canadianquilter.com/) celebrates quilting and Canadian quilters across the country.
QUOTA: Fishing quotas play an important role in managing Canada’s marine resources. In 1992, the federal government placed a major moratorium on the Atlantic cod fishery after decades of overfishing led to the collapse of cod stocks, dramatically impacting communities across Newfoundland and Labrador. Since then, strict quotas and management measures have been used to help protect remaining fish populations and support the long-term sustainability of Canada’s fisheries.
RABBI: Canada’s Jewish community has long been shaped by remarkable rabbis. In 1846, Rabbi Abraham de Sola became the first to settle permanently here, leading Montreal’s Spanish and Portuguese Synagogue and even preaching before Queen Victoria. In Ottawa, Rabbi Reuven Bulka built on that legacy – founding Kindness Week, now a national celebration of compassion passed into law in 2021. Today, rabbis across Canada continue to serve as spiritual leaders, educators, and advocates, helping to enrich the diverse fabric of Canadian life.
RADIO: Canadian inventor Reginald A. Fessenden is best known for his pioneering work developing radio technology, including the foundations of amplitude modulation (AM) radio. On 23 December 1900, he was the first person to send audio (wireless telephony) by means of electromagnetic waves, successfully transmitting speech by radio over a distance of about a 1.6 kilometres.
RAISE: Yesterday would have been Terry Fox's 65th birthday! Terry Fox is one of the most prominent figures in all of Canada. In 1977, 18-year-old Terry Fox was diagnosed with bone cancer and gave up his right leg to prevent the spread of the disease. The Canadian Cancer Society helped sponsor his run across Canada to raise funds and awareness for cancer research. The Marathon of Hope raised $24.2 million for cancer research and Terry became an inspiration to millions of people worldwide. To date, the [Terry Fox Foundation](https://terryfox.org/) has raised over 600 million dollars for cancer research.
RALLY: May 17 marks the [International Day Against Homophobia, Biphobia, and Transphobia](https://may17.org/). Canada has a rich history of rallies and protests, where citizens come together to advocate for change and raise awareness about important social and political issues. The 'We Demand' rally, which took place on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, Ontario on August 28, 1971, was the first large-scale LGBTQ2+ rally in Canadian history. The rally marked a pivotal moment in Canada's LGBTQ2+ rights movement. Today, rallies and protests remain an important part of Canada's democratic process, providing a platform for citizens to voice their concerns and hold their government accountable.
RAMEN: Did you know that ramen has found a special place in Canada’s diverse culinary landscape? While traditionally a Japanese dish, ramen shops have popped up across Canadian cities, from Vancouver to Toronto, with many chefs adding local twists. The first dedicated ramen shop in Canada opened in Vancouver in 1996, and since then, the dish has been embraced coast to coast. Whether it’s the cold winters that call for a warm, comforting bowl or the multicultural nature of the country, Canadians have welcomed ramen as part of their rich food scene!
RANGE: Canada is home to some incredible mountain ranges, including the famous Rocky Mountains. The Canadian Rockies house over 50 high mountains whose elevation exceeds the 11,000 ft (3,350 m) mark. The highest peak of this range of mountains is Mount Robson, which stands at 12,972 ft (3,954 m) above mean sea level.
RANTS: Canadians might be known for being polite, but we do love a good rant! Rick Mercer's iconic "Rick’s Rant" segments hilariously tackled politics and Canadian quirks from back alleys across the country. And who could forget the famous rant from the Molson Canadian commercial back in 2000, where Joe proudly declared "[I AM CANADIAN!](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WMxGVfk09lU)" Every good rant tells a story and carries a touch of Canadian pride.
RAVEN: The raven is of high importance to Indigenous Peoples throughout Canada, appearing in myths, legends, art and traditions. It is particularly important to Aboriginal people of the British Columbia coast, where it symbolizes creation, knowledge and prestige. The raven was adopted as the Yukon's official bird in 1985.
READS: [Canada Reads](https://www.cbc.ca/books/canadareads) is an annual "battle of the books" competition organized and broadcast by Canada's public broadcaster, the CBC. During Canada Reads, five Canadian personalities champion five different books, with each advocate extolling the merits of one of the titles. The Canada Reads 2023 winner was ["Ducks: Two Years in the Oil Sands"](https://www.cbc.ca/books/ducks-by-kate-beaton-1.6559688) by author Kate Beaton, championed by Jeopardy super-champion Mattea Roach.
REALM: Canada is unique among countries in that it borders three marine realms: the Arctic, Temperate Northern Atlantic, and Temperate Northern Pacific. These realms can be further subdivided into three marine biomes and fifteen marine ecoregions based upon biological distinctiveness.
REBEL: Today is Louis Riel Day - a day to reflect on [Louis Riel](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/louis-riel), and his important role for the advocacy of the Métis Nation and his help in building the Canada we know today. Louis Riel was a Canadian politician, a founder of the province of Manitoba, and a political leader of the Métis people. He led two resistance movements - the Red River Rebellion of 1869-70 and the North-West Rebellion of 1885 - against the Government of Canada and its first prime minister John A. Macdonald. Riel's historical reputation has long been polarized between portrayals as a dangerous religious fanatic and rebel opposed to the Canadian nation, and, by contrast, as a charismatic leader intent on defending his Métis people. November 16 is the anniversary of Riel's execution in 1885. In Manitoba, Louis Riel Day takes place on the third Monday of February and commemorates his life.
REEFS: Canada is home to rare glass sponge reefs off the coast of British Columbia, some of the only living reefs of their kind in the world. These ancient underwater structures can be thousands of years old and provide vital habitat for marine life, forming complex ecosystems in the deep, cold waters of the Pacific.
REELS: Today is [National Canadian Film Day](https://canfilmday.ca/)! Canada has a rich film history full of memorable stories and incredible talent - both in front of and behind the camera. Before digital editing, movies were physically cut and spliced on film reels, which became a lasting symbol of the film industry. Today, Canadian filmmakers continue to spin powerful stories on screens big and small. So grab some popcorn and press play on a Canadian classic to celebrate the creativity and talent of Canadian filmmakers!
REGAL: Tomorrow is Commonwealth Day! It is the annual celebration of the Commonwealth of Nations. We join our Commonwealth partners around the world to celebrate the shared values and the strong bonds of cooperation and friendship that bind us together. The Governor General of Canada is the federal viceregal representative of the Canadian monarch, currently King Charles III.
REIGN: The reign of Canada's new monarch, King Charles III, began when Queen Elizabeth II died on September 8. Queen Elizabeth II was Canada's monarch for over 70 years, making her the longest reigning monarch in Commonwealth history.
RELIC: Robert Allan Clothier was a Canadian stage and television actor most famous for his role as Relic on the CBC television series, The Beachcombers. He portrayed Bruno Gerussi's rival beachcomber, Relic - a curmudgeonly, conniving man of Welsh descent who lived on a house boat and used his jetboat to outrun and challenge Nick's claims to logs. After landing this memorable role, Clothier became a household face among viewers, as the show originally aired from 1972 to 1990, one of the longest running Canadian television dramas of all time.
REVEL: Each March 17, communities across Canada revel in the spirit of St. Patrick’s Day! From lively parades to seas of green, people across the country join in celebrating Irish heritage. In fact, Canada is home to one of the largest Irish diasporas outside Ireland, with millions of Canadians tracing at least some of their roots to the Emerald Isle.
REVUE: Revue has a rich history in Canada, both on stage and on screen! The theatrical revue - a variety show featuring music, dance, and comedy - has entertained Canadians for over a century. One of the most famous was Spring Thaw, a beloved comedy revue that ran from 1948 to 1971. Meanwhile, Toronto's [Revue Cinema](https://revuecinema.ca/) has been a film-lover's gem since 1912, making it one of Canada's oldest continuously operating movie theatres. Saved from closure by the community in 2006, the Revue continues to shine as a cherished landmark for cinephiles.
RIDER: [Canadian equestrian](https://equestrian.ca/) riders have shone brightly on the world stage in both dressage and eventing! [Ian Millar](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/ian-millar/), affectionately known as "Captain Canada," has competed in a record 10 Olympic Games, winning a team silver medal in show jumping at the 2008 Beijing Olympics. In dressage, Canada brought home a bronze medal in team dressage from the 1988 Seoul Olympics. Canada’s equestrian success continues to inspire and showcase the dedication and talent of its riders.
RIDGE: The Battle of Vimy Ridge, during the First World War, is Canada's most celebrated military victory – an often mythologized symbol of the birth of Canadian national pride and awareness.
RIVER: Annually, Canada’s Rivers discharge 7% of the world’s renewable water supply at a flow rate per second more than four times that of Niagara Falls.
ROADS: If you want to drive on a road in Canada, there is no better place than Saskatchewan. All in all, Saskatchewan consists of over 250,000 km of roads, the highest length of road surface compared to any other Canadian province. That is enough to circle the Earth's equator over 6 times! On top of being a landlocked province, a wide dispersion of population over a vast area has led to Saskatchewan having this record.
ROAST: Happy [Saint-Jean-Baptiste Day](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/celebrate-canada/saint-jean-baptiste-day.html)! On June 24, Francophones across the country show their pride on the National Day of Quebec by celebrating their language and their traditions. Canada boasts a rich culinary tradition of hearty roasts, including the iconic Quebecois dish known as Bouilli! Similar to the French pot-au-feu, Bouilli, which translates to 'boiled' in English, is a traditional Quebecois pot roast or stew made with beef and an assortment of root vegetables such as carrots, potatoes, and turnips. This comforting and flavourful dish is typically slow-cooked until the beef is tender and infused with the rich flavors of the vegetables and aromatic spices. Bouilli has deep roots in Quebecois cuisine and is often enjoyed as a warm and satisfying meal during the cold winter months.
ROCKS: Canada is home to some stunning rock formations, including New Brunswick's Hopewell Rocks, Ontario's Flowerpot Rocks, the Hoodoos found in Alberta's Badlands, Balancing Rock in Nova Scotia, and Rocher Percé (Pierced Rock) in Quebec.
ROCKY: The Rocky Mountains, also known as the Rockies, are the largest mountain system in North America!
ROLLS: On the East Coast of Canada, fresh lobster rolls are the epitome of local comfort food. With succulent chunks of fresh lobster meat, nestled in a buttery toasted bun, this iconic dish is a true delicacy that evokes the charm and flavour of the Atlantic shoreline. The classic East Coast lobster roll is a culinary masterpiece that captures the essence of coastal living.
ROOST: In Canada, chickens don’t just roost on farms - they help support a multi-billion-dollar industry! The country's poultry sector thrives under supply management, a system that balances production with demand to keep grocery shelves stocked with fresh, high-quality chicken. This approach supports thousands of jobs while maintaining strict food safety and animal welfare standards. From coast to coast, [Canadian chicken farmers](https://www.chickenfarmers.ca/) ensure there's always a perfect perch for poultry!
ROOTS: Roots Canada opened its first store in 1973 selling footwear, and started using the beaver logo in 1985 with the launch of their athletic brand.
ROSES: The Farine Five Roses sign is a feature of the Montreal skyline, first erected above the Ogilvie flour mill in 1948. The unmistakeable symbol is over 75 years old, making it older than the Canadian flag. Its shining neon lights, which overlook the Lachine Canal, call out to Montreal drivers and pedestrians and remind them that they are, in fact, home.
ROUGE: In the Canadian Football League (CFL), a rouge is a one-point score that is awarded for certain plays that involve the ball being kicked into the end zone. The rouge is uniquely Canadian!
ROUGH: The Canadian Football League (CFL) once had two teams with nearly identical names: the Ottawa Rough Riders and the Saskatchewan Roughriders. This led to some confusion among fans and broadcasters, especially during games between the two teams. In 1996, the Ottawa team folded, leaving Saskatchewan as the sole "Roughriders" in the CFL. The Ottawa franchise returned in 2002 as the Ottawa Renegades, and later became the Ottawa Redblacks in 2014. Despite the name changes, the legacy of the "Rough Riders" and "Roughriders" remains a unique chapter in Canadian football history.
ROUND: On National Donut Day, Canadians celebrate the sweet, round treat found in bakeries and coffee shops across the country. From classic glazed rings to filled and frosted varieties, donuts are a popular indulgence enjoyed with coffee or hot chocolate. Canada is also among the highest donut-consuming countries in the world, with Canadians enjoying roughly a billion donuts each year. Their familiar round shape is part of what makes them so iconic and instantly recognizable.
ROWAN: The rowan tree, also known as mountain ash, is one of Canada’s most widespread native trees, found from Newfoundland to British Columbia. In autumn, its bright red berry clusters become an important food source for migrating birds such as cedar waxwings, robins, and pine grosbeaks. In Atlantic Canada, Scottish settlers often planted rowans near their homes, carrying with them a Highland tradition that believed the trees brought protection and good fortune. The berries have also been used in Maritime kitchens for generations, turned into jams, jellies, and even rowan wine.
ROYAL: Canada is one of the oldest continuing monarchies in the world. The title “Royal” is a sign of honour and distinction, and the granting of this distinction is a prerogative of the Sovereign. In Canada, we have the Royal Canadian Navy, the Royal Canadian Air Force, the Royal Canadian Regiment in the Canadian Army, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Royal Canadian Legion, the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada, and the Royal Architectural Institute of Canada. In Canada's legislative process, a bill can only become law once it has received royal assent.
RUDDY: The Ruddy Duck is one of Canada’s smallest diving ducks, with a compact chestnut body, sky-blue bill, and stiff, upright tail. About 86% of its breeding population nests in wetlands and reservoirs of the prairie pothole region. Males are known for lively courtship displays, sometimes drumming the water with their bills to impress a mate!
RULER: Happy [Victoria Day](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/services/important-commemorative-days/victoria-day.html)! Celebrated on the last Monday before May 25, the day honours Queen Victoria, the longest-reigning monarch in British history at the time. Known as the 'Mother of Confederation,' her rule from 1837 to 1901 helped shape the modern Canadian nation. As Canada's first monarch after Confederation, her leadership paved the way for a future where Canada would become a self-governing dominion within the British Empire.
SABLE: [Sable Island](https://parks.canada.ca/pn-np/ns/sable), a remote sandbar about 300 km southeast of Halifax, is famous for its wild horses, which have roamed free for centuries! These resilient animals have adapted to the island's harsh conditions, grazing on its unusual vegetation. Sable Island is also known as the "Graveyard of the Atlantic," with over 350 recorded shipwrecks scattered along its shifting shores. Today, it is a protected National Park Reserve, with visitor access carefully managed by Parks Canada to help safeguard its delicate ecosystem. Even trees don't thrive here - except for a single Scots pine, planted in the 1960s, standing as the island's only tree!
SAFER: On May 17, we mark [International Day Against Homophobia, Transphobia and Biphobia](https://may17.org/), a global day dedicated to raising awareness of discrimination and promoting dignity, inclusion, and respect for 2SLGBTQIA+ communities. Across Canada, ongoing efforts in schools, workplaces, and public spaces focus on building safer environments where people can live openly and authentically, without fear of harassment or exclusion. The goal is simple but vital: safer communities where understanding, education, and respect help reduce harm and support everyone’s right to belong.
SALTY: Known as the "Dead Sea of Canada", the waters of Little Manitou Lake near Saskatoon are roughly five times saltier than the ocean - and approximately half as salty as the Dead Sea in Israel and Jordan. Fed by underground springs, the lake is so high in sodium, magnesium and potassium salts that it's almost impossible for swimmers to sink. Locals and visitors alike swear by Little Manitou Lake's ability to cure skin conditions, arthritis and joint pain, although the science on its healing powers is up for debate.
SAUNA: Sauna culture is picking up steam across Canada! While modern sauna houses and mobile units are rising in popularity for wellness and relaxation, heat-based traditions have deep roots here: Indigenous communities have long used sweat lodges for ceremony, healing and spiritual renewal. Today’s revival of sauna culture reflects both new trends and timeless practices that connect people through warmth, reflection and community.
SCION: In Canada, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau is often considered a scion - a descendant of a prominent family. His father, Pierre Elliott Trudeau, was one of Canada's most famous and influential prime ministers, serving for 15 years. Justin followed in his father's footsteps, becoming the second Trudeau to hold the country's highest office. November 4th marked the 9th anniversary of Justin Trudeau being sworn in as Canada's 23rd prime minister.
SEATS: Today is [Election Day](https://www.elections.ca/)! In Canada's 2025 federal election, the House of Commons expanded to 343 seats, reflecting the country's growing population. This change underscores the dynamic nature of Canada's democracy, ensuring that representation in Parliament keeps pace with demographic shifts. Each seat represents a unique riding, and the party that secures at least 172 seats forms a majority government. This adjustment emphasizes the importance of every vote, as even a single seat can influence the balance of power in Parliament.
SEDGE: In Canada, marshy areas known as sedges are important habitats for wildlife, especially for cranes! The term "sedge" not only refers to grassy wetlands but also to a group of cranes gathering in these lush areas. Canada is home to two species of cranes - the Sandhill Crane and the endangered Whooping Crane. Each fall, Sandhill Cranes flock to Canadian wetlands, where sedges provide the perfect mix of cover and food as they prepare for migration. These crane gatherings are a beautiful sight, showcasing how Canada’s diverse ecosystems support unique wildlife year-round.
SEEDS: Canada is the world's largest producer of mustard seed, most of it farmed in the southern prairie regions of Alberta and Saskatchewan. Canada is also the largest producer of flaxseed in the world, representing about 40% of world production.
SERGE: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police, or “Mounties,” are known for their iconic uniforms that feature the iconic scarlet tunic called a red serge.
SEWED: On [National Flag of Canada Day](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/national-flag-canada-day.html), we remember the woman who literally sewed Canada’s identity into history. In 1964, Ottawa civil servant Joan O’Malley stayed late into the night at her Singer sewing machine to sew the first Canadian flag, turning cloth and thread into a symbol that would unite a nation. Every stitch carried pride, purpose, and the promise of a flag that would fly over homes, schools, and Parliament – and, of course, soar above Canadian athletes at the Olympics!
SHAFT: Goderich, Ontario is home to the world's largest salt mine! Located beneath Lake Huron, the mine shaft is as deep as the height of the CN Tower. Operating since 1959, the rock salt produced at the Sifto Salt Mine is used to keep citizens in North America safe as they travel through winter snow and ice.
SHAKE: Did you know Canada has an island that literally shakes? Tremble Island, located in British Columbia’s Seymour Inlet, experiences a phenomenon where the ground quivers due to the power of the water currents surrounding it. This inlet has some of the fastest tidal surges in the world, and at peak tides, the force of the water is so intense that it causes the entire island to tremble! Visitors to Tremble Island are in for a unique (and slightly shaky) experience, showcasing the raw power of Canada’s incredible natural landscapes.
SHALE: The Burgess Shale is a fossil-bearing deposit exposed in the Canadian Rockies of British Columbia, Canada. Found in Canada's Yoho National Park, it is one of the most important fossil sites in the world! The rocks here preserve not only the usual hard shells of ancient organisms, but also soft skin and tissue, allowing for stunning impressions of the strange creatures of 500 million years ago!
SHAWL: Powwow dances are beautiful expressions of Indigenous spirituality, history and culture. There are a variety of regional dance styles performed by men, women and children across North America. Women were traditionally required to wear shawls as a sign of proper etiquette when in a dancing arena. The characteristic feature of the women's [Fancy Shawl Dance](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/powwow-dances#WomensFancyShawlDance) - the elaborate shawl - is uniquely decorated by the dancer with distinct ornaments, beadwork and fringes. Though diverse in terms of regalia, footwork and origin stories, powwow dances remain a testament to Indigenous history, heritage and identity.
SHELF: The [Scotian Shelf](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/scotian-shelf) is a geological formation, part of the Continental shelf, located southwest of Nova Scotia, Canada. It covers an area of 120,000 square kilometres, is 700 kilometres long and has an average depth of 90 metres. The Scotian Shelf contains the ecologically important Scotian Shelf Large Marine Ecosystem (LME) and the Scotian Shelf Waters (SSW).
SHELL: Happy Easter from Canuckle! The [Vegreville egg](https://www.vegreville.com/worlds-largest-pysanka) is a giant sculpture of a pysanka, a Ukrainian-style Easter egg, in the town of Vegreville, Alberta. Designed by Canadian artist Paul Maxym Sebaliu, the egg's shell is made up of an intricate set of two-dimensional anodized aluminum tiles in the shape of congruent equilateral triangles and star-shaped hexagons. The egg is 9 metres (31 feet) long and three and a half storeys high, weighing in at 2.5 tonnes (5,512 lb) making it the largest pysanka in the world! It was constructed in 1975 in honour of the early Ukrainian settlements east of Edmonton.
SHINE: During Canada’s Prohibition era in the early 1900s, some crafty Canadians made their own “moonshine” – illegally distilled liquor that often shone with a powerful kick! Hidden stills and daring rum-runners kept the trade alive until the ban ended in the 1930s. Today, Canada’s craft distilleries legally carry on that spirit of innovation, producing small-batch whiskies, vodkas, and gins that truly let Canadian craftsmanship shine.
SHINY: Big Shiny Tunes is a series of rock albums compiled and released by the Canadian music television station MuchMusic, and through MusiquePlus in Quebec, from 1996 to 2009. The best-selling album of the series was Big Shiny Tunes 2, which was certified Diamond in Canada (1,000,000 units). It has been cited as the best-selling album series in Canadian history, with 5 million albums sold in ten years.
SHIRT: Feb 22 is Anti-Bullying Day, also known as [Pink Shirt Day](https://www.pinkshirtday.ca/), where people wear a pink-coloured shirt to stand against bullying. The initiative was started in Canada in 2007 by two Nova Scotia teenagers when a fellow Grade 9 student in Berwick was being teased and bullied for wearing a pink shirt on the first day of school.
SHOVE: In bobsleigh, the race can be decided in the opening seconds – you might even say it’s when push comes to shove. [Canadian bobsleigh teams](https://olympic.ca/sports/bobsleigh/) have captured Olympic and World Championship medals by turning the shove into an art, sprinting alongside the sled to generate explosive speed before jumping in. That powerful push start is trained endlessly, because one great shove can launch a run all the way to the podium.
SIGNS: The [Neon Sign Museum](https://www.edmonton.ca/city_government/edmonton_archives/neon-sign-museum), the first of its kind in Canada, features a collection of functional historic signs that tell a story about Edmonton's neon past. The City of Edmonton has collected 20 neon signs, all of which have been restored and installed on the east wall of the Telus building and the south wall of the Mercer Warehouse building. The signs chosen are iconic and represent the commercial signage from Edmonton's history.
SIXTY: In Canada, the 60th parallel forms the southern mainland boundary of the northern territories of Yukon, Northwest Territories, and Nunavut. Accordingly, "North of 60" is an expression often used for the territories. There was even 1990s TV show on CBC called North of 60, a drama depicting life in the sub-Arctic northern boreal forest.
SKATING: In Ottawa, winter means skating on the [Rideau Canal](https://ncc-ccn.gc.ca/places/rideau-canal-skateway), officially recognized as the world’s largest skating rink! Stretching through the heart of the capital, this UNESCO World Heritage Site transforms into a frozen pathway each winter, inviting Canadians and visitors alike to glide past historic landmarks in a truly one-of-a-kind skating experience.
SKILL: [Skills Canada](https://www.skillscompetencescanada.com/) is a Canadian non-profit organization dedicated to the promotion of careers in technology and skilled trades. One of their major initiatives is the annual Skills Canada National Competition. This is an Olympic-style event in which competitors from across the country take part in various skilled trades and technology contests.
SKIRT: Ribbon skirts represent an important part of the identity and history of Indigenous women and girls. January 4th marked the first [National Ribbon Skirt Day in Canada](https://www.ctvnews.ca/canada/article/canada-marks-national-ribbon-skirt-day-inspired-by-10-year-old-saskatchewan-girl/). Every Jan 4 going forward will be a day where Indigenous women across the country are encouraged to wear ribbon skirts to celebrate their culture, their strength and their connection as women.
SLANG: Canada has some very unique slang words, sayings and phrases that make the Great White North a little bit different! Do you know how to speak Canadian? [Check out this video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=o34VzENNPic) to learn how! Don't be a hoser, eh?
SLATE: In Canada’s early one-room schoolhouses, students didn’t have notebooks or tablets – they used slates! These small, handheld chalkboards were a reusable and affordable way for kids to practise writing and arithmetic. With a slate pencil in hand, students could solve math problems, copy sentences, or spell out their lessons, then simply wipe it clean and start again. Slates were especially common in rural schools, where supplies were scarce and learning had to be practical. It’s a little piece of classroom history that helped shape generations of Canadian students!
SLEDS: “Toboggan” is from the Mi'kmaq word “tobakun,” which means sled. In fact, the Inuit made the first toboggans out of whale bone and used it to transport people and belongings across the snowy tundra. Guy Martin holds the world record for fastest speed on a gravity powered snow sled at over 134 km/h in 2014!
SLEET: Sleet is a familiar part of Canadian winters, forming when snowflakes melt into raindrops and then refreeze before hitting the ground. Canada experiences some of the widest temperature swings on Earth, which makes mixed precipitation like sleet especially common in late fall and early spring. In fact, parts of southern Canada can see all four types of precipitation – rain, snow, sleet, and freezing rain – within the same day!
SLEIGH: Sleighs have been a part of Canadian winters for centuries, helping people travel across snow-covered landscapes long before cars and snowmobiles. From sturdy horse-drawn sleighs to festive holiday sleighs, they capture the imagination and charm of the season. Today, sleigh rides remain a popular winter tradition in Canada, bringing families together to enjoy the crisp air, sparkling snow, and a little holiday magic.
SMACK: Did you know that a group of jellyfish is called a "smack"? In Canada, jellyfish can be found along the Atlantic, Pacific, and Arctic coasts. One of the most notable species is the Lion's Mane jellyfish, which is commonly seen in the colder waters off the coast of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. These jellyfish can have tentacles that extend over 30 metres, making them one of the largest jellyfish species in the world. Encountering a smack of jellyfish is a mesmerizing experience, showcasing the diversity of marine life in Canadian waters.
SMART: Canada is the most educated country globally, with over 56% of adults meeting the OECD criteria of residents aged 25 to 64 who have completed some form of tertiary education.
SMILE: Canadians have lots of reasons to smile! Canada is the 13th happiest country in the world out of 157 countries ranked according to the 2023 World Happiness Report. This week is [Smile Cookie](https://www.timhortons.ca/smile-cookie) week at Tim Hortons! From May 1st through May 7th, 100% of proceeds from every Smile Cookie support charities and community groups across Canada. The Smile Cookie campaign has raised over $92 million across North America since 1996 and last year, restaurant owners raised a record-breaking $15 million! Get your #SmileCookie this week and put a smile on someone's face!
SMOKE: Today is National Indigenous Peoples Day! Smoke is used in different ways by all three Indigenous groups in Canada. Whether it is to smoke fish and meat, to burn sage and tobacco or for sacred ceremonies or celebrations, it is a significant symbol in Indigenous culture.
SNAKE: Canada is home to the largest known congregations of snakes anywhere in the world. In spring and fall, over 50,000 red-sided gartersnakes congregate at hibernation sites in the Narcisse Wildlife Management Area in Manitoba.
SONGS: The [2024 Juno Awards](https://junoawards.ca/) are taking place in Halifax, Nova Scotia tonight to honour achievements in Canadian music in 2023. The ceremony will be hosted by Nelly Furtado. The Canadian Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences (CARAS) votes and awards outstanding Canadian artists for their top songs, videos, and albums released throughout the year.
SORRY: Canadians apologize so much, Canada passed the Apology Act in 2009.
SOUND: Clayoquot Sound, on the west coast of Vancouver Island in British Columbia, is a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve known for its stunning fjords, ancient temperate rainforests, and rich marine life. This protected area is home to whales, sea otters, and bears, and its waterways are popular for kayaking, sailing, and wildlife watching. Clayoquot Sound’s dramatic landscapes and thriving ecosystems make it one of Canada’s most spectacular coastal regions.
SPACE: Canada's contributions to space exploration include one of Canada’s most celebrated and iconic technological advances: The Canadarm - a remote-controlled robotic arm used to help build and maintain the International Space Station (ISS).
SPARK: Sparks is a [Girl Guides of Canada](https://www.girlguides.ca/) program is for five and six-year-old girls. Sparks were given their own branch in 1988, although they didn’t get their name until 1989. The program aims to spark curiosity, creativity, and confidence in young girls as they embark on their Girl Guides journey. A Spark is a reference to a Celtic Fairy spirit, which would be encountered in natural areas such as forests. The Sparks Promise is to share and be a friend.
SPAWN: Every fall, Canada's rivers and streams come alive with the incredible sight of salmon spawning! These resilient fish travel upstream, often covering hundreds of kilometres, to lay their eggs in the same waters where they were born. British Columbia's Fraser River is one of the most famous spawning grounds in the world, where millions of sockeye salmon return each year. This natural cycle is crucial to the ecosystem, supporting wildlife from eagles to bears. Watching the salmon spawn is a quintessential Canadian experience and a celebration of nature's perseverance!
SPEAK: Did you know that during the Prohibition era in the 1920s, Canada had its own network of secret bars called speakeasies? These hidden establishments provided Canadians with a place to enjoy alcoholic beverages despite the nationwide ban on alcohol. From Montreal to Vancouver, speakeasies popped up in basements, back rooms, and secret locations, often requiring a special password for entry. Today, the legacy of Canada's speakeasies lives on in the country's vibrant nightlife scene, with modern bars paying homage to this clandestine era through their decor, cocktails, and atmosphere.
SPEAR: Canada's easternmost point is found at Cape Spear, Newfoundland, near the province's capital of St. John's. The [Cape Spear Lighthouse National Historic Site](https://parks.canada.ca/lhn-nhs/nl/spear) is home to the oldest surviving lighthouse in Newfoundland and Labrador.
SPEED: In Canada's olympic history, its athletes have received a total medal count of 79 in speed skating making it Canada's most successful Olympic sport! Charles Hamelin (short track) and Cindy Klassen (long track) are Canada's most decorated winter olympians with 6 medals each.
SPICE: Emerging spice crops in Saskatchewan include coriander, caraway, dill, anise, and fenugreek, but mustard seed is the most important spice crop in Saskatchewan. Canada is the second largest producer in the world with over 200,000 tonnes per year, and the largest exporter with 160,000 tonnes per year. Saskatchewan produces 80–90% of the Canadian mustard seed and is known worldwide for the production of a high-quality product.
SPIEL: Curling season is in full swing in Canada, and that means spiels (short for bonspiels) are taking place in curling clubs across the country! The two biggest curling spiels in Canada take place in February and March: the [2023 Scotties Tournament of Hearts](https://www.curling.ca/2023scotties/) in Kamloops, BC and the [2023 Tim Hortons Brier](https://www.curling.ca/2023brier/) in London, Ontario.
SPIKE: The Last Spike was the final and ceremonial railway spike driven into the Canadian Pacific Railway (CPR) track by company director Donald Smith on the morning of 7 November 1885. Contemporaries and historians have viewed the Last Spike as a moment when national unity was realized.
SPINY: Canada's most unique terrestrial animal is probably not what you might think. A recent study published in the journal The [Canadian Field-Naturalist](https://www.canadianfieldnaturalist.ca/index.php/cfn/article/view/2673) has found the country's most evolutionarily distinct Canadian animal is the spiny softshell turtle! These turtles can be found in Ontario and Quebec, and are one of the largest freshwater turtle species in North America. But unfortunately, they have been listed as one of Canada's rarest species for over 20 years. If we let them disappear from Canada, we would lose almost 180 million years of unique evolutionary history. This shows how important it is to prioritize the conservation of this species and its unique legacy amongst Canadian wildlife.
SPIRE: Canada is home to stunning spires found both in cities and in nature. Architectural landmarks like the Peace Tower in Ottawa and the CN Tower in Toronto soar above city skylines, while the rugged Bugaboo Spire in British Columbia draws climbers worldwide with its dramatic alpine peak. From innovative structures and beautiful church towers to majestic mountain peaks, these spires showcase the remarkable blend of natural wonder and architectural brilliance that defines Canada’s landscape.
SPLIT: Split pea soup is an authentic French Canadian dish that is made with yellow peas, ham, and veggies. This traditional pea soup is the ultimate in Quebec-style comfort food. This early settler soup became a staple item on the menu for Quebec's settlers as it was a filling and nutritious meal that helped them survive harsh Canadian winters.
SPORT: Canada's official national sports are ice hockey (winter) and lacrosse (summer).
SPOTS: Spotted Lake (Lake Kliluk) in British Columbia’s Similkameen Valley is made up of hundreds of separate pools that contain some of the world’s highest concentrations of Epsom salts, calcium, sodium sulphates and magnesium sulphates. When the warm summer months roll in, much of the water evaporates, leaving behind concentrations of the minerals that form spots across the lake. The spots can change in size and colour from blue to green to yellow, as minerals within each spot alter with further evaporation. According to Destination Osoyoos, Spotted Lake is a sacred place of healing for the people of the Syilx Okanagan Nation.
SPRAY: In Canada’s backcountry, bear spray is a safety tool carried by hikers, campers, and outdoor workers in areas where bears may be present. When deployed, it releases a wide spray designed to deter close wildlife encounters and allow time to retreat safely. It has become a standard part of outdoor safety practices in many of Canada’s wilderness regions.
SQUAD: Cold Squad is a Canadian police television series that premiered on CTV on January 23, 1998, and ran for seven seasons. Known for its gripping stories and compelling characters, Cold Squad follows a team of homicide detectives from the Vancouver Police Department that reopen long-unsolved, or "cold" cases, using present-day forensic technology and psychological profiling to help crack them. Cold Squad was the first prime time national series produced out of Vancouver. With a total of 98 episodes, it became the longest-running prime time drama series on Canadian television and won several Gemini awards, Canada's highest television honours.
STACK: The Hopewell Rocks in New Brunswick (also known as flowerpots) are rock formations known as sea stacks caused by tidal erosion. They are located on the shores of the Bay of Fundy in [Hopewell Rocks Provincial Park](https://www.nbparks.ca/en/parks/33/hopewell-rocks-provincial-park) and come in an astounding variety of shapes and sizes. No Atlantic Canadian vacation is complete without experiencing these icons!
STALK: As Halloween approaches, corn stalks take centre stage in Canada, especially in the form of sprawling corn mazes! These mazes, crafted from towering stalks of corn, provide a fun challenge for families and friends seeking some spooky excitement. Many Canadian farms transform their fields into intricate designs, inviting visitors to get lost among the twisting paths. So, this Halloween, as you navigate through a corn maze, remember the importance of corn stalks in celebrating the harvest season in true Canadian style!
STAND: Happy Canada Day from Canuckle! Today we stand together to celebrate our country’s strength and spirit. The word stand is at the heart of our national pride - from the famous line ”We stand on guard for thee” in O Canada to the uplifting anthem ”A Place to Stand” written for Expo 67 celebrating Canada’s Centennial. That song’s message of growth and belonging perfectly matches the unity and joy we feel each July 1st as Canadians come together to honour our shared home. Here’s to standing tall, proud, and united - today and every day!
STATE: Canada's political system is based on that of the United Kingdom. It is a constitutional monarchy, which means that we recognize the Queen or King as the Head of State, while the Prime Minister is the Head of Government. Currently, His Majesty King Charles III is King of Canada and Canada's Head of State. He is the personal embodiment of the Crown in Canada. A state funeral for former Prime Minister Brian Mulroney is being held today in Montreal. Wayne Gretzky will be among the high-profile figures to eulogize the former PM. Mulroney passed away on Feb 29, 2024 at the age of 84. He served as the 18th prime minister of Canada from 1984 to 1993.
STAVE: The NHL Stanley Cup Playoffs began on Saturday, April 18, launching a grueling postseason where every series is a best-of-seven battle. From coast to coast to coast, teams will try to stave off elimination in pursuit of the Stanley Cup, arguably the hardest trophy in sports to win. Canadian fans will be cheering on their teams throughout the chase for hockey’s ultimate prize.
STEAD: [Homesteading](https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/homesteading) was a cornerstone of Canada’s western expansion. Settlers were given land to cultivate and build a life, transforming untouched prairies into farms and communities (though this land had long been home to Indigenous Peoples). Through hard work and resilience, thousands of families built homes, broke ground, and established new lives on the Prairies. Their efforts helped shape Canada’s rural landscape and agricultural heritage, leaving a legacy that still thrives today.
STEAK: Alberta has become synonymous with choice cuts of AAA beef, and chowing down on a delicious and tender steak is at the top of most people's list when they first come to the province. Beef produced in Alberta is recognized around the world for its rich taste, even fat distribution and consistent quality.
STEAM: Steam transportation allowed people in Canada to move beyond their immediate communities and interact with a wider world. The years from 1900 to 1960 were the last great age of steam locomotion. Steamships and steam-powered railways were at the height of their power, efficiency, and reliability. These technologies were fundamental to the lives of Canadians.
STEEL: Steel plays an extremely important role in the Canadian economy as a whole: in 2019, the Canadian steel industry contributed $4.2 billion to Canada's GDP. According to the Canadian Steel Producers Association, the Canadian steel industry employs, directly and indirectly, more than 120,000 Canadians.
STEER: At the [Calgary Stampede](https://www.calgarystampede.com/), steer wrestling is a fan-favourite event that puts cowboy courage to the test! In this thrilling rodeo challenge, a rider leaps from a galloping horse and attempts to wrestle a sprinting steer to the ground using strength, speed, and precision. It’s a heart-pounding highlight of the Stampede, showcasing the daring skills rooted in Canada’s ranching traditions.
STEPS: The [Last Steps Memorial Arch](https://www.veterans.gc.ca/eng/remembrance/memorials/national-inventory-canadian-memorials/details/9408) is located on a Halifax pier behind the Maritime Museum of the Atlantic. The Halifax waterfront is where thousands of Canadian men and women took their last steps as they embarked on ships to Europe during the First World War. There were around 350,000 Canadian men and women who boarded ships in Halifax to be taken overseas. About 60,000 never returned. The wooden arch bears the words "The Last Steps," immortalizing the place where many of those soldiers last stood on Canadian soil.
STERN: Located in Kaslo, British Columbia, the [S.S. Moyie stern wheeler](https://www.klhs.bc.ca/) is the oldest intact passenger steam vessel of its type in the world. The machinery and the steel frames of its hull were built by the Bertram Engine Works of Toronto, shipped west by rail and assembled in Vancouver. Launched at Nelson on 22 October 1898 by the Canadian Pacific Railway, the S.S. Moyie carried passengers and freight on Kootenay Lake for 59 years. It was retired from service in 1957. Rescued and preserved by the people of Kaslo, the "sweetheart of the lake" recalls the role of sternwheelers in the history of western Canada. 2023 marks the 125th birthday celebration of the S.S. Moyie, which was designated a national historic site of Canada in 1958 and reaffirmed in 1983.
STEWS: Caribou stew is a traditional Canadian stew and a specialty of Nunavut cuisine. The stew is usually made with a combination of boneless caribou (wild North American reindeer) cubes, red wine, tomato paste, root vegetables and herbs. Caribou provide one of the most important food sources for Inuit in Canada and have been a major part of Inuit diet and culture for many generations. Today, caribou stew remains a cherished part of Canadian culinary heritage, celebrated for its rich flavours and cultural significance.
STICK: Hockey and Canada are synonymous with each other, and the sport remains integral to the country’s culture. Hockey sticks go back to the 1800’s where sticks were hand carved from a single piece of wood. The first commercial sticks were said to be created by the Mi’kmaq carvers in Nova Scotia and were made from birch and hornbeam trees.
STING: Today marks the start of the [Ontario Hockey League](https://chl.ca/ohl/) (OHL) regular season in Canada! The [Sarnia Sting](https://chl.ca/ohl-sting/) are a junior ice hockey team based in Sarnia, Ontario. They are one of the 20 teams that make up the OHL. The franchise was granted in 1969 as one of the inaugural teams of the Quebec Major Junior Hockey League. At the time, the team was located in Cornwall, Ontario and known as the Cornwall Royals.
STOCK: The Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX) is a stock exchange located in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. It is the 10th largest exchange in the world and the third largest in North America based on market capitalization. The Montreal Exchange is Canada's oldest exchange and was formerly called the Montreal Stock Exchange.
STONE: A building material used in Manitoba for nearly 200 years, from trading forts to the modern-day architecture of the Canadian Museum for Human Rights, received international recognition in 2023 as a global heritage stone resource. Tyndall Stone - a fossil-laden limestone dating back 450 million years - has also been used at the parliament buildings in Ottawa, the Canadian Museum of History in Quebec and the legislative buildings in Regina and Winnipeg. Canada is the only source in the world for the stone, and Manitoba is the only place it is quarried. The designation means that the Tyndall stone is considered a culturally significant material.
STORE: The local convenience store has been the backbone of Canadian communities for generations. In fact, our convenience store roots can be traced back to Quebec in the 1600s when Samuel de Champlain founded the first store outside of Quebec City. The more than 22,500 stores across Canada act as gathering places in many communities. Those community hubs generate more than $54 billion in sales, employ more than 200,000 Canadians and sell everything from fuel, EV charging, to lottery, energy drinks, bottled water, salty snacks and in Quebec and Newfoundland and Labrador, beer. Find out more about Canada’s convenience industry from its chief advocate, The Convenience Industry Council of Canada at [convenienceindustry.ca](https://convenienceindustry.ca/).
STORM: Canada is as tall as it is wide, creating a wide range of climate conditions. From blistering cold winters to hot muggy summers; torrential rain, blinding snowstorms, deadly tornadoes and scorching drought, Canadians experience some of the planet's most diverse weather systems. Windsor, Ontario is the thunderstorm capital of Canada and has more lightning strikes than any other major city across the country.
STORY: Winterlude 2026’s [Lantern Grove](https://www.lanterngrove.ca/) transforms Confederation Park into a magical, light-filled story-driven experience built around a winter tale of community and generosity. Produced by Immersive International and presented by [Ottawa Tourism](https://ottawatourism.ca/en/event-calendar/lantern-grove), visitors can wander among sculptural installations, dynamic lighting, whimsical sound design, and the enchanting Cinema Forest. A short film expands the story on Friday, Saturday, and Sunday evenings, making Lantern Grove feel like stepping inside a living Canadian winter story.
STOUT: Happy [Canadian Beer Day](https://canadianbeerday.ca/)! During the early period of Canada’s brewing history, heavier ales, porters and stouts were the more popular brews, owing to the traditional preferences of the English, Irish, Welsh and Scottish immigrants who comprised an increasing proportion of Canada’s population following the takeover of New France by Britain in 1763.
STRAY: The Parliament Hill cat colony was a clowder of stray cats living on Parliament Hill in Ottawa, Ontario, in a cat sanctuary set aside for them. The care of the cats and maintenance of the sanctuary was carried out by volunteers, and the effort was funded by donations. The colony was closed in January 2013 after the remaining cats were adopted into homes.
STRIP: Did you know that Canada has a rich history of producing iconic comic strips? One of the most famous Canadian comic strips is '[For Better or For Worse](https://fbofw.com/)' created by Lynn Johnston. This heartwarming comic strip, which debuted in 1979, follows the daily lives of the Patterson family and addresses relatable themes such as family dynamics, relationships, and social issues. 'For Better or For Worse' became widely syndicated and beloved by readers around the world, earning numerous awards and accolades for its authenticity and humour.
STUMP: In Canada, the word stump can mean much more than just the leftover part of a tree. Historically, stumps were common sights in logging areas, where trees were felled and the trunks removed. In political circles, stumping is a term for giving speeches on the campaign trail, a tradition that has deep roots in Canada's political landscape, with leaders traveling across the country to connect with citizens.
SUEDE: The [Blue Suede Music Festival](https://bluesuedemusicfestival.com/) is held in northern Alberta, Canada at the Ag Grounds in the town of Westlock. This festival was started as a way to keep the memory of Elvis and his music alive and to allow tribute artists to come and pay homage to the King of Rock and Roll in a non-competitive setting. It takes place outdoors in the province that has the most Elvis fans in Canada! This year's festival runs from July 26-28, 2024.
SUNNY: Canada’s North is particularly well-known as being the fabled “land of the midnight sun.” Due to its proximity to the Arctic Circle, northern days can entail up to 24 straight hours of sunlight in the summer. Calgary is the sunniest of Canada's large cities, enjoying an average of 2,400 hours of bright sun each year, spread over 333 days.
SUPER: It's a Bird... It's a Plane... It's Superman! The Superman character was co-created by Canadian artist Joseph Shuster. Born in Toronto, he is a cousin of Wayne Shuster, one-half of the beloved Canadian comedy duo Wayne and Shuster. Joseph, who passed away in 1992 at the age of 78, said Metropolis was modelled on Toronto and the Daily Planet was inspired by the Toronto Star, which he delivered as a kid.
SURGE: The [Calgary Surge](https://www.calgarysurge.ca/) is a Canadian professional basketball team based in Calgary, Alberta, that competes in the [Canadian Elite Basketball League](https://www.cebl.ca/) (CEBL). In 2023 they relocated from Guelph, where they were known as the Guelph Nighthawks. The Surge lost to the Scarborough Shooting Stars in the 2023 CEBL Championship game. The CEBL boasts the highest percentages of Canadian players of any pro league in the country with 75 percent of its players being Canadian.
SUSHI: Although sushi may not come immediately to mind when discussing Canadian food, the California Roll - evolved from the Japanese sushi tradition and given an American-sounding name - is Canadian! Vancouver sushi chef Hidekazu Tojo invented the California roll and popularized the "inside-out" sushi technique in North America. There are thousands of sushi restaurants across Canada - more than 600 of them are in Vancouver alone.
SWANS: Royal mute swans came to Ottawa in 1967, Canada’s centennial year, as a gift to the nation’s capital from Queen Elizabeth II. The city also received a pair of Australian Black swans in a trade with a Montreal zoo in 1974. The swans graced the Rideau River for more than five decades, and in 2019 the remaining swans were gifted to Parc Safari in Hemmingford, Quebec.
SWEEP: In the sport of [curling](https://www.curling.ca), sweeping helps control the speed and direction of the curling stone, a skill Canadian curlers have mastered. Canada has an impressive Olympic track record in curling, with both men's and women's teams sweeping their way to Olympic glory and consistently reaching the podium. Highlights include the men's team winning gold in 2006, 2010, and 2014, and the women's team securing gold in 1998 and 2014. Canada also won gold in mixed doubles curling at the 2018 PyeongChang Olympics.
