SWIMS: Canada is a nation that swims! Canada's Olympic swimmers have truly made a splash on the world stage! [Canadian swimming](https://www.swimming.ca/) stars have dazzled with their impressive performances at the 2024 Paris Olympics, including [Summer McIntosh](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/summer-mcintosh/) who won three gold medals and a silver, setting new Olympic records in both the 200m butterfly and 400m individual medley. [Penny Oleksiak](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/penny-oleksiak/) won a remarkable four medals at the Rio 2016 Olympics, including a gold in the 100m freestyle. [Maggie Mac Neil](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/margaret-mac-neil/) won gold in the 100m butterfly at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics and [Mark Tewksbury](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/mark-tewksbury/) brought home gold in the 100m backstroke from the 1992 Barcelona Games. At the Los Angeles 1984 Olympics, Canada won 10 medals in swimming, including gold medal performances by [Alex Baumann](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/alex-baumann/), [Victor Davis](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/victor-davis/), and [Anne Ottenbrite](https://olympic.ca/team-canada/anne-ottenbrite-muylaert/). With such remarkable achievements, it's clear that Canada not only swims but excels at it!
SWINE: Canada is one of the top producers of pork in the world, with millions of pigs raised across the country, especially in provinces like Quebec, Ontario, and Manitoba. Canadian pork is a popular export, found on dinner tables across the globe! On Super Bowl Sunday, pigs make an appearance in more ways than one! While you’re enjoying pulled pork sliders or crispy bacon, it's interesting to note that the term "pigskin" for footballs originates from the early days of the sport. Originally, footballs were made from inflated pig bladders, which served as the ball's core. These bladders were encased in leather to form the ball. This "pigskin" ball was standard for football for many years before modern synthetic materials took over.
SWING: [Oscar Peterson](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/oscar-peterson) is one of Canada's most honoured musicians and is widely regarded as one of the greatest jazz pianists of all time. Born and raised in Montreal, Peterson began playing piano at the age of five. Known as the "master of swing" or the "king of inside swing," Peterson made a name for himself with his incredible dexterity, speed and ornate technique on the keys. Over the course of Peterson’s acclaimed career, he won seven Grammy Awards, was awarded the Order of Canada and the Order of Ontario, won the Martin Luther King Jr. Achievement Award, received numerous honorary degrees, and was inducted into the Canadian Music Hall of Fame. A public statue of Oscar Peterson was unveiled by Queen Elizabeth II in Ottawa in 2007. Check out this [Heritage Minutes video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7cdXEhR9dd4) that recounts the early years of Peterson’s music career.
SWISH: Basketball fans know the satisfying sound of a perfect shot aka the "swish," but did you know that basketball itself was invented by a Canadian? In 1891, Dr. James Naismith from Almonte, Ontario, created the game, and over a century later, Canada continues to be a major part of basketball's story. As the NBA season tips off today, the Toronto Raptors and fans across the country celebrate the legacy of Naismith's invention. From amateur courts to the pros, every swish is a tribute to Canada’s hoop heritage!
SYRUP: Canada produces 71% of the world's maple syrup, 91% of it coming from Quebec.
TABLE: Arguably Canada's most famous piece of furniture, Canada's historic Confederation Table is on display in the Saskatchewan Legislative Library Reading Room in Regina. The table was believed to be from the 1864 Quebec Conference where the Fathers of Confederation wrote the British North America Act, creating Canada as a country. The Confederation Table is a golden-hued oak and basswood library or refectory table constructed circa 1837 to 1864 in a Victorian Gothic Revival style.
TACKS: The [Tacks hockey skate](https://ca.ccmhockey.com/en/Skates/Shop-All-Skates/Tacks-Skates) has deep Canadian roots! It all started with George Tackaberry, a Manitoba shoemaker who crafted a better-fitting, more durable skate for professional players in the early 1900s. His design became so popular that CCM (Canada Cycle and Motor Company) took over production, making Tacks their signature hockey skate for decades. Though the brand was retired in 2006, it made a comeback in 2014, proving that a great Canadian innovation never stays on the bench for long!
TAFFY: Maple taffy (tire d'érable or tire sur la neige in French-speaking Canada) is a sugar candy made by boiling maple sap past the point where it would form maple syrup, but not so long that it becomes maple butter or maple sugar. It is part of traditional culture in Québec, Eastern Ontario, New Brunswick, and Nova Scotia. In these regions, maple syrup is boiled, poured into rows on a snow-lined tray, and rolled onto sticks to make this chewy, irresistible candy.
TAILS: Today marks the start of [Winterlude](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/winterlude.html), the annual winter festival in Ottawa-Gatineau featuring ice, snow, and BeaverTails! [BeaverTails](https://beavertails.com/about-beavertails-pastries/) are world famous Canadian fried dough pastries that are individually stretched to resemble beaver's tails, with sweet toppings like cinnamon & sugar, chocolate hazelnut, and maple spread. They are the ultimate way to keep warm during Winterlude!
TANKS: 79 years ago today on D-Day, Canadian soldiers and tanks landed on Juno Beach, one of five beaches of the Allied invasion of German-occupied France in the Normandy landings on June 6, 1944 during the Second World War. June 6th is a day to remember those who fought and fell so we could be free.
TARPS: In Canadian hockey slang, tarps are the jerseys players wear on the ice. At the Olympics, Team Canada’s tarps stand out as some of the best-looking in the tournament, with their iconic red and white design, bold maple leaf, and crisp stripes. Striking, unmistakably Canadian, and steeped in tradition, these tarps are a symbol of hockey excellence.
TARTS: A butter tart is a delicious pastry tart, which generally consists of butter, sugar, syrup, and egg, filled into a flaky pastry. The earliest published recipe for a butter tart is from Barrie, Ontario dating back to 1900 in the Women's Auxiliary of the Royal Victoria Hospital Cookbook.
TAXES: Lottery & gambling winnings in Canada are treated as windfalls and are not subject to Canadian income tax. Turns out taxes aren't always certain after all!
TAXIS: Taxis have played an important role in Canadian urban history since the early 20th century, with cities like Winnipeg and Toronto among the first to introduce motorized taxi services. During World War II, Canadian taxi fleets were repurposed for civil defense – transporting supplies, volunteers, and even serving as emergency vehicles when needed. Today, while rideshares are popular, classic yellow cabs remain a familiar sight in many of Canada’s biggest cities.
TEACH: Today is World Teachers' Day! Celebrated annually on October 5th, this day celebrates the incredible role that teachers play all over the world and their important contribution to society. In Canada, there are over 400,000 full-time and part-time educators in public elementary and secondary schools. Thank a teacher today for everything they do!
TEAMS: Fifty [Canadian Paralympians](https://paralympic.ca/games/milano-cortina-2026/athletes/) are bound for the 2026 Winter Paralympics, which open on March 6! They’ll compete across six sports: para alpine skiing, para biathlon, para cross-country skiing, para ice hockey, para snowboarding, and wheelchair curling. From individual races to medal-contending teams on the ice and snow, they’ll challenge 665 athletes from around the world across 79 medal events. Together, these teams and athletes bring skill, strategy, and teamwork to every course and match, representing the strength and resilience of the Canada Paralympic Team.
TEMPO: The tempo is picking up for women's basketball in Canada! The WNBA is expanding north with the [Toronto Tempo](https://tempo.wnba.com/), the league's first-ever Canadian franchise. Set to debut in 2026, the Tempo will bring top-tier professional women's basketball to Toronto, igniting excitement among fans across the country. The team's ownership group includes tennis legend Serena Williams, who is bringing her influence to the sport. With Canada's strong basketball talent and growing support for the sport, the Tempo are sure to make an impact on the court!
TENTS: Camping is a cherished Canadian tradition, with tents set up each summer in provincial and national parks from coast to coast to coast. From lakeside campgrounds to remote backcountry sites, Canadians head outdoors to paddle, hike, and sleep under the stars. Pitching a tent is one of the simplest ways many people connect with Canada’s vast natural landscapes and seasonal wilderness culture.
TERRY: While 'terry' can refer to a type of soft, absorbent fabric, it also carries special meaning in Canada as the name of Terry Fox, a true Canadian hero whose Marathon of Hope continues to inspire millions. In 1980, Terry set out to run across Canada to raise money for cancer research after losing his leg to the disease. Although he was forced to stop early, his legacy lives on through the annual [Terry Fox Run](https://terryfox.org/terry-fox-run/), held every September, including this year on September 15. So, when you think of Terry, remember the determination and courage that have united Canadians from coast to coast in support of a great cause!
THANK: Today we are celebrating Canuckle #1500! Reaching this milestone was a moment to pause and thank the community that has made 1500 daily puzzles possible. From coast to coast to coast, and around the world, Canuckle has become a shared part of many people’s daily routine – a quick challenge, a few guesses, and a lot of connection along the way. We’re incredibly grateful to everyone who has played, shared, and supported the game since day one. Thank you!
THEIR: [Their Opportunity](https://www.theiropportunity.com/) is a national children's charity in Canada that uses sport and generosity to educate, uplift, and support children facing barriers. Their programs break down obstacles to participation and promote a lifestyle of giving back, empowering youth to grow, belong, and thrive. Their Opportunity is one of the charities supported by the [Sach In Motion](https://sachinmotion.ca/) fund, as Sachin Latti completes his coast-to-coast run in St. John’s, Newfoundland today, raising awareness and support for mental health and community causes.
THEME: "The Hockey Theme" is a Canadian piece of instrumental theme music composed in 1968 by Dolores Claman and orchestrated by Jerry Toth. The theme was associated with CBC Television's Hockey Night in Canada and it was widely recognized as Canada's unofficial second national anthem.
THORN: Canada has a deep-rooted love for roses, particularly the hardy Canadian Explorer rose series, developed to withstand cold winters. The [Canadian Rose Society](https://canadianrosesociety.org/), founded in 1946, promotes the appreciation and cultivation of roses across the country. Thorny roses are celebrated at the annual "Festival of Roses" held at Montréal Botanical Garden, which showcases hundreds of beautiful rose varieties. While roses have their thorns, they are a symbol of perseverance and beauty, much like the spirit of Canadian gardeners who cultivate them in challenging climates.
THROW: It may not be the sport that Canadians have globally been known for, but it's official now: Canada is a hammer throw powerhouse! At the 2023 World Athletics Championships in Budapest, Camryn Rogers from Richmond, BC won gold in the women's hammer throw event and Ethan Katzberg from Nanaimo, BC won gold in the men's hammer throw event. It was Canada's first-ever hammer-throw double gold on the world athletics stage.
TIGER: The [Hamilton Tiger-Cats](https://ticats.ca/) are a professional Canadian football team in the CFL based in Hamilton, Ontario. The Ticats have over 153 years of history & tradition and have won 15 Grey Cup championships. Oskee Wee Wee!
TIGHT: William Leonard Hunt, also known by the stage name The Great Farini, was a well-known 19th- and early 20th-century Canadian funambulist, aka a tightrope walker extraordinaire. Hunt was an entertainment promoter, an inventor, a circus impresario, and he became known for high-flying stunts, most famously for crossing Niagara Falls on a tightrope in 1860. He is also credited with inventing the human cannonball circus trick.
TIPSY: Sometime around World War II, people along the south coast of Newfoundland began to associate December 23rd with the phrase "Tibb's Eve" and deemed it the first night during Advent when it was appropriate to have a drink. Sometimes called Tip's Eve or Tipsy Eve, it's one of several extensions of the Christmas holidays. For many Newfoundlanders, this day is the official opening of Christmas, and it is customary to have a couple of drinks in the company of friends.
TITAN: The [Ottawa Titans](https://www.ottawatitans.com/) are one of three Canadian baseball teams that play in the MLB Partner [Frontier League](https://www.frontierleague.com/). Formed in 1993, it is the oldest currently running independent league in the United States. The Can-Am League merged with the Frontier League in 2019.
TOMBS: Across Canada, historic tombs and cemeteries take on an eerie charm each Halloween. From Montreal’s Mount Royal Cemetery to Halifax’s Old Burying Ground, some of the country’s oldest tombs date back centuries - resting places that tell stories of settlers, sailors, and soldiers. Many offer lantern-lit tours in October, blending history and haunting in true Canadian fashion.
TONNE: Canada officially uses the metric system of measurement, and tonne is the standard spelling of the metric unit for weight. One tonne is equal to 1000kg, or the size of a fully grown bison!
TOOLS: Happy Father's Day from Canuckle! Across Canada, tools are a familiar part of garages, workshops, and weekend projects – because if something breaks, there’s a good chance a dad has already said, “I’ve got just the tool for that!” For many, they’ve also been part of passing down practical skills, problem-solving, and hands-on learning from one generation to the next. On Father's Day we’re celebrating all the dads and father figures across the country for everything they build, fix, and figure out along the way.
TOONIE: Canada’s two-dollar coin, affectionately called the “toonie,” was introduced in 1996 to replace the $2 bill. It features an adult polar bear, designed by Ontario wildlife artist Brent Townsend, standing on an Arctic ice floe. Its name comes from a playful mix of “two” and “loonie,” the one-dollar coin. In 2002, a giant toonie statue was unveiled in Campbellford, Ontario, honouring one of the country’s most recognizable coins.
TOOTH: [Diamond Tooth Gerties Gambling Hall](https://diamondtoothgerties.ca/) is a casino in Dawson City, Yukon, Canada. It was first opened in 1971 by the Klondike Visitors Association, making it Canada's oldest casino. Gerties, as it is popularly known, is reminiscent of the area's Klondike Gold Rush history, and is home to Canada's best cancan show!
TOQUE: Toque (or tuque) is the official name for a winter hat in Canada!
TORCH: The [2024 Summer Olympic Games](https://www.olympics.com/en/olympic-games/paris-2024) start tomorrow in Paris, France! Canada has had the honour of hosting the Olympic Games three times over the years: Montreal (1976), Calgary (1988) and Vancouver (2010). During these historic events, the [Olympic torch relay](https://olympic.ca/2020/02/21/faq-the-olympic-torch-relay/) travelled thousands of kilometres across Canada, passing through cities, towns, and remote regions, symbolizing unity, friendship, and the spirit of the Games. The torch relay provided Canadians from coast to coast with the opportunity to participate in the Olympic excitement and showcase their pride in being part of this global celebration of sport. Whether it's the thrill of the Games or the warmth of the torch, Canada has left an indelible mark on the Olympic movement.
TORSO: Canada is home to a remarkable group of mammals known as mustelids, including wolverines, badgers, otters, minks, martens, weasels, ermines, and fishers. These animals are instantly recognizable for their signature build: long, slender, tube-like torsos paired with remarkably short legs. This distinctive shape gives them exceptional flexibility, allowing them to twist, turn, and slip through narrow crevices and burrows in pursuit of prey in forests, wetlands, rivers, and tundra throughout the country.
TOURS: World Tourism Day, created by the United Nations World Tourism Organization, is celebrated each year on September 27th to spread awareness about the importance of tourism and its impact on our society. Canada is a country filled with famous landmarks, historical wonders, delicious food, incredible culture, and all the outdoor exploration you could want. Whether you are touring the Parliament Buildings in Ottawa, touring one of Canada's many national parks and historic sites, touring Niagara Falls, or taking a tour through the Canadian Rockies, there are so many natural and cultural wonders to enjoy in our country!
TOWER: Toronto's CN Tower held the record for the world's tallest free-standing structure for 32 years, from 1975 until 2007.
TOXIC: During the First World War, a Canadian innovation helped protect soldiers from toxic gases on the battlefield. The [Hypo Helmet](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/hypo-helmet), invented by Newfoundland doctor Captain Cluny Macpherson in 1915, was an early type of gas mask designed to filter out toxic gases like chlorine gas. It was made of a chemically treated flannel hood with a mica visor, and was a crucial development in protecting soldiers from the harmful effects of chemical warfare. This Canadian invention was an important step in the evolution of gas masks, helping to save countless lives during the war.
TRACE: [Leave No Trace Canada](https://leavenotrace.ca/) is a non-profit organization dedicated to promoting outdoor ethics and the seven Leave No Trace principles with the goal of encouraging Canadians to enjoy the benefits of the outdoors while protecting Canada's natural and cultural heritage. The mission of Leave No Trace Canada is to promote and inspire responsible outdoor recreation through science-based education and partnerships throughout Canada.
TRACK: Canada's best summer Olympic sport is athletics, which includes running, hurdles, long jump, high jump, decathlon and other track & field events. Canada has earned 66 medals in athletics since 1900, including 16 gold, 17 silver and 33 bronze.
TRAIN: Canada has a large and well-developed railway system that includes transcontinental freight train services by Canadian National (CN) and Canadian Pacific (CP), and nationwide passenger train services by Via Rail.
TRAMP: The [Capilano Suspension Bridge](https://www.capbridge.com/) in Vancouver, British Columbia has been a popular destination for adventurers since the late 1890s. Back then, reaching the bridge was no easy feat. Hikers had to first cross the Burrard Inlet by steamboat, then trek through a 12km path winding through dense rainforest to get to the bridge. Those who made the long journey were said to 'tramp' their way to the bridge and were dubbed 'Capilano Tramps', earning the nickname for their determination and endurance. Today, visitors still experience the beauty of the bridge, but thankfully, they don’t have to tramp their way through the wilderness to get there!
TRAWL: Dragging large fishing nets through the water, a method known as trawling, is widely used in Canadian fisheries along both coasts. From the Atlantic provinces to British Columbia, trawling supports important commercial fishing communities and contributes significantly to Canada’s seafood industry. But it’s not just about catching fish – sustainable trawling practices are essential for protecting marine ecosystems, helping ensure these waters remain rich and vibrant for generations to come.
TRIAL: [Brain Cancer Awareness Day](https://www.braintumour.ca/get-involved/raising-awareness/brain-cancer-awareness-day/) in Canada, which occurs in Canada on October 24th, and Brain Tumor Awareness Week, which occurs globally during October 28 - November 4, highlight the challenges in brain tumour and cancer treatment, as well as the need for increased research efforts into these diseases. Through clinical trials, Canadian researchers are contributing to major scientific advancements in brain research so that Canadians with cancer and those at risk will have the best available cancer treatments. You can support the cause and the [Brain Tumour Foundation of Canada](https://www.braintumour.ca/) by buying a hat or hoodie at [hatsforhopecanada.ca](https://hatsforhopecanada.ca/).
TRIBE: In Canada, Indigenous tribes, also called nations or bands, have rich cultures, languages, and histories that stretch back thousands of years. The name tribe has also inspired modern artists, such as the Canadian group A Tribe Called Red (now The Halluci Nation), who blend traditional Indigenous music with electronic beats to celebrate culture and community.
TRIKE: Aqua trikes are making waves across Canada! These big-wheeled, pedal-powered water tricycles let riders glide across lakes and ponds with ease - a fun, stable ride that’s popular with families and adventurers alike. You can find them in Collingwood, Ontario, Cardigan, Prince Edward Island, and Kelowna, British Columbia, just to name a few. Aqua Trikes give Canadians of all ages a playful, unique way to enjoy the water and the outdoors.
TROOP: The Canadian Armed Forces has personnel deployed across Canada and around the world. Since 1947, Canadian troops have completed 72 international missions.
TULIP: The Canadian Tulip Festival in Ottawa features 100 tulip varieties with more than one million blooms over 14,000 m². The celebration is a symbol of friendship between Canada and the Netherlands, with 20,000 bulbs being gifted by the Netherlands each year.
TUNIC: Did you know that the RCMP's red serge tunic is a symbol of Canadian pride and history? Introduced in the 1870s, the red tunic was part of the uniform for the North-West Mounted Police, the RCMP's predecessor. The bold colour was chosen for its high visibility and as a symbol of authority and strength. Over time, the red serge became a lasting emblem of the RCMP's commitment to service and law enforcement across Canada. Today, it remains an iconic part of their ceremonial dress and is instantly recognized worldwide as a representation of Canada's national identity.
TURBO: The TurboTrain was an early high-speed passenger train that operated in Canada from 1968 to 1982. The TurboTrain was powered by a gas turbine engine and could attain a maximum speed of over 270 km/h. The TurboTrain was one of the first "tilting trains" to enter service in North America. It operated on the Montreal–Toronto route, and under optimal conditions was supposed to complete the trip in less than four hours, though it often took about four and a half hours.
TURTLE: Many Indigenous Peoples across the land now called Canada refer to North America as Turtle Island. In these traditional teachings, the turtle carries the world on its back, symbolizing creation, resilience, and connection to the land. The shell’s 13 large scutes are said to represent the lunar cycles, while the 28 smaller sections reflect the days between them. These teachings continue to inspire respect for the land and a sense of belonging within the natural world.
TUTOR: The CT-114 Tutor jet is the aircraft flown by the [Canadian Forces Snowbirds](https://www.canada.ca/en/air-force/services/showcasing/snowbirds.html)! The Tutor was the primary jet trainer for the Royal Canadian Air Force until 2000. The Tutors flown by the Snowbirds are slightly modified for show features and enhanced performance during low-level aerobatic flying.
TWICE: April 11th is National Poutine Day, and what better way to enjoy this iconic Canadian dish than with twice-fried potatoes! Most traditional poutine recipes call for the potatoes to be fried twice, creating that perfect balance of crispy on the outside and soft on the inside. This ensures the fries can hold up to the rich gravy and squeaky cheese curds without getting soggy. Whether you stick with the classic or get creative, twice-fried fries are the key to the ultimate poutine experience!
TWINE: Today marks the start of the NHL regular season in North America! In hockey, "twine" is a common slang term for the net, and "tickling the twine" refers to scoring a goal - a thrill that no player delivered more than Canadian hockey legend Wayne Gretzky! Known as "The Great One," Gretzky tickled the twine a jaw-dropping 894 times, setting the record for the most career goals in NHL history.
TWINS: The Edison Twins is a Canadian children's television program which ran for six seasons on CBC Television from March 3, 1984 to December 17, 1986. The series featured the adventures of Tom and Annie Edison (played by Andrew Sabiston and Marnie McPhail respectively), a pair of teenage scientific prodigy siblings who face a variety of challenges which they overcome with their expertise of science. McPhail won the Gemini Award for Best Performance by a Lead Actress in a Continuing Dramatic Series in 1986.
UDDER: Cows are at the heart of the [Canadian dairy industry](https://dairyfarmersofcanada.ca/), which produces everything from milk and butter to cheese and yogurt. Milk is collected from the udder, the part of the cow where it's stored before being carefully cooled and transported. Canada is home to over 10,000 dairy farms, and its farmers follow some of the highest standards in the world for quality, safety, and animal care. So the next time you pour a glass of milk or bite into a gooey grilled cheese, you can thank a Canadian cow!
ULTRA: [Ray Zahab](https://www.rayzahab.com/) is a Canadian explorer, ultra distance runner, and founder of non-profit [impossible2Possible](https://www.impossible2possible.com/). A recent recipient of the Meritorious Service Cross of Canada, Ray is an Explorer in Residence of the Royal Canadian Geographical Society, and Fellow of the Royal Geographical Society. In 2015 Canadian Geographic recognized Ray as one of Canada's Top Explorers. He has ran 17,000+ km across the world's deserts, and unsupported expeditions in some of the coldest places on the planet. From ultra marathons to crossing the Sahara and beyond, Ray's journey has taught him that we can truly exceed any limits we think we might have.
UMBRA: Happy Total Solar Eclipse Day! Today, Canada will experience its first [total solar eclipse](https://www.asc-csa.gc.ca/eng/astronomy/eclipses/total-solar-eclipse.asp) since 1979. Only during a total solar eclipse, when the Moon blocks all of the Sun, does a smaller, darker conical shadow called the umbra project onto Earth. The width of the umbra (the path of totality) and the penumbra (the partial eclipse zone) depend on the moon's distance from Earth during the eclipse. The path of the umbra for today's total solar eclipse will be about 185 kilometres wide. All of Canada will see at least a partial solar eclipse, but parts of Ontario, Quebec and Atlantic Canada will experience totality.
UNCLE: [Mon oncle Antoine](https://www.nfb.ca/film/mon_oncle_antoine_en/) (My Uncle Antoine) is a 1971 French-language Canadian drama film directed by Claude Jutra for the National Film Board of Canada. The film depicts life in a rural mining town in Québec before the Asbestos Strike of 1949. Mon oncle Antoine has twice been voted the greatest Canadian film in the Sight & Sound poll, conducted once each decade. The Toronto International Film Festival placed it first in the Top 10 Canadian Films of All Time three times.
UNITY: [National Flag of Canada Day](https://www.canada.ca/en/canadian-heritage/campaigns/national-flag-canada-day.html) is observed every year on February 15. This day marks the inauguration of the present flag of Canada with the red maple leaf. The flag signifies the common values that unite all citizens of Canada - equality, diversity, and inclusion. Officially adopted as Canada's national flag in 1965, George Stanley's vision for Canada's flag was simple, easily recognizable and served as a rallying symbol for unity.
UPPER: In Canadian history, Upper Canada (also called Canada West) was the region in Canada now known as Ontario. You can travel back in time to one of Canada's largest living-history sites and experience life in the 1860s at [Upper Canada Village](https://www.uppercanadavillage.com/) near Morrisburg, Ontario.
URANIUM: Canada is the world’s second-largest uranium producer, contributing roughly 13–18% of global supply. High-grade deposits in northern Saskatchewan’s Athabasca Basin provide fuel for nuclear power plants that generate clean, low-carbon electricity. Canadian uranium powers energy systems at home and abroad while supporting communities in the North.
URBAN: In 2021, 81 per cent of Canadians lived in an urban centre, compared to 45 per cent in 1911. The three largest cities in Canada are Toronto, Montréal and Vancouver.
VAULT: [Qaumajuq](https://www.wag.ca/about/qaumajuq/) is an innovative new museum in Winnipeg, Manitoba, home of the largest public collection of contemporary Inuit art in the world. The first thing you’ll see when you step inside Qaumajuq is the stunning, three-storey glass vault filled with thousands of Inuit carvings. The [Visible Vault](https://vault.wag.ca/) provides unprecedented access to close to 5,000 Inuit stone carvings, providing a unique, immersive art-viewing experience. It is the world's only visible vault of its kind.
VEGAN: Did you know that vegetarians and vegans now account for nearly 10 per cent of Canada’s population? The number of vegans in Canada has doubled in two years. Canada is ranked 9th globally as a vegan friendly country. The most vegan-friendly Canadian province is British Columbia with the most vegans per capita. With 2.3 million people identifying as vegetarian and just under 1 million as vegan, together with government and market responses, Canada is arguably very vegan-friendly.
VIDEO: Launched in 1984, [MuchMusic](https://www.bellmedia.ca/the-lede/tv/muchmusic/) made video culture a daily ritual in Canada, earning its reputation as the country’s answer to MTV. Broadcasting from its iconic street-level studio in Toronto, it brought music videos to life with VJs, live fan interaction, and countdown shows. It helped launch Canadian artists through the MuchFACT grant program and played a major role in promoting homegrown music across the country.
VIEWS: Vancouver is known around the world as a modern, cosmopolitan city set against the spectacular backdrop of the North Shore Mountains. These views remind residents of their connection to nature and, together with select views to important landmark buildings, reinforce the city's unique civic identity. Since 1989, Vancouver has maintained a series of Council-approved [protected public views](https://vancouver.ca/home-property-development/protecting-public-views.aspx) to shape development in the city's downtown and central neighbourhoods. It does this in a way that balances the need for economic growth and housing while also preserving landmark views for future generations.
VINYL: Randy Bachman's [Vinyl Tap](https://www.cbc.ca/listen/live-radio/1-135-randy-bachman-s-vinyl-tap) radio show on CBC is two hours of music and stories from one of Canada's musical legends. Randy Bachman has been an integral part of Canada’s music scene for more than 40 years as part of The Guess Who, Bachman Turner Overdrive and as a solo artist. Vinyl Tap was previously CBC’s top rated show for 16 years and features Randy's favourite tunes and candid stories from his life on the road and in the studio.
VIPER: There are 3 endemic venomous snake species in Canada that fall within the pit viper family: the Western rattlesnake, the Prairie rattlesnake, and the Eastern Massasauga rattlesnake. These pit vipers are equipped with heat-sensing pits that help them hunt small mammals even in the cooler Canadian climate. Though they might seem intimidating, all three rattlesnakes are shy creatures that avoid human contact and play an essential role in controlling rodent populations. Conservation efforts, particularly for the endangered Eastern Massasauga, help protect these unique members of Canada's wildlife. So, next time you think of "viper," remember these important native species, quietly helping keep Canada's ecosystems balanced!
VISTA: Canada’s stunning scenery and mind-defying vistas are a well-known draw to the country. Rugged mountain ranges, thundering rivers and turquoise lakes surrounded by alpine forests – Canada is an absolute wonder to behold! From sweeping grasslands to crashing ocean tides to craggy snow-covered mountains, Canada’s diverse landscapes offer awe-inspiring vistas for every taste.
VOCAL: Today is International Inuit Day! It is a holiday that was created to celebrate Inuit and amplify their voices. Inuit throat singing, or katajjaq, is a distinct vocal style uniquely found among the Inuit. It is a form of musical performance, traditionally consisting of two women who sing duets in a close face-to-face formation with no instrumental accompaniment. Their technique relies on short, sharp, rhythmic inhalations and exhalations of breath. The Inuit recognize katajjaniq as part of their cultural heritage.
VOICE: February is Black History Month in Canada! "Voice of the Fugitive" was Canada's first Black newspaper and it was used to communicate with Underground Railroad supporters. Founded and edited by Henry Bibb and his wife Mary Bibb, it was first published in 1851 in Sandwich, and moved to Windsor shortly after.
VOLTS: Tomorrow marks the start of the [Quebec Maritimes Junior Hockey League](https://chl.ca/lhjmq/) (QMJHL) regular season in Canada! The [Drummondville Voltigeurs](https://chl.ca/lhjmq-voltigeurs/) (aka "Volts") are a Canadian junior ice hockey team of the QMJHL. The franchise was originally granted for the 1982–83 season, and is based in Drummondville, Quebec, playing its home games at the Centre Marcel Dionne. The team won the QMJHL's President's Cup in 2009 and 2024.
VOTER: Canadian citizens who are at least 18 years old on election day can vote in their electoral district in municipal, provincial/territorial, and federal elections. Did you know that on the day of a federal election, [Elections Canada](https://www.elections.ca/) becomes the largest employer in the country? The agency hires about 250,000 people in communities across Canada.
WAFER: Yesterday was World Chocolate Day! The popular Canadian chocolate bar, "Coffee Crisp," features layers of vanilla wafer and coffee-flavoured cream covered in milk chocolate. It's a unique Canadian treat, and it rarely ventures beyond Canada's borders. The candy has largely been made exclusively for Canadian markets - over 150 million Coffee Crisp bars are produced every year in the Nestlé Canada factory in Toronto. How do Canadians like their coffee? Crisp!
WALKS: Canada has some amazing areas, trails, and parks you can walk, but did you know there are a couple that are among the world’s happiest walks? Inghams, a UK travel company that specializes in active holidays around the lakes and mountains of Europe and Canada, looked at social media posts taken on popular walking trails around the world and used facial detection software to find and compare the size of the smiles captured in the posts, generating a happiness score and providing a tangible measurement of how happy travellers are as they embark on different walks around the world! Two trails in Canada made the list of '[The World's Happiest Walks](https://www.inghams.co.uk/walking-holidays/insider-guides/happiest-walks)', with the Bruce Trail in Tobermory, Ontario and the Canadian Rockies in BC & Alberta coming in with a happiness score of 93.67!
WATER: With around 80,423 cubic metres per capita, Canada has about 9% of the world's total renewable fresh water supply. When glacier, underground and lake water is included, Canada actually has 20% of the world's fresh water supply.
WAVES: August 30th is National Beach Day! It is estimated that Canada has around 2,000 surfers, and they all get their share of waves on the west (British Columbia) and east (Nova Scotia) coasts and on the Great Lakes (Ontario). The wave-rich region of Tofino, BC played a fundamental role in the development of surfing in the country. The so-called surf capital of Canada is home to a vibrant and active community of cold-water wave riders. Surf's up!
WEAVE: There are an estimated 7,000 or 8,000 weavers in Ontario, Québec and British Columbia, and weavers' guilds exist in most large communities in Canada. Over thousands of years, Indigenous peoples of North America perfected the art of basket weaving. Weavers manipulated grasses, bark, roots, and other plant materials into baskets that served a variety of functions. The Salish peoples of the Northwest Coast have had a long history of weaving and textile manufacture, using mountain-goat hair, fireweed and woolly dog hair.
WHALE: There are more than 33 species of whale that live in Canada's oceans.
WHEAT: Close to half of all Canadian wheat is grown in Saskatchewan, followed by Alberta and Manitoba.
WHIPS: [Canada Whips](https://www.canadawhips.ca/) is a Canadian resource for whip crackers worldwide. Canada Whips was formed with one specific goal in mind: to increase skill, knowledge, and participation in whip cracking across Canada and beyond! They offer tutorials, guides, glossaries, and more to whip crackers around the globe.
WHITE: Red and white, the colours that adorn the National Flag of Canada, have undeniably come to represent Canada both at home and abroad. Red and white have truly become Canada’s national colours, through common use and collective pride, even if they are not officially enshrined in law. The "Great White North" is one of Canada's nicknames, and also used as the title of a [Second City Television](https://www.secondcity.com/network/category/sctv) (SCTV) comedy sketch featuring our favourite two hosers, [Bob & Doug McKenzie](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=X-ZvAVcBIrQ)!
WHOOP: Every August, Lethbridge, Alberta celebrates [Whoop-Up Days](https://www.agrifoodhub.ca/events/whoop-up) – a high-energy festival full of rodeos, concerts, midway rides, and pancake breakfasts galore. The name comes from the wild days of frontier trading, when “whooping it up” meant a real party. Today, it’s all about community, cowboy spirit, and letting loose – prairie style! Whoop-Up Days 2025 takes place from August 19 to 23, so mark your calendars for five days of fun and celebration.
WINDS: "Four Strong Winds" is a song written by Ian Tyson and recorded by Canadian folk duo Ian and Sylvia. It was a top 10 single in Canada in 1963. The song has a clear Canadian context and subtext, including an explicit mention of the province Alberta as well as references to long, cold winters. In 2005, CBC Radio One listeners chose this song as the greatest Canadian song of all time, and is considered the unofficial anthem of Alberta.
WINES: Canadians drink more than 1 billion glasses of Canadian wine every year. Because of our cold climate, Canada is the largest Icewine producer in the world.
WINGS: Wings are a Super Bowl staple in Canada. According to Chicken Farmers of Canada, Canadians are expected to eat around 90 million chicken wings on Super Bowl Sunday, making it the country's biggest wing-eating day of the year. Whether they’re saucy, spicy, or extra crispy, wings have become just as much a part of the big game north of the border as the kickoff itself.
WIRED: Canada's early internet networks relied on being wired to telephone lines and later advanced to fibre optics, connecting the nation's vast geography. In 1984, NetNorth, Canada's first digital network, linked universities using dial-up lines, allowing researchers to exchange data across provinces. This wired system laid the foundation for CA*net in 1990, Canada's first national internet backbone, which revolutionized communication and collaboration across the country. From these humble beginnings, Canada's internet infrastructure has grown into one of the most advanced in the world!
WOMAN: Happy International Women's Day! It's a global day to recognize and celebrate women's and girls' social, economic, cultural, and political achievements. It's also a time to raise awareness of the progress made towards achieving gender equality and the work remaining to be done. The 'Day of the Woman' was first proclaimed in 1910 at an international women’s conference in Copenhagen. However, it was only until the United Nations recognized the 8th of March as an official day of celebration in 1978. The Government of Canada's theme for [International Women's Day 2024](https://www.canada.ca/en/women-gender-equality/commemorations-celebrations/international-womens-day.html) is "Invest in women: Accelerate progress". It's a call to action and a reminder that gender equality is one of the most effective ways to build healthier, more prosperous, and more inclusive communities. We all have a role to play in building a future where everyone can reach their full potential!
WOODS: Canada is famously covered in vast woods – with nearly 40% of the country blanketed by forests, making it one of the world’s greenest nations. These woods are home to countless species and provide endless opportunities for outdoor adventures. Since 1926, the Canadian company [Woods](https://www.woods.ca/) has been a trusted name for camping gear, helping adventurers connect with nature across these expansive woodlands. Whether exploring or camping, the woods are truly at the heart of Canada’s great outdoors!
WORSE: Canada’s most acclaimed cartoonist, Lynn Johnston, is internationally known for her comic strip "[For Better or For Worse](https://fbofw.com/)." The stories revolving around the lives of Elly Patterson and her family had at its peak over 220 million readers of more than 2,000 newspapers in more than 20 countries.
WOUND: Established in 1995, [Wounds Canada](https://www.woundscanada.ca/) is a charitable organization dedicated to the advancement of wound prevention and management. Wound Canada's mission is to build a healthier Canada by advancing skin health and excellence in wound management. Learn more at [woundscanada.ca](https://www.woundscanada.ca/)!
WOVEN: Today is [Red Dress Day](https://www.thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/red-dress-day) in Canada – a day to honour and remember Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women, Girls, and Two-Spirit People (MMIWG2S). The red dresses hanging in windows and trees across the country serve as powerful symbols of those whose lives have been taken and those still missing. Traditional Indigenous clothing is often woven with deep cultural meaning, with intricate designs and patterns that reflect stories, spiritual beliefs, and connections to the land. These garments are more than just clothing – they are a form of storytelling, passed down through generations. On Red Dress Day, the red dresses themselves are a modern reflection of these woven traditions, symbolizing strength, resilience, and the ongoing call for justice.
WRITE: Happy International Literacy Day! Canada is full of amazing storytellers, and CBC Books celebrates their voices through [Canada Writes](https://www.cbc.ca/books/canadawrites). This platform showcases Canadian writers of all backgrounds, offering contests, resources, and a space for both emerging and established authors to share their work. It’s a reminder of how the written word continues to connect us, inspire us, and shape Canada’s cultural identity.
YACHT: Yachting refers to races of watercraft using sail power only. One of the most glorious chapters in Canadian yachting was written by the Bluenose out of Lunenburg, Nova Scotia, which dominated the races for the Halifax Herald's International Fisherman's Trophy from 1921 until her retirement in 1938. Canada has a rich sailing history, and Canadian sailors have achieved success in various international competitions, including the Olympics. [Sail Canada](https://www.sailing.ca/) (formerly the Canadian Yachting Association) is Canada's governing body for the sport of sailing.
YAHOO: The [Calgary Stampede](https://www.calgarystampede.com/) starts today! Did you know that "Yahoo!" is a spirited shout famously associated with the Stampede? This annual rodeo and exhibition, held every July in Calgary, Alberta, is one of Canada's largest and most famous events. During the Stampede, "Yahoo!" becomes a rallying cry for excitement and celebration, heard from cowboys, cowgirls, and spectators alike. The Stampede features thrilling rodeo events, chuckwagon races, parades, and concerts, drawing visitors from all over the world. The enthusiastic "Yahoo!" shout encapsulates the vibrant and festive spirit of this iconic Canadian event. The official Stampede mascot, Harry the Horse has been saying "Yahoo!" since he debuted with his bell and signs on March 14, 1985.
YEAST: December 10th is National Lager Day! Lagers are some of the most popular beer styles in the world and Canada is no exception. Pale lagers are the most popular beer in Canada. Most lagers are distinguished by the use of a "bottom-fermenting" yeast that ferments at relatively cold temperatures. The term "lager" comes from the German word for "storage", as the beer was stored before drinking, traditionally in the same cool caves in which it was fermented. Celebrate the day with a lager from your favourite Canadian brewery!
YOUTH: International Youth Day is celebrated annually on August 12th to recognize the important role that young people play in promoting positive change and development around the world. The day was established by the United Nations General Assembly in 1999, and is celebrated in more than 100 countries worldwide. In Canada, International Youth Day is an opportunity to raise awareness about the unique challenges and opportunities facing young people in the country. It is also a time to celebrate their achievements, and to recognize the important role they play in shaping the future of the country.
ZEBRA: Zebra is a slang term for a referee, particularly for the sports of hockey, basektball and football. The term comes from the black and white striped jerseys that they wear during the game. Did you know that 80% of the NHL's current referees and linesmen are Canadian? The NHL Officials Association even has a charitable organization called [Zebras Care](https://nhlofficials.com/zebras-care/)!
